arXiv:2003.10320v2 [math.PR] 29 Jul 2022
Random walks on mated-CRT planar maps
and Liouville Brownian motion
Nathanaël Berestycki
University of Vienna
Ewain Gwynne
University of Chicago
Abstract
We prove a scaling limit result for random walk on certain random planar maps with its natural time parametrization.
In particular, we show that for  $\gamma\in(0,2)$ , the random walk on the mated-CRT map with parameter  $\gamma$  converges to  $\gamma$ -Liouville Brownian motion, the natural quantum time parametrization of Brownian motion on a  $\gamma$ -Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surface.
Our result applies if the mated-CRT map is embedded into the plane via the embedding which comes from SLE / LQG theory or via the Tutte embedding (a.k.a. the harmonic or barycentric embedding). In both cases, the convergence is with respect to the local uniform topology on curves and it holds in the quenched sense, i.e., the conditional law of the walk given the map converges.
Previous work by Gwynne, Miller, and Sheffield (2017) showed that the random walk on the mated-CRT map converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization.
This is the first work to show the convergence of the parametrized walk.
As an intermediate result of independent interest, we derive an axiomatic characterisation of Liouville Brownian motion, for which the notion of Revuz measure of a Markov process plays a crucial role.

1 Introduction
1.1 Background
The mathematical study of random walks on random planar maps goes back to the seminal paper of Benjamini and Schramm [BS01].
This paper was motivated by contemporary works by Ambjørn et al. [AAJ+99, ANR+98] which introduced and studied (in a nonrigorous way) a notion of diffusion in the geometry of Liouville quantum gravity. As we will discuss in more detail below (and partly make rigourous in this paper), this diffusion can heuristically be thought of as a continuum limit of random walk on random planar maps.
Benjamini and Schramm proved recurrence of any local limit of a sequence of randomly rooted planar graphs, subject to a bounded degree assumption, and initiated a remarkably fruitful program of research aiming to describe properties of random walks on random planar maps, especially random walks on the so-called Uniform Infinite Planar Triangulation (UIPT) as well as other models of random planar maps in the same universality class.
In the years since then, this program of research has blossomed into a very rich and quickly expanding area of probability theory.
We will not attempt to give a complete review of this literature here. Instead, we mention a few highlights and refer to [Cur16, GHS19b] as well as the excellent lecture notes by Nachmias [Nac20] for relevant expository articles.
The UIPT was constructed by Angel and Schramm in [AS03]. Gurel-Gurevich and Nachmias [GGN13] removed the bounded degree assumption of [BS01] and replaced it by an exponential tail on the degree of the root vertex of the map (in particular applying to the UIPT). The random walk on the UIPT was proved to be subdiffusive by Benjamini and Curien in [BC13] through the consideration of the so-called pioneer points which were analyzed in great detail. More recently, the exact value of the diffusivity exponent on the UIPT (equal to  $1/4$ ) was obtained through the combination of two works: a paper by Gwynne and Miller [GM21] which proves the lower bound for the diffusivity exponent and also computes the spectral dimension, and a paper by Gwynne and Hutchcroft [GH20] which proves the upper bound for the diffusivity exponent.
Naturally, these developments cannot be dissociated from the remarkable progress in the understanding of the purely geometric features of these random maps, culminating for instance in the convergence of random planar maps (viewed as random metric spaces) to the Brownian map which was proven by Le Gall [Le 13] and Miermont [Mie13], see for instance the survey [LG14].
On the continuum side, the paper by Duplantier and Sheffield [DS11] provided a framework (corresponding to the DDK ansatz [Dav88, DK89]) for building a continuum theory of Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) based on a rigorous construction of the volume form associated with the formal metric tensor
$e^{\gamma h}\,(dx^{2}+dy^{2})$
(1.1)
where  $h$  is a variant of the Gaussian free field on a planar domain,  $dx^{2}+dy^{2}$  is the Euclidean metric tensor on that domain, and  $\gamma\in(0,2)$  is a constant (which is related to the type of random planar map being considered). In [DS11], the volume for associated with (1.1) is understood as a random measure (in fact, this random measure is a special case of the theory of Gaussian multiplicative chaos, which was initiated in [Kah85]; see [RV11] and [BP] for additional context and a modern approach).
A rigorous construction of a continuum diffusion in the geometry associated with (1.1) was proposed in [GRV16, Ber15], for every parameter  $\gamma\in(0,2)$ . This diffusion, called Liouville Brownian motion (LBM) and described in more details below, is widely conjectured to be the scaling limit of simple random walks on many models of random planar maps. Much is now known about the behaviour of LBM, including a rigorous verification in [RV14b] of the predictions made in [ANR+98] about the spectral dimension; as well as several works considerably refining our understanding of its heat kernel: see, e.g., [GRV14, DZZ19, AK16, Jac18, MRVZ16, BGRV16].
There are also known scaling limit results for discrete approximations of (analogues of) Liouville Brownian motion on tree-like spaces and low-dimensional fractals: see, e.g. [CHK17], which is in the spirit of earlier works on the Bouchaud trap model and its scaling limit to the so-called FIN diffusion in dimension one [FIN02] and to fractional kinetics in higher dimensions [BAČ07].
However, prior to the present paper there were no rigorous results relating the behaviour of simple random walk on natural models of random planar maps to Liouville Brownian motion. The main purpose of this paper is to establish the first such result, in the case of random walk on the so-called mated-CRT random planar maps. These random planar maps are in some sense more directly connected to Liouville quantum gravity than other random planar map models (thanks to the results of [DMS21]) and will be described in more detail below. Interestingly, mated-CRT maps also provide a coarse-grained approximation to many other models of random planar maps (see Remark 1.1). The main result of this paper is that for any parameter  $\gamma\in(0,2)$ , the scaling limit of simple random walk on the mated-CRT planar map with parameter  $\gamma$  is Liouville Brownian motion with the same parameter. See Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 for precise statements, including the topology of convergence. Our results build on the earlier work [GMS21], which shows that the random walk on the mated-CRT map converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization.
1.2 Setup
Infinite-volume mated-CRT maps.
Mated-CRT maps are a one-parameter family of random planar maps, indexed by  $\gamma\in(0,2)$ , which were first used implicitly in [DMS21] and studied more explicitly in [GHS19a, GMS21].
We start with a brief description of infinite-volume mated-CRT maps, with the topology of the plane.
In this case, the basic data is provided by a pair of correlated real-valued two-sided Brownian motions  $(L_{t},R_{t})_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}$  such that  $L_{0}=R_{0}=0$  and with correlation coefficient given by  $-\cos(\pi\gamma^{2}/4)$ , i.e.,
$\operatorname{cov}(L_{t},R_{t})=-\cos\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\pi\gamma^{2}}{4}}}\right)|t|.$
The mated-CRT map is the map obtained by gluing discretized versions of the the (non compact) Continuum Random Trees defined by  $L$  and  $R$ . More precisely, for a given  $\varepsilon>0$ , the mated-CRT map with scale  $\varepsilon$  is the random graph  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  whose vertex set is  $\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  and where there is an edge between two vertices  $x,y\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  (with  $x<y$ ) if and only if:
$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}X_{t}}}\right)\vee\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\inf_{t\in[y-\varepsilon,y]}X_{t}}}\right)\leq\inf_{t\in[x,y-\varepsilon]}X_{t}$
(1.2)
where  $X$  can be either  $L$  or  $R$ . Note that in this definition  $x$  is always connected to  $x+\varepsilon$  via both  $L$  and  $R$ , but we only include one such edge in this case (let us call such an edge trivial).
If  $y>x+\varepsilon$  it is possible that (1.2) is satisfied for neither, one, or both of  $L$  and  $R$ : in the case when (1.2) is satisfied for both  $L$  and  $R$  there are two edges joining  $x$  and  $y$ .
When  $y>x+\varepsilon$  and (1.2) is satisfied we call the corresponding edge nontrivial.
A nontrivial edge can be of two types: type  $L$  or type  $R$  depending on whether (1.2) is satisfied with  $X=L$  or  $X=R$ .
By Brownian scaling, it is clear that the law of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  viewed as a graph does not depend on  $\varepsilon$ , but for reasons we will explain just below it is convenient to consider the whole family of graphs  $\{\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0}$  constructed from the same pair  $(L,R)$ .
Note that the condition (1.2) says that there are times  $s\in[x-\varepsilon,x]$  and  $t\in[y-\varepsilon,y]$  such that  $s$  and  $t$  are identified in the equivalence relation used to construct the CRT associated with  $L$  or  $R$ . The definition of the mated-CRT map can therefore indeed be thought of as a gluing of discretized versions of the CRT’s associated to  $L$  and  $R$ .
Figure 1: Left: A geometric description of the definition of the mated-CRT map. We consider the restrictions of  $L$  and  $R$  to some interval (in this case,  $[0,12\varepsilon]$ ). We then draw the graphs of the restrictions of  $L$  and  $C-R$  to this interval in the same rectangle in the plane, where  $C$  is a large constant chosen so that the graphs do not intersect. The adjacency condition (1.2) for  $L$  (resp.  $R$ ) is equivalent to the condition that there is a horizontal line segment under the graph of  $L$  (resp. above the graph of  $C-R$ ) which intersects the graph only in the vertical strips  $[x-\varepsilon,x]\times[0,C]$  and  $[y-\varepsilon,y]\times[0,C]$ . For each pair  $(x,y)$  for which this adjacency condition holds, we have drawn the lowest (resp. highest) such horizontal line segment in green.
Right: Illustration of a proper planar embedding of the given portion of the mated-CRT map which realizes its planar map structure. Trivial edges (resp.  $L$ -edges,  $R$ -edges) are shown in black (resp. red, blue). A similar illustration appeared as [GMS19, Figure 1].
In order to turn the graph  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  into a (rooted) planar map we first specify the root vertex to be the trivial edge from  $0$  to  $\varepsilon$ . In a planar map there is also a notion of counterclockwise cyclical order on the edges surrounding a given vertex. For the mated-CRT map, this ordering is obtained as follows. We order the  $L$ -edges emanating from a given vertex  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  by giving them the order they inherit from their endpoints on  $\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ . We order the  $R$ -edges in the reverse way, and declare that the  $L$ -edges come before the  $R$ -edges. The  $L$ -edges and the  $R$ -edges are separated by the two trivial edges emanating from  $x$ . With this order, it is easy to see why a proper planar embedding of this graph exists (i.e., an embedding in which the edges do not overlap). Simply draw the  $R$ -edges on one side of  $\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  in the plane and the  $L$ -edges on the other, and observe that the  $R$ -edges (and equivalently the  $L$ -edges) can be drawn without overlapping: if  $s_{1}<s_{2}$  and  $t_{1}<t_{2}$  are identified in  $R$ , then either  $s_{1}<s_{2}<t_{1}<t_{2}$  or  $s_{1}<t_{1}<t_{2}<t_{2}$ . See Figure 1 for an illustration. We note that with this planar map structure, the mated-CRT map is in fact a triangulation; see the caption of [GMS19, Figure 1] for an explanation.
Remark 1.1 (Connection to other random planar map models).
The above construction of the mated-CRT map is motivated by a class of combinatorial bijections called mating of trees bijections. Basically, such bijections tell us that certain natural random planar maps decorated by statistical mechanics models can be constructed via discrete analogs of the above construction of the mated-CRT map, with the two coordinates of a random walk on  $\mathbbm{Z}^{2}$  (with an increment distribution depending on the map) used in place of  $(L,R)$ .
Examples of planar maps which can be encoded in this way include uniform triangulations decorated by site percolation configurations [Ber07a, BHS18] as well as planar maps decorated by spanning trees [Mul67, Ber07b], the critical Fortuin-Kasteleyn cluster model [DS11, Ber07b], or bipolar orientations [KMSW19].
Due to the convergence of random walk to Brownian motion, the mated-CRT map can be viewed as a coarse-grained approximation of these other random planar maps.
This coarse-graining can sometimes be used to transfer results from the mated-CRT map to other random planar maps, as is done, e.g., in [GHS20, GM21, GH20]. Currently, however, the estimates comparing mated-CRT maps to other maps are not sufficiently precise to transfer scaling limit results like the one proven in this paper.
Finite volume mated-CRT maps.
Mated-CRT planar maps can also be defined in finite volume with other topologies such as the disk.
In this version,  $L$  and  $R$  are two correlated Brownian motions over the time-interval  $[0,1]$  (instead of the entire real line  $\mathbbm{R}$ ), start from  $L_{0}=R_{0}=0$  and
are conditioned so that  $(L_{t},R_{t})_{0\leq t\leq 1}$  remains in the positive quadrant  $[0,\infty)^{2}$  until time 1 and ends up in the position  $(1,0)$  at time one. (This is a degenerate conditioning; see [MS19] for a construction, building on the cone excursions studied by Shimura in [Shi85].) We call such a pair a Brownian excursion in the quadrant. The vertex set of the mated-CRT map with the disk topology is then taken to be  $\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\cap[0,1]$  instead of  $\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ , but apart from that the definitions above stay the same.
Note that the tree encoded by  $R$  is a standard (compact) Continuum Random Tree, whereas the one encoded by  $L$  also comes with a natural boundary. More precisely, we define boundary vertices  $\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  as the set of vertices  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\cap[0,1]$  such that
$\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}\leq\inf_{t\in[x,1]}L_{t}.$
(1.3)
See Figure 2 for an illustration.
Figure 2: Left: The conditioned correlated Brownian motion  $(L,R)$  used to construct the mated-CRT map with the disk topology.
Right: The analog of Figure 1, left, for the disk topology, with  $\varepsilon=1/12$ . We have  $x\in\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  if and only if there is a horizontal line segment under the graph of  $L$  which intersects the graph of  $L$  only in  $[x-\varepsilon,x]\cap[0,C]$  and also intersects  $\{1\}\times[0,C]$ . Here the boundary vertices are  $\varepsilon,2\varepsilon,10\varepsilon,11\varepsilon,$  and  $12\varepsilon$ .
Tutte embedding.
The advantage of working in the finite volume setup discussed above (as opposed to say the earlier whole plane setup) is that the Tutte embedding can be defined in a straightforward way. The Tutte embedding of a graph is a planar embedding which has the property that each interior vertex (i.e., a vertex not on the boundary) is equal to the average of its neighbours. Equivalently, the simple random walk on the graph is a martingale. A concrete construction in the case of a finite volume mated-CRT map is as follows. We first choose a marked root vertex of the mated-CRT map by sampling  $\mathbbm{t}$  uniformly from  $[0,1]$  and letting  $\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}\in(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})\cap[0,1]$  be chosen so that  $\mathbbm{t}\in[\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}-\varepsilon,\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}]$ .
Let  $x_{1}<\ldots<x_{k}$  denote the vertices of the boundary  $\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , in numerical order.
Let  $\mathfrak{p}(x_{k})$  denote the probability that simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , started from  $\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}$ , first hits  $\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  in the arc  $\{x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\}$ . Then the boundary vertices  $x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}$  are mapped (counterclockwise) respectively to  $z_{1}=e^{2i\pi\mathfrak{p}(x_{1})},\ldots,z_{k}=e^{2i\pi\mathfrak{p}(x_{k})}$ . This makes it so that the harmonic measure from  $\mathbbm{x}^{\varepsilon}$  approximates Lebesgue measure on  $\partial\mathbbm{D}$ . As for the interior vertices, if  $x\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}$ , let  $\psi^{\varepsilon}:\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathbbm{C}$  denote the unique function which is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\partial\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  and whose boundary values are given by  $\psi^{\varepsilon}(x_{i})=z_{i}$ . This gives an embedding of the vertices of the graph (into the unit disk  $\mathbbm{D}$ , by an argument similar to the maximum principle). A theorem of Tutte [Tut63] then guarantees that if the edges of the graph are drawn as straight lines then the edges can overlap but not cross.
SLE/LQG embedding.
One of the reasons the mated-CRT maps (either in finite or infinite volume) are convenient is that, due to the main result of [DMS21], they admit an elegant alternative description given by a certain type of  $\gamma$ -LQG surface (represented by a random distribution  $h$  in a portion  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$  of the complex plane), decorated by an independent space-filling version of a Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) curve  $\eta$  with parameter  $\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}\in(4,\infty)$ . The notion of LQG surfaces will be described in greater details in Section 2.2, but let us nevertheless describe the embedding as succinctly as possibly, deferring the definitions to that section. See Figure 3 for an illustration.
Figure 3:  Illustration of the LQG / SLE embeddding of the mated-CRT map in the disk case (a similar figure appears in [GMS21]). Left: A segment of a space-filling curve  $\eta:[0,1]\rightarrow\overline{\mathbbm{D}}$ , divided into cells  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  for  $x\in(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})\cap(0,1]$ . The order in which the cells are hit is shown by the orange path. This figure looks like what we would expect to see for  $\kappa\geq 8$  ( $\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}$ ), since the cells are simply connected. Middle: To get an embedding of the mated-CRT map, we draw a red point in each cell and connect the points whose cells share a corresponding boundary arc. Right: Same as the middle picture but without the original cells, so that only the embedded mated-CRT map is visible.
We start with the infinite volume case, which is slightly easier to explain. In that case,  $D=\mathbbm{C}$  and  $h$  is the random distribution corresponding to a so-called  $\gamma$ -quantum cone.
Since the law of  $h$  is locally absolutely continuous with respect to that of a Gaussian free field one can define a volume measure  $\mu_{h}$  which is a version of the LQG measure (or Gaussian multiplicative chaos) associated to  $h$ .
One way to define this measure is as follows.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ , let  $h_{\varepsilon}(z)$  be the average of  $h$  over the circle of radius  $\varepsilon$  centered at  $z$ .
Then for any open set  $A\subset\mathbbm{C}$ ,
$\mu_{h}(A)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{A}\varepsilon^{\gamma^{2}/2}e^{\gamma h_{\varepsilon}(z)}dz$
(1.4)
in probability (see, e.g., [DS11, Ber17]). In fact the convergence was shown to be a.s. in [SW16].
The curve  $\eta$  mentioned above is in the whole-plane case a whole-plane space-filling SLEκ from  $\infty$  to  $\infty$ , sampled independently from  $h$ . When  $\kappa\geq 8$ , i.e. when  $\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}$ , whole-plane SLEκ is already space-filling and  $\eta$  is then nothing but an ordinary whole-plane SLE from  $\infty$  to  $\infty$ . However, when  $\kappa\in(4,8)$  ordinary SLE is not space-filling and the construction is more complicated, see [MS17, Section 1.2.3] and Section 2.2.2. This choice of  $(h,\eta)$  corresponds to the setting of the whole-plane mating of trees theorem [DMS21, Theorem 1.9].
Let us now describe the disk case, which is slightly more involved. In this case,  $D=\mathbbm{D}$  is the unit disk and  $h$  is the random distribution corresponding to a type of quantum surface known as a quantum disk with unit area and unit boundary length. Such a surface does not normally come with a specified marked point either on the boundary or in the bulk, but we add a marked point on the boundary by sampling from the boundary length measure (the appropriate analogue of (1.4) restricted to the boundary).
The curve  $\eta$  is a space-filling SLEκ loop from the marked boundary point to itself (with loops being filled in clockwise). Such a curve is obtained as the limit of a chordal space-filling SLEκ between two boundary points  $x$  and  $y$ , as  $y\to x$ ; see Section 2.2.2 for more details.
This setup corresponds essentially to the (finite volume) mating of trees theorem proved by Ang and Gwynne [AG21, Theorem 1.1], with two unessential differences: one is that the loops of  $\eta$  are filled counterclockwise in [AG21] (corresponding to the Brownian pair  $(L,R)$  ending on the  $R$  axis instead of the  $L$  axis as is the case here). The second is
that the paper [AG21] describes the situation corresponding to unit boundary length (but random area). The corresponding mating of trees theorem for the case we need here is naturally obtained by conditioning on the total area, whose law is described in [AG21, Theorem 1.2].
In both setups, since the curve  $\eta$  is space-filling, it can be reparametrized by  $\mu_{h}$ -area: in any time interval of length  $t$ , the curve covers an area of mass  $t$ . The LQG embedding of mated-CRT planar maps is then as follows. Each vertex  $x\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}$  corresponds to a cell  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  with appropriate modifications for the last cell if  $\varepsilon$  is not of the form  $1/n$  for some  $n\geq 1$ . Two cells are declared adjacent if their intersection is nonempty and contains a nontrivial curve11
1
When  $\kappa\geq 8$ , this second condition is in fact not necessary.
On the other hand, when  $\kappa\in(4,8)$ , an SLEκ curve is self-touching, resulting in pinch points for the cells formed by the space-filling curve.
On either side of such a pinch point could be two different cells, but our definition ensures that these are nevertheless not declared adjacent, even though they intersect at the pinch point.. It is not hard to see via the mating of trees theorems mentioned earlier (Theorem 1.9 in [DMS21] and Theorem 1.1 in [AG21]) that this gives an alternative and equivalent construction of the mated-CRT planar maps in the respective setups. Concretely, this gives an a priori embedding of the mated-CRT planar map into the domain  $D$  (either the whole plane or the disk) obtained by sending each vertex  $x$  to a point of the corresponding cell.
This embedding is extremely useful to carry out concrete computations on the mated-CRT planar maps. Furthermore, it is closely related to the Tutte embedding: indeed, one of the main results of [GMS21] implies that the Tutte embedding converges uniformly to the SLE embedding. More precisely, if  $\psi^{\varepsilon}$  denotes the Tutte embedding of the mated-CRT map with the disk topology, as above, then
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}}|\psi^{\varepsilon}(x)-\eta(x)|\to 0$
(1.5)
in probability; see (3.3) in Section 3.4 of [GMS21].
Convergence of the random walk modulo time parametrization.
Most of the work in [GMS21] goes into proving that that the random walk on the mated-CRT map converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization under the LQG embedding discussed above.
More precisely, it is shown in [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] that for each compact set  $K\subset\mathbbm{C}$ , the Prokhorov distance between the following two probability measures converges to zero in probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , uniformly over all  $z\in K$ :
•
The law of standard planar Brownian motion started from  $z$ , viewed modulo time parametrization;
•
The conditional law given  $(h,\eta)$  of the random walk on the mated-CRT map under the LQG embedding with cell size  $\varepsilon$ , started from the (a.s. unique) vertex  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  such that  $z\in\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$ , extended to be a continuous curve by piecewise linear interpolation, and viewed modulo time parametrization.
See [GMS21, Section 2.1.2] for a discussion of the topology on curves modulo time parametrization. The proof of the above convergence result is based on a general scaling limit result for random walks in planar random environments which are in some sense “translation invariant modulo scaling” [GMS18, Theorem 3.10].
Due to the relationship between random walk and discrete harmonic functions, the convergence of random walk on the mated-CRT map to Brownian motion implies that, under the LQG embedding, discrete harmonic functions on the mated-CRT map approximate their continuum counterparts when  $\varepsilon$  is small. This, in turn, allows one to show that the Tutte embedding is close to the LQG embedding, in the sense of (1.5).
This paper will build on the result of [GMS21] to get convergence of the parametrized walk on the mated-CRT map. Let us now discuss the limiting object.
Liouville Brownian motion.
Let  $h$  be either field considered in the preceding section, i.e., a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone with circle average embedding or a unit quantum disk. Along with an area measure  $\mu_{h}$  on  $D$ , it is possible to associate to the field  $h$  a diffusion  $X$ , called Liouville Brownian motion. We give a few more details now. Let  $z\in D$ , let  $B^{z}$  denote a standard planar Brownian motion in  $D$  started from  $z$  and let  $\tau$  denote its exit time from  $D$ . By definition22
2
In fact, the works [Ber15, GRV16] focus on slightly different versions of the field  $h$  where instead of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone or quantum disk,  $h$  is a Dirichlet GFF. Extending this definition to the case of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone or to a quantum disk is relatively straightforward: in particular, in the case of the quantum cone one needs to check that the process does not stay stuck at zero (due to the  $\gamma$ -log singularity). This is easily confirmed since the expected time for the LBM started from 0 to reach the boundary of the unit disk, say, given the quantum cone  $h$ , is given by  $\int_{\mathbbm{D}}\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbbm{D}}(0,y)\mu_{h}(dy)<\infty$  a.s. (where  $\operatorname{Gr}_{\mathbbm{D}}$  is the Green’s function on the disk). The finiteness of this last integral can be checked by splitting the disk into dyadic annuli and considering the contribution of each annulus. (see, e.g., [Ber15, GRV16]), Liouville Brownian motion is defined as the time-change  $B^{z}_{\phi^{-1}(t)}$ , where the Liouville clock  $\phi$  satisfies
$\phi(t)=\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\int_{0}^{t\wedge\tau}\varepsilon^{\gamma^{2}/2}e^{\gamma h_{\varepsilon}(B^{z}_{s})}ds.$
In fact, for technical reasons our results will require applying a fixed global rescaling of time, chosen so that the median of the time needed by Liouville Brownian motion on a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone to leave a fixed Euclidean ball, say the ball  $B_{1/2}$  of radius  $1/2$  centered at zero, is one. In other words, if  $h$  is the circle average embedding of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone,
$\tau_{1/2}=\inf\{t>0:|B_{\phi^{-1}(t)}|\geq 1/2\},$
and if  $m_{0}$  is its (annealed) median, then our scaled Liouville Brownian motion is by definition
$X^{z}_{t}=B^{z}_{\phi^{-1}(tm_{0})}.$
(1.6)
Note that  $m_{0}$  is defined w.r.t. the circle average embedding of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone, regardless of what field  $h$  we are using to define the Liouville Brownian motion.
1.3 Main results
Our main result will come in two versions, corresponding respectively to the whole plane and disk setups. We start with the whole-plane case.
In this case, we work only with the SLE/LQG embedding since the Tutte embedding is harder to define if we do not have a boundary.
Let  $(h,\eta)$  denote the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone decorated by an independent space-filling SLE describing the SLE/LQG embedding of the whole plane mated-CRT planar maps  $(\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0}$  with parameter  $\gamma$ , as described above. We assume that  $h$  is the circle-average embedding of the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ , let  $X^{z,\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{N}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  be the simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from  $x$ , where  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  is chosen so that  $z$  belongs to the cell  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  (there is a.s. a unique such  $x$  for each fixed  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ ; for the atypical points for which there are multiple possibilities, we arbitrarily choose the smallest possible value of  $x$ ).
We extend the domain of definition of the embedded walk  $\mathbbm{N}_{0}\ni j\mapsto\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{j})$  from  $\mathbbm{N}_{0}$  to  $[0,\infty)$  by piecewise linear interpolation.
Also let
$m_{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{median exit time of $\eta(X^{0,\varepsilon})$ from $B_{1/2}$}}}\right)$
(1.7)
where  $B_{1/2}$  is the Euclidean ball of radius  $1/2$  centered at 0.
Note that this is an annealed median, i.e., we are not conditioning on  $(h,\eta)$  and so  $m_{\varepsilon}$  is deterministic.
In this whole plane setup, our main result is the following theorem.
Theorem 1.2.
For each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , the conditional law of the embedded, linearly interpolated walk  $(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(L_{t},R_{t})_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}$  (equivalently, given  $(h,\eta)$ ) converges in probability to the rescaled law of  $\gamma$ -Liouville Brownian motion started from  $z$  associated with  $h$ , defined in (1.6), with respect to the Prokhorov topology induced by the local uniform metric on curves  $[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$ .
In fact, the convergence occurs uniformly over all points  $z$  in any compact subset of  $\mathbbm{C}$ .
Remark 1.3.
Our proof shows that there is a constant  $C>1$  depending only on  $\gamma$  such that the time scaling constants  $m_{\varepsilon}$  of (1.7) satisfy
$C^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1}\leq m_{\varepsilon}\leq C\varepsilon^{-1},\quad\text{for all sufficiently small $\varepsilon>0$.}$
(1.8)
We do not know that  $\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}$  converges, so we do not get convergence in Theorems 1.2 and 1.4 when we scale time by  $1/\varepsilon$  instead of by  $m_{\varepsilon}$ .
See, however, Section 1.4.
We now give our theorem statement in the disk case.
The theorem is similar to the whole-plane case except that we state it for the more intrinsic Tutte embedding (rather than the a priori LQG embedding, although the result is also valid for this latter embedding).
Let  $(h,\eta)$  denote the quantum disk decorated by an independent space-filling SLE describing the SLE/LQG embedding of the mated-CRT maps  $(\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon})_{\varepsilon>0}$  with the disk topology and parameter  $\gamma$ , as described above.
We assume that the marked point for  $h$  (equivalently, the starting point for  $\eta$ ) is 1.
Let  $\psi^{\varepsilon}:\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}\to\mathbbm{C}$  be the Tutte embedding of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , as defined in Section 1.2.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{D}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ , let  $X^{z,\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{N}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  be the simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from  $x$ , where  $x=x(z,\varepsilon)\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\cap[0,1]$  is chosen to be a vertex such that  $z$  is closest to  $\psi^{\varepsilon}(x)$ . In case of ties, pick  $x$  arbitrarily among the possible choices.
We extend the domain of definition of the embedded walk  $\mathbbm{N}_{0}\ni j\mapsto\psi(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{j})$  from  $\mathbbm{N}_{0}$  to  $[0,\infty)$  by piecewise linear interpolation.
Let  $m_{\varepsilon}$  be as in (1.7) (note that we define  $m_{\varepsilon}$  in terms of the whole-plane mated-CRT map in both the whole-plane and disk settings).
Theorem 1.4.
For each  $z\in\mathbbm{D}$ , consider the conditional law of the embedded, linearly interpolated walk  $(\psi^{\varepsilon}(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0}$ , given  $(L_{t},R_{t})_{t\in[0,1]}$  (equivalently, given  $(h,\eta)$ ). As  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , these laws converge in probability to the rescaled law of  $\gamma$ -Liouville Brownian motion started from  $z$  associated with   $h$ , defined in (1.6), stopped upon leaving the unit disk  $\mathbbm{D}$ , with respect to the Prokhorov topology induced by the local uniform metric on curves  $[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$ .
In fact, the convergence occurs uniformly over all points  $z$  in any compact subset of  $\overline{\mathbbm{D}}\setminus\{1\}$ .
Due to (1.5), Theorem 1.4 is equivalent to the analogous statement with the SLE/LQG embedding in place of the Tutte embedding.
Note that we only claim uniform convergence on compact subsets of  $\overline{\mathbbm{D}}\setminus\{1\}$  in Theorem 1.4, not uniform convergence on all of  $\overline{\mathbbm{D}}$ . We know that the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  converges to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization uniformly over all starting points in  $\overline{\mathbbm{D}}$  [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] (in the quenched sense). We expect that the result of Theorem 1.4 also holds uniformly over all  $z\in\overline{\mathbbm{D}}$ , but in order to prove this one would need some arguments to prevent the walk started near the marked point  $1$  from getting “stuck” and staying in a small neighborhood of  $1$  for an unusually long time without hitting  $\partial\mathbbm{D}$ .
As we explain below, our proof of Theorem 1.2 relies on the one hand on proving a tightness result for the conditional law of  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ , and on the other hand on a characterization statement for the subsequential limits, which is stated below as Theorem 1.5.
Our proof of convergence to Liouville Brownian motion is restricted to mated-CRT maps and does not apply in full to other natural models of random planar maps such as the UIPT.
Nevertheless, several aspects of our proof might be useful in this more general setting.
In particular, the following characterization of Liouville Brownian motion is of independent interest and may be useful for identifying (subsequential) limits of random walk on other models of conformally embedded random planar maps.
We state this result somewhat informally, deferring the actual necessary definitions and full statement to Section 7 and in particular Proposition 7.10.
Theorem 1.5.
Let  $h$  be the random distribution associated with the circle average embedding of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone.
Suppose that we are given a coupling of  $h$  and a random continuous function  $P=\{P_{z}:z\in\mathbbm{C}\}$  which takes each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  to a (random) element  $P_{z}$  of the space  $\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  of probability measures on random continuous paths in  $\mathbbm{C}$  started from  $z$ .
Suppose that the following conditions hold:
•
Conditional on  $(h,P)$ , a.s. for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  the process with the law  $P_{z}$  is Markovian;
•
For each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ ,  $P_{z}$  has the law of a (random) time-change of a standard Brownian motion starting from  $z$ ;
•
$P$  leaves the Liouville measure  $\mu=\mu_{h}$  associated to  $h$  invariant.
Then there is a (possibly random) constant  $c$  such that for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ ,  $P_{z}$  coincides with the law of  $(X^{z}_{ct},t\geq 0)$ , where  $X^{z}$  is a Liouville Brownian motion associated with  $h$ , starting from  $z$ .
1.4 Outline
Most of the paper is devoted to the proof of Theorem 1.2. See Section 7.4 for an explanation of how one deduces Theorem 1.4 from Theorem 1.2 using (1.5) and a local absolute continuity argument.
It is shown in [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] that, in the setting of Theorem 1.2, the conditional law of  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$  converges in probability to the law of Brownian motion started from  $z$  with respect to the Prokhorov topology induced by the metric on curves in  $\mathbbm{C}$  modulo time parametrization. It is also shown there that the convergence is uniform over  $z$  in any compact subset of  $\mathbbm{C}$ .
We need to show that the walk in fact converges uniformly to  $\gamma$ -LBM.
Most of the work in the proof goes into proving an appropriate tightness result, which says that the conditional law of  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$  admits subsequential limits as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (Proposition 6.1).
This is done in Sections 3 through 6 and requires us to establish many new estimates for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , building on the results of [GMS21, GMS19].
The identification of the subsequential limit, summarized in Theorem 1.5, is carried out in Section 7. A crucial role is played in particular by the notion of Revuz measure associated to a Positive Additive Continuous Functional (PCAF) for general Markov processes.
Before outlining the proof, we make some general comments about our arguments.
•
Only a few main results from each section (usually stated at the beginning of the section) are used in subsequent sections. So, the different sections can to a great extent be read independently of each other.
•
Our proofs give quantitative estimates for random walk on the mated-CRT map which are stronger than what is strictly necessary to prove convergence to Liouville Brownian motion. Such estimates include up-to-constants bounds for exit times from Euclidean balls (Propositions 4.1 and 5.1), bounds for the Green’s function (Lemmas 4.4, 5.4, and 5.6), and modulus of continuity estimates for random walk paths (Proposition 6.5) and for the law of the walk as a function of its starting point (Proposition 6.12).
•
For most of the proof of Theorem 1.2, we will scale time by  $1/\varepsilon$  instead of by  $m_{\varepsilon}$ , i.e., we will work with  $(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon}))_{t\geq 0}$ .
We switch to scaling time by  $m_{\varepsilon}$  at the very end of the proof, in Section 7.3, for reasons which will be explained at the end of this outline.
In order to establish tightness of  $(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon}))_{t\geq 0}$ , we need up-to-constants estimates for the conditional law given  $(h,\eta)$  of the exit time of the (embedded) random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from a Euclidean ball.
Moreover, these estimates need to hold uniformly over all Euclidean balls contained in any given compact subset of  $\mathbbm{C}$ .
Moments of exit times from Euclidean balls can be expressed as sums involving the discrete Green’s function for random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  stopped upon exiting the ball.
Hence we need to prove up-to-constants estimates for the discrete Green’s function.
The results of [GMS19] allow us to bound the discrete Dirichlet energies of discrete harmonic functions on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , which leads to bounds for effective resistances (equivalently, for the values of the discrete Green’s function on the diagonal).
The main task in the proof of tightness is to transfer from these estimates to bounds for the behavior of the Green’s function off the diagonal.
Section 3 contains the two key estimates which allow us to do this.
•
Lemma 3.4 says that for any finite graph  $G$  and any vertex sets  $A\subset B\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$ , the following is true.
The maximum (resp. minimum) value on the boundary  $\partial A$  of the Green’s function for random walk killed upon exiting  $B$  is bounded below (resp. above) by the effective resistance from  $A$  to  $B$ .
•
Proposition 3.8 is a Harnack-type inequality which says that the maximum and minimum values of the discrete Green’s function on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  on the boundary of a Euclidean ball differ by at most a constant factor.
Combined, these two estimates reduce the problem of estimating the Green’s function to the problem of estimating effective resistances, which we can do (with a non-trivial amount of work) using tools from [GMS19].
In Sections 4 and 5, we use the ideas discussed above to establish a lower (resp. upper) bound for the Green’s function, which in turn leads lower (resp. upper) bounds for the exit times of the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from Euclidean balls.
In Section 6, we use these estimates to establish the tightness of the conditional law of  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon})\}_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ .
The arguments involved in these steps are non-trivial, but we do not outline them here; see the beginnings of the individual sections and subsections for outlines.
In Section 7, we show that the subsequential limit must be LBM as follows.
Since we already know the convergence of the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization, every subsequential limit of the conditional law of  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon})\}_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$  is a probability measure on curves  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  in  $\mathbbm{C}$  which are time-changed Brownian motions, with a continuous time change function.
Our estimates show that the time change function is in fact strictly increasing.
Furthermore, it can be checked using the Markov property for random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  that  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is Markovian (Lemma 7.4).
Finally, since the counting measure on vertices of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  weighted by their degree is reversible for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , it is easily seen that the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure  $\mu_{h}$  is invariant (in fact, reversible) for  $\widehat{X}^{z}$ .
The properties of the subsequential limit process described in the preceding paragraph are all also known to hold for Liouville Brownian motion [GRV16, GRV14, Ber15].
It turns out that these properties are in fact sufficient to uniquely characterize LBM up to a time change of the form  $t\mapsto ct$  for a deterministic  $c>0$  which does not depend on the starting point.
This is a consequence of a general proposition (Proposition 7.10, which is a generalization of Theorem 1.5), which says that two Markovian time changed Brownian motions with a common invariant measure agree in law modulo such a time change. In our setting, the two Markovian time changed Brownian motions are the subsequential limit process and the LBM and the common invariant measure is the LQG measure.
As explained in Section 7.2, Proposition 7.10 is a (in our view surprisingly simple) consequence of known results in general Markov process theory.
In particular, the time change function for a time changed Brownian motion is a positive continuous additive functionals (PCAF) of the Brownian motion with the standard parametrization. The Revuz measure associated with the PCAF is an invariant measure for the time changed Brownian motion, and is in fact the unique such invariant measure up to multiplication by a deterministic constant.
Since the Revuz measure uniquely determines the PCAF, this shows that two different time changed Brownian motions with the same invariant measure must agree in law modulo a linear time change, as required.
The above argument shows that for any sequence of positive  $\varepsilon$ ’s tending to zero, there is a subsequence  $\mathcal{E}$  and a deterministic33
3
We are glossing over a technicality here — as explained in Section 7.3, some argument is needed to show that the constant  $c$  is deterministic rather than just a random variable which is determined by  $(h,\eta)$  and the limiting law on random paths. constant  $c>0$  which may depend on  $\mathcal{E}$  along which  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{t/\varepsilon})\}_{t\geq 0}$  converges in law to LBM started from  $z$  pre-composed with the linear time change  $t\mapsto ct$  (in the quenched sense).
This does not yet give Theorem 1.2 since  $c$  can depend on the subsequence.
To get around this, we need to scale time by  $m_{\varepsilon}$  instead of by  $1/\varepsilon$ .
Indeed, by the definition (1.7), the median exit time of the process  $\{\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t})\}_{t\geq 0}$  from  $B_{1/2}$  is equal to 1, so all of the possible subsequential limits of the laws of this process must be LBM with the same linear time change.
Appendix A contains some basic estimates for the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure and for space-filling SLE cells which are used in our proofs.
The proofs in this appendix are routine and do not use any of the other results in the paper, so are collected here to avoid distracting from the main ideas of the argument.

2 Preliminaries
2.1 Basic notation
We write  $\mathbbm{N}=\{1,2,3,\dots\}$  and  $\mathbbm{N}_{0}=\mathbbm{N}\cup\{0\}$ .
For  $a<b$ , we define the discrete interval  $[a,b]_{\mathbbm{Z}}:=[a,b]\cap\mathbbm{Z}$ .
For a graph  $G$ , we write  $\mathcal{V}(G)$  and  $\mathcal{E}(G)$  for its vertex and edge sets, respectively.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $r>0$ , we write  $B_{r}(z)$  for the Euclidean ball of radius  $r$  centered at  $z$ .
We abbreviate  $B_{r}=B_{r}(0)$ .
If  $f:(0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{R}$  and  $g:(0,\infty)\rightarrow(0,\infty)$ , we say that  $f(\varepsilon)=O_{\varepsilon}(g(\varepsilon))$  (resp.  $f(\varepsilon)=o_{\varepsilon}(g(\varepsilon))$ ) as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  if  $f(\varepsilon)/g(\varepsilon)$  remains bounded (resp. tends to zero) as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ . We similarly define  $O(\cdot)$  and  $o(\cdot)$  errors as a parameter goes to infinity.
If  $f,g:(0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty)$ , we say that  $f(\varepsilon)\preceq g(\varepsilon)$  if there is a constant  $C>0$  (independent from  $\varepsilon$  and possibly from other parameters of interest) such that  $f(\varepsilon)\leq Cg(\varepsilon)$ . We write  $f(\varepsilon)\asymp g(\varepsilon)$  if  $f(\varepsilon)\preceq g(\varepsilon)$  and  $g(\varepsilon)\preceq f(\varepsilon)$ .
Let  $\{E^{\varepsilon}\}_{\varepsilon>0}$  be a one-parameter family of events. We say that  $E^{\varepsilon}$  occurs with
•
polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  if there is a  $p>0$  (independent from  $\varepsilon$  and possibly from other parameters of interest) such that  $\mathbbm{P}[E^{\varepsilon}]\geq 1-O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{p})$ .
•
superpolynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  if  $\mathbbm{P}[E^{\varepsilon}]\geq 1-O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{p})$  for every  $p>0$ .
We similarly define events which occur with polynomially, superpolynomially, and exponentially high probability as a parameter tends to  $\infty$ .
We will often specify any requirements on the dependencies on rates of convergence in  $O(\cdot)$  and  $o(\cdot)$  errors, implicit constants in  $\preceq$ , etc., in the statements of lemmas/propositions/theorems, in which case we implicitly require that errors, implicit constants, etc., appearing in the proof satisfy the same dependencies.
2.2 Background on Liouville quantum gravity and SLE
Throughout this paper we fix the LQG parameter  $\gamma\in(0,2)$  and the corresponding SLE parameter  $\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}>4$ .
2.2.1 Liouville quantum gravity
We will give some relatively brief background on LQG. We will in particular focus on quantum cones (which are the main types of quantum surfaces considered in this paper) and also briefly discuss quantum disks.
The following definition is taken from [DS11, She16, DMS21].
Definition 2.1.
A  $\gamma$ -Liouville quantum gravity (LQG) surface is an equivalence class of pairs  $(D,h)$ , where  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$  is an open set and  $h$  is a distribution on  $D$  (which will always be taken to be a realization of a random distribution which locally looks like the Gaussian free field), with two such pairs  $(D,h)$  and  $(\widetilde{D},\widetilde{h})$  declared to be equivalent if there is a conformal map  $f:\widetilde{D}\rightarrow D$  such that
$\widetilde{h}=h\circ f+Q\log|f^{\prime}|\quad\text{for}\quad Q=\frac{2}{\gamma}+\frac{\gamma}{2}.$
(2.1)
More generally, for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  a  $\gamma$ -LQG surface with  $k$  marked points is an equivalence class of  $k+2$ -tuples  $(D,h,x_{1},\dots,x_{k})$  where  $x_{1},\dots,x_{k}\in D\cup\partial D$ , with the equivalence relation defined as in (2.1) except that the map  $f$  is required to map the marked points of one surface to the corresponding marked points of the other.
We think of different elements of the same equivalence class in Definition 2.1 as representing different parametrizations of the same surface.
If  $(D,h,x_{1},\dots,x_{k})$  is a particular equivalence class representative of a quantum surface, we call  $h$  an embedding of the surface into  $(D,x_{1},\dots,x_{k})$ .
Suppose now that  $h$  is a random distribution on  $D$  which can be coupled with a GFF on  $D$  in such a way that their difference is a.s. a continuous function.
Following [DS11, Section 3.1], we can then define for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$  the circle average  $h_{\varepsilon}(z)$  of  $h$  over  $\partial B_{\varepsilon}(z)$ .
It is shown in [DS11, Proposition 3.1] that  $(z,\varepsilon)\mapsto h_{\varepsilon}(z)$  a.s. admits a continuous modification.
We will always assume that this process has been replaced by such a modification.
One can define the  $\gamma$ -LQG area measure  $\mu_{h}$  on  $D$ , which is defined to be the a.s. limit
$\mu_{h}=\lim_{\varepsilon\rightarrow 0}\varepsilon^{\gamma^{2}/2}e^{\gamma h_{\varepsilon}(z)}\,dz$
with respect to the local Prokhorov distance on  $D$  as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  along powers of 2 [DS11].
One can similarly define a boundary length measure  $\nu_{h}$  on certain curves in  $D$ , including  $\partial D$  [DS11] and SLE ${}_{\underline{\kappa}}$ -type curves for  $\underline{\kappa}=\gamma^{2}$  which are independent from  $h$  [She16]. If  $h$  and  $\widetilde{h}$  are related by a conformal map as in (2.1), then  $f_{*}\mu_{\widetilde{h}}=\mu_{h}$  and  $f_{*}\nu_{\widetilde{h}}=\nu_{h}$ .
Hence  $\mu_{h}$  and  $\nu_{h}$  are intrinsic to the LQG surface — they do not depend on the choice of parametrization.
The measures  $\mu_{h}$  and  $\nu_{h}$  are a special case of a more general theory of regularized random measures called Gaussian multiplicative chaos which originates in work of Kahane [Kah85]. See [Ber17] for an elementary proof of convergence (and independence of the limit with respect to the regularization procedure) and [RV14a] for a survey of this theory.
The main type of LQG surface which we will be interested in in this paper is the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone, which is the surface appearing in the SLE/LQG embedding of the mated-CRT map.
The  $\gamma$ -quantum cone is a doubly marked LQG surface  $(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty)$  introduced in [DMS21, Definition 4.10].
Roughly speaking, the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone is the surface obtained by starting with a general  $\gamma$ -LQG surface, sampling a point  $z$  uniformly from the  $\gamma$ -LQG area measure, then “zooming in” near the marked point and re-scaling so that the  $\mu_{h}$ -mass of the unit disk remains of constant order [DMS21, Proposition 4.13(ii) and Lemma A.10].
This surface can be described explicitly as follows.
Definition 2.2 (Quantum cone).
The  $\gamma$ -quantum cone is the LQG surface  $(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty)$  with the distribution  $h$  defined as follows.
Let  $B$  be a standard linear Brownian motion and let  $\widehat{B}$  be a standard linear Brownian motion conditioned so that  $\widehat{B}_{t}+(Q-\gamma)t>0$  for all  $t>0$  (here  $Q=2/\gamma+\gamma/2$ , as in (2.1)).
Let  $A_{t}=B_{t}-\alpha t$  for  $t\geq 0$  and let  $A_{t}=\widehat{B}_{-t}+\gamma t$  for  $t<0$ .
The circle average process of  $h$  centered at the origin satisfies  $h_{e^{-t}}(0)=A_{t}$  for each  $t\in\mathbbm{R}$ .
The “lateral part”  $h-h_{|\cdot|}(0)$  is independent from  $\{h_{e^{-t}}(0)\}_{t\in\mathbbm{R}}$  and has the same law as  $\widetilde{h}-\widetilde{h}_{|\cdot|}(0)$ , where  $\widetilde{h}$  is a whole-plane GFF.
By Definition 2.1, one can get another embedding of the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone by replacing  $h$  by  $h(a\cdot)+Q\log|a|$  for any  $a\in\mathbbm{C}\setminus\{0\}$ .
The particular embedding  $h$  appearing in Definition 2.2 is called the circle average embedding and is characterized by the condition that  $\sup\{r>0:h_{r}(0)+Q\log r=0\}=1$ .
The circle average embedding is especially convenient to work with since for this embedding,  $h|_{\mathbbm{D}}$  agrees in law with the corresponding restriction of a whole-plane GFF plus  $-\gamma\log|\cdot|$ , normalized so that its circle average over  $\partial\mathbbm{D}$  is 0.
Indeed, this is essentially immediate from Definition 2.2 since the process  $A_{t}$  has no conditioning for  $t>0$ .
Since we can only compare  $h$  to the whole-plane GFF on the unit disk  $\mathbbm{D}$ , for many of our estimates we will restrict attention to a Euclidean ball of the form  $B_{\rho}$  for  $\rho\in(0,1)$ .
It is possible to transfer these estimates to larger Euclidean balls using the scale invariance property of the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone, which is proven in [DMS21, Proposition 4.13(i)].
Lemma 2.3.
Let  $h$  be the circle average embedding of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone.
For  $b>0$ , define
$R_{b}:=\sup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{r>0:h_{r}(0)+Q\log r=\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b}}\right\}.$
(2.2)
Then  $h^{b}:=h(R_{b}\cdot)+Q\log R_{b}-\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b\overset{d}{=}h$ .
Lemma 2.3 says that the law of  $h$  is invariant under the operation of scaling areas by a constant (i.e., adding  $\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b$  to  $h$ ), then re-scaling space and applying the LQG coordinate change formula (2.1) so that the new field is embedded in the same way as  $h$ .
In addition to the  $\gamma$ -quantum wedge we will also have occasion to consider the quantum disk, which appears in Theorem 1.4.
To define the quantum disk, one first defines an infinite measure  $\mathcal{M}^{\operatorname{disk}}$  on doubly quantum surfaces  $(\mathbbm{D},h,-1,1)$  using the Bessel excursion measure.
We will not need the precise definition here, so we refer to [DMS21, Section 4.5] for details.
The infinite measure  $\mathcal{M}^{\operatorname{disk}}$  assigns finite mass to quantum surfaces with boundary length  $\nu_{h}(\partial\mathbbm{D})\geq L$  for any  $L>0$ .
By considering the regular conditional law of  $\mathcal{M}^{\operatorname{disk}}$  given  $\{\nu_{h}(\partial\mathbbm{D})=L,\mu_{h}(\mathbbm{D})=A\}$  for any  $L,A>0$ , one defines the doubly marked quantum disk with boundary length  $L$  and area  $A$ . We define the singly marked quantum disk or the unmarked quantum disk by forgetting one or both of the marked boundary points. By Proposition [DMS21, Proposition A.8], the marked points of a quantum disk are uniform samples from the LQG boundary length measure. That is, if  $(\mathbbm{D},h)$  is an unmarked quantum disk (with some specified area and boundary length) and conditional on  $h$  we sample  $x,y$  independently from the probability measure  $\nu_{h}/L$ , then  $(\mathbbm{D},h,x)$  is a single marked quantum disk and  $(\mathbbm{D},h,x,y)$  is a doubly marked quantum disk.
2.2.2 Space-filling SLEκ
The Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLEκ) for  $\kappa>0$  is a one-parameter family of random fractal curves originally defined by Schramm in [Sch00].
SLEκ curves are simple for  $\kappa\in(0,4]$ , self-touching, but not space-filling or self-crossing, for  $\kappa\in(4,8)$ , and space-filling but still not self-crossing for  $\kappa\geq 8$  [RS05].
One can consider SLEκ curves between two marked boundary points of a simply connected domain (chordal), from a boundary point to an interior point (radial), or between two points in  $\mathbbm{C}\cup\{\infty\}$  (whole-plane). We refer to [Law05] or [Wer04] for an introduction to SLE.
We first consider the whole-plane space-filling SLEκ from  $\infty$  to  $\infty$ , which was introduced in [MS17, Sections 1.2.3 and 4.3].
This is a random space-filling curve  $\eta$  in  $\mathbbm{C}$  which travels from  $\infty$  to  $\infty$  which fills all of  $\mathbbm{C}$  and never enters the interior of its past.
Moreover, its law is invariant under spatial scaling: for any  $r>0$ ,  $r\eta$  agrees in law with  $\eta$  viewed as curves modulo time parametrization.
This is essentially the only information about space-filling SLEκ which is needed to understand this paper — we do not use any detailed information about the geometry of the curve.
However, we briefly describe how space-filling SLEκ is defined (without details) to give the reader some more intuition about what this curve is.
See [GHS19b, Section 3.6] for a detailed review of space-filling SLEκ.
When  $\kappa\geq 8$ , in which case ordinary SLEκ is already space-filling, whole-plane SLEκ from  $\infty$  to  $\infty$  describes the local behavior of an ordinary chordal SLEκ curve near a typical interior point.
For any  $a<b$ , the set  $\eta([a,b])$  has the topology of a closed disk and its boundary is the union of four SLE ${}_{\underline{\kappa}}$ -type curves for  $\underline{\kappa}=16/\kappa$  which intersect only at their endpoints.
When  $\kappa\in(4,8)$ , the definition of space-filling SLEκ is more involved.
Roughly speaking, chordal space-filling SLEκ can be obtained by starting with an ordinary chordal SLEκ curve and iteratively “filling in” the bubbles which it disconnects from its target point by SLEκ-type curves.
It is shown in [MS17] that the curve one obtains after countably many iterations is space-filling and continuous when parameterized so that it traverses one unit of Lebesgue measure in one unit of time.
The whole-plane space-filling SLEκ from  $\infty$  to  $\infty$  for  $\kappa\in(4,8)$  describes the local behavior of the chordal version near a typical interior point, as in the case  $\kappa\geq 8$ .
The topology of the curve is much more complicated for  $\kappa\in(4,8)$  than for  $\kappa\geq 8$ .
For  $a<b$ , neither the interior of the set  $\eta([a,b])$  nor its complement  $\mathbbm{C}\setminus\eta([a,b])$  is connected. Rather, each of these sets consists of a countable union of domains with the topology of the open disk (or the punctured plane in the case of the unbounded connected component of  $\mathbbm{C}\setminus\eta([a,b])$ .
The boundary of  $\eta([a,b])$  is the union of four SLE ${}_{\underline{\kappa}}$ -type curves for  $\underline{\kappa}=16/\kappa$ , but these curves typically intersect each other.
If  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$  is a simply connected domain and  $a\in\partial D$ , we can similarly define the clockwise space-filling SLEκ loop in  $D$  based at  $a$ . This is a random curve in  $D$  from  $a$  to  $a$  which is the limit of chordal space-filling SLE from  $a$  to  $b$  in  $D$  as  $a\rightarrow b$  from the counterclockwise direction. See Section A.3 for details.
2.3 Mated-CRT map setup
Throughout most of this paper we will work with the following setup.
Let  $(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty)$  be a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone with the circle average embedding.
Let  $\eta$  be a whole-plane space-filling SLEκ with  $\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}$  sampled independently from  $h$  and then parametrized so that  $\eta(0)=0$  and  $\mu_{h}(\eta([a,b]))=b-a$  for every  $a<b$ . We define the cells
$H_{x}^{\varepsilon}:=\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]),\quad\forall\varepsilon>0,\quad\forall x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}.$
(2.3)
For  $\varepsilon>0$ , we let  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  be the mated-CRT map associated with  $(h,\eta)$ , i.e.,  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  and two distinct vertices  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  are connected by one (resp. two) edges if and only if  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\cap H_{y}^{\varepsilon}$  has one (resp. two) connected component which are not singletons.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , we define
$x_{z}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{smallest $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ such that $z\in H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$}}}\right)$
(2.4)
and we note that for a fixed  $z\in\mathbbm{C}\setminus\{0\}$ ,  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  is in fact the only  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  for which  $z\in H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  (this is related to the fact that the boundaries of the cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  have zero Lebesgue measure).
For a set  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$ , we define
$\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D):=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{subgraph of $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ induced by $\{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}:H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\cap D\not=\emptyset\}$}}}\right).$
(2.5)
We write  $X^{\varepsilon}$  for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
For  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , we define
$\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{conditional law given $(h,\eta)$ of $X^{\varepsilon}$ started from $X_{0}^{\varepsilon}=x$}}}\right)$
(2.6)
and we write  $\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for the corresponding expectation.
For  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$ , we define
$\tau_{D}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{first exit time of $X^{\varepsilon}$ from $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$}}}\right).$
(2.7)
Since  $h|_{B_{1}}$  agrees in law with the corresponding restriction of a whole-plane GFF plus  $\gamma\log|\cdot|^{-1}$ , it will be convenient in most of our arguments to restrict attention to a proper subdomain of  $B_{1}$ .
Consequently, throughout the paper we fix  $\rho\in(0,1)$  and work primarily in  $B_{\rho}$ .
We will frequently need the following estimate for the Euclidean diameters of space-filling SLE cells.
Lemma 2.4 (Cell diameter estimates).
Fix a small parameter  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ . With polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the Euclidean diameters of the cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which intersect  $B_{\rho}$  satisfy
$\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2-\gamma)^{2}}+\zeta}\leq\operatorname{diam}H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\leq\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2+\gamma)^{2}}-\zeta},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(2.8)
Proof.
The upper bound for cell diameters is proven in [GMS19, Lemma 2.7].
To get the lower bound, use Lemma A.1 with  $\delta=\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2-\gamma)^{2}}+\zeta}$ , which implies that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , each Euclidean ball of radius  $\varepsilon^{\frac{2}{(2-\gamma)^{2}}+\zeta}$  contained in  $\mathbbm{D}$  has  $\mu_{h}$ -mass at most  $\varepsilon$ .
If this is the case then no such Euclidean ball can contain one of the cells  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  (since each such cell has  $\mu_{h}$ -mass  $\varepsilon$ ).
∎
3 Green’s function, effective resistance, and Harnack inequalities
3.1 Definitions of Dirichlet energy, Green’s function, and effective resistance
In this subsection we review some mostly standard notions in the theory of electrical networks and fix some notation.
Definition 3.1.
For a graph  $G$  and a function  $f:\mathcal{V}(G)\to\mathbbm{R}$ , we define its Dirichlet energy to be the sum over unoriented edges
$\operatorname{Energy}(f;G):=\sum_{\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))^{2},$
with edges of multiplicity  $m$  counted  $m$  times.
Definition 3.2.
For a graph  $G$ , a set of vertices  $V\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$ , and two vertices  $x,y\in G$ , we define the Green’s function for random walk on  $G$  killed upon exiting  $V$  by
$\operatorname{Gr}_{V}(x,y):=\mathbbm{E}_{x}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{number of times that $X$ hits $y$ before leaving $V$}}}\right]$
(3.1)
where  $\mathbbm{E}_{x}$  denotes the expectation for random walk on  $G$  started from  $x$ .
Note that  $\operatorname{Gr}_{V}(x,y)=0$  if either  $x$  or  $y$  is not in  $V$ .
We also define the normalized Green’s function
$\operatorname{gr}_{V}(x,y):=\frac{\operatorname{Gr}_{V}^{G}(x,y)}{\operatorname{deg}(y)}.$
(3.2)
By, e.g., [LP16, Proposition 2.1], the function  $\operatorname{gr}_{V}(x,\cdot)$  is the voltage function when a unit of current flows from  $x$  to  $V$ . In particular,  $\operatorname{gr}_{V}(x,\cdot)$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus(V\cup\{x\})$ .
To define effective resistance, we view a graph  $G$  as an electrical network where each edge has unit resistance.
For a vertex  $x\in\mathcal{V}(G)$  and a set  $Z\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$  with  $x\notin Z$ , the effective resistance from  $x$  to  $Z$  in  $G$  is defined (using Definition 3.2) by
$\displaystyle\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow Z}}\right):=\operatorname{gr}_{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus Z}(x,x),$
(3.3)
i.e.,  $\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow Z}}\right)$  is the expected number of times that random walk started at  $x$  returns to  $x$  before hitting  $Z$ , divided by the degree of  $x$ .
For two disjoint vertex sets  $W,Z\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$ , we define  $\mathcal{R}(W\leftrightarrow Z)$  to be the effective resistance from  $\overline{w}$  to  $Z$  in the graph  $\overline{G}$  obtained from  $G$  by identifying all of the vertices of  $W$  to a single vertex  $\overline{w}$ .
There are several equivalent definitions of effective resistance which will be useful for our purposes.
1.
Dirichlet’s principle. Let  $\mathfrak{f}=\mathfrak{f}_{Z,x}:\mathcal{V}(G)\rightarrow[0,1]$  be the function such that  $\mathfrak{f}(x)=1$ ,  $\mathfrak{f}|_{Z}\equiv 0$ , and  $\mathfrak{f}$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus(Z\cup\{x\})$ . Then (see, e.g., [LP16, Exercise 2.13])
$\mathcal{R}^{G}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow Z}}\right)=\frac{1}{\operatorname{Energy}(\mathfrak{f};G)}.$
(3.4)
2.
Thomson’s principle. A unit flow from  $x$  to  $Z$  in  $G$  is a function  $\theta$  from oriented edges  $e=(y,z)$  of  $G$  to  $\mathbbm{R}$  such that  $\theta(y,z)=-\theta(z,y)$  for each oriented edge  $(y,z)$  of  $G$  and
$\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\mathcal{V}(G)\\
z\sim y\end{subarray}}\theta(y,z)=0\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus(\{x\}\cup Z)\quad\operatorname{and}\quad\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}z\in\mathcal{V}(G)\\
z\sim x\end{subarray}}\theta(x,z)=1.$
One has (see, e.g., [LPW09, Theorem 9.10] or [LP16, Page 35])
$\mathcal{R}^{G}(x\leftrightarrow V)=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}(G)}[\theta(e)]^{2}:\text{$\theta$ is a unit flow from $x$ to $Z$}}}\right\}.$
(3.5)
Notation 3.3.
In the case when  $G=\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  is the mated-CRT map, we will typically include a superscript  $\varepsilon$  in the above notations, so, e.g.,  $\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}$  denotes effective resistance on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
We will commonly apply the above definitions in the case when the vertex sets  $V,Z,W$  are of the form  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A)$  for some set  $A\subset\mathbbm{C}$ .
To lighten notation we will simply write  $A$  instead of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A)$ .
So, for example,  $\operatorname{Gr}_{A}^{\varepsilon}$  denotes the Green’s function for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  killed upon exiting  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A)$ .
3.2 Comparison of Green’s function and effective resistance
The results of [GMS19, GM21] give us good control on effective resistances in the mated-CRT map.
In this subsection we will prove a general lemma which allows us to convert estimates for effective resistance to estimates for the Green’s function.
To state the lemma, we first introduce some notation.
For a graph  $G$  and a set  $A\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$ , we write
$\partial A:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in A:\text{$\exists y\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A$ with $x\sim y$}}}\right\}.$
(3.6)
We also write
$\overline{A}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{subgraph of $G$ induced by $A\cup\partial(\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A)$}}}\right).$
(3.7)
The following lemma bounds the maximum and minimum of the Green’s function on  $\partial A$  in terms of effective resistances.
It will be used in conjunction with Lemma 3.9 to get a uniform bound for the Green’s function on  $\partial A$ .
Lemma 3.4.
Let  $G$  be a finite graph and let  $A\subset B\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$  be a finite sets of vertices.
Let  $x\in A$  and define (using the notation of Definition 3.2)
$a:=\min_{y\in\partial A}\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y),\quad b:=\max_{y\in\partial A}\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y),\quad\delta:=\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{|\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u)-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v)|:u,v\in B,u\sim v}}\right\}.$
(3.8)
Then for any  $x\in A$ ,
$\frac{a^{2}}{a+\delta}\leq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(A\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)\leq b+\delta.$
(3.9)
Lemma 3.4 is a discrete version of [Gri99, Proposition 4.1], and is proven in a similar manner.
It can be checked that the error term  $\delta$  in Lemma 3.4 is at most 1; see Lemma 3.7.
This is the only bound for  $\delta$  which is needed for our purposes.
To prove Lemma 3.4, we need some preparatory lemmas.
Lemma 3.5.
Let  $G$  be a graph, let  $x\in G$ , and let  $A\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$  be a finite set of vertices with  $x\in A$ .
If  $\theta$  is a unit flow from  $x$  to  $Z\subset\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A$ , then
$\sum\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\theta(u,v):u\in A,v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A,u\sim v}}\right\}=1.$
Proof.
Since  $\theta$  is a unit flow, we have  $\sum_{v\sim x}\theta(x,v)=1$  and for any  $y\in A\setminus\{x\}$ ,  $\sum_{v\sim y}\theta(y,v)=0$ .
Therefore,
$\sum_{u\in A}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\\
v\sim u\end{subarray}}\theta(u,v)=1.$
We can break up the double sum on the left into two parts: the sum over the pairs  $(u,v)\in A\times A$  with  $u\sim v$  and the sum over the pairs  $(u,v)\in A\times(\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A)$  with  $u\sim v$ . The first sum is zero since  $\theta(u,v)=-\theta(v,u)$  for every  $u,v\in A$ .
Therefore the second sum is equal to 1.
∎
Lemma 3.6 (Discrete Green’s identity).
Let  $G$  be a graph, let  $A\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$  be a finite set of vertices, let  $f,\mathfrak{g}:\mathcal{V}(G)\rightarrow\mathbbm{R}$  and suppose that  $\mathfrak{g}$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A$ . Then
$\sum_{\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))=-\sum_{x\in A}f(x)\Delta\mathfrak{g}(x),$
(3.10)
where  $\Delta$  is the discrete Laplacian and the sum is over all unoriented edges of  $G$ .
Proof.
Write  $\mathcal{E}^{\shortrightarrow}$  for the set of oriented edges of  $G$ . We have
$\displaystyle\sum_{\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))$
$\displaystyle\qquad=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{E}^{\shortrightarrow}(G)}(f(x)-f(y))(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))$
$\displaystyle\qquad=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{E}^{\shortrightarrow}(G)}f(x)(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{E}^{\shortrightarrow}(G)}f(y)(\mathfrak{g}(y)-\mathfrak{g}(x))$
$\displaystyle\qquad=\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}(G)}f(x)\sum_{y\sim x}(\mathfrak{g}(x)-\mathfrak{g}(y))$
$\displaystyle\qquad=-\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}(G)}f(x)\Delta\mathfrak{g}(x)=-\sum_{x\in A}f(x)\Delta\mathfrak{g}(x),$
where in the last inequality we used that  $\Delta\mathfrak{g}=0$  on  $\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A$ .
∎
Proof of Lemma 3.4.
For  $c>0$ , let
$F_{c}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{y\in B:\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y)\geq c}}\right\},\quad\forall c\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[0,\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,x)}}\right].$
(3.11)
Note that each  $F_{c}$  contains  $x$ ,  $F_{c}$  is non-increasing in  $c$ , and  $F_{0}=B$ .
We claim that with  $a,b$  as in the lemma statement, we have  $F_{b^{\prime}}\subset A\subset F_{a}$  for each  $b^{\prime}>b$ .
Indeed, since  $\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,\cdot)$  is discrete harmonic on  $B\setminus A$  and vanishes outside of  $B$ , its maximum value on  $B\setminus A$  is by the maximum principle at most its maximum value on  $\partial A$ , which is  $b$ . Hence  $F_{b^{\prime}}\cap(B\setminus A)=\emptyset$  for  $b^{\prime}>b$ , i.e.,  $F_{b^{\prime}}\subset A$ .
Similarly, since  $\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,\cdot)$  is discrete harmonic on  $A\setminus\{x\}$  and attains its maximum value at  $x$  (again by the maximum principle, on all of  $B$ ), its minimum value on  $A$  is the same as its minimum value on  $\partial A$ , which is  $a$ . Hence  $A\subset F_{a}$ .
In particular, by Rayleigh’s monotonicity principle (see Chapter 2.4 in [LP16]),
$\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{a}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)\leq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(A\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)\leq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{b^{\prime}}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right).$
(3.12)
We claim that
$\frac{c^{2}}{c+\delta}\leq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{c}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)\leq c+\delta,\quad\forall c\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,x)}}\right].$
(3.13)
Once (3.13) is established, (3.9) follows from (3.12) upon letting  $b^{\prime}$  decrease to  $b$ .
It remains to prove (3.13).
To this end, consider the function  $\mathfrak{f}(y):=c^{-1}\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y)$ . Then  $\mathfrak{f}$  is discrete harmonic on  $B\setminus\{x\}$ , it vanishes outside of  $B$ , its values on  $F_{c}$  are at least 1, and its values on  $\partial F_{c}$  are at most  $(c+\delta)/c$ .
We first argue that
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f};\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)^{-1}\leq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{c}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)\leq c^{2}\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f};\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right).$
(3.14)
Indeed, the function  $\mathfrak{f}\wedge 1$  vanishes outside of  $B$  and is identically equal to 1 on  $F_{c}$ .
By Dirichlet’s principle (3.4),
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f};\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)\geq\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}\wedge 1;\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)\geq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{c}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right)^{-1}.$
(3.15)
Recalling that  $\mathfrak{f}(y):=c^{-1}\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y)$ , we have that  $\theta(u,v):=c(\mathfrak{f}(u)-\mathfrak{f}(v))$  is a unit flow from  $x$  to  $B\setminus\mathcal{V}(G)$  (here we use that the gradient of  $\operatorname{gr}(x,\cdot)$  is a unit flow [LP16, Proposition 2.1]).
By Lemma 3.5,
$\sum\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\theta(u,v):u\in F_{c},v\in B\setminus F_{c},u\sim v}}\right\}=1.$
(3.16)
Hence  $\theta|_{\mathcal{E}(\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}})}$  is a unit flow from  $\partial F_{c}$  to  $\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B$ .
By Thomson’s principle (3.5),
$c^{2}\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f};\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)=\sum_{\{u,v\}\in\mathcal{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)}[\theta(u,v)]^{2}\geq\mathcal{R}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(F_{c}\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B}}\right).$
(3.17)
From (3.15) and (3.17), we obtain (3.14).
We now need to bound  $\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f};\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)$ .
By Lemma 3.6 applied to the graph  $\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}$ , the vertex set  $\partial F_{c}$ , and the functions  $f=\mathfrak{g}=\mathfrak{f}$ ,
$\displaystyle\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f};\overline{\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}}}}\right)$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{u\in\partial F_{c}}\mathfrak{f}(u)\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c},u\sim v}(\mathfrak{f}(u)-\mathfrak{f}(v))$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{c+\delta}{c}\sum\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\mathfrak{f}(u)-\mathfrak{f}(v):u\in F_{c},v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c},u\sim v}}\right\}\quad\text{(recall $\mathfrak{f}\leq\frac{c+\delta}{c}$ on $\partial F_{c}$)}$
$\displaystyle\leq\frac{c+\delta}{c^{2}},\quad\text{by~\eqref{eqn-green-unit-flow}}.$
(3.18)
Plugging (3.18) into (3.14) gives (3.13).
∎
The following crude estimate is useful when applying Lemma 3.4.
Lemma 3.7.
In the setting of Lemma 3.7, we have  $\delta\leq 1$ .
Proof.
Consider an edge  $\{u_{0},v_{0}\}\in\mathcal{E}(G)$  with  $\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u_{0})>\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v_{0})$ .
We need to show that  $\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u_{0})-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v_{0})\leq 1$ .
To this end, let  $c=\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u_{0})$  and let  $F_{c}=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{y\in B:\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,y)\geq c}}\right\}$ , as in (3.11).
Then  $u_{0}\in F_{c}$  and  $v_{0}\notin F_{c}$ .
Since  $\theta(u,v):=\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u)-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v)$  is a unit flow from  $x$  to  $\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus B$  and  $x\in F_{c}$ , we can apply Lemma 3.5 to get that
$\sum\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u)-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v):u\in F_{c},v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c},u\sim v}}\right\}=1.$
(3.19)
For each  $u\in F_{c}$  and each  $v\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus F_{c}$ , we have  $\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u)-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v)\geq 0$ .
Therefore, each term in the sum (3.19) is at most 1.
In particular,  $\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,u_{0})-\operatorname{gr}_{B}(x,v_{0})\leq 1$ .
∎
3.3 Harnack inequality for the mated-CRT map
Lemma 3.4 gives an upper (resp. lower) bound for the minimum (resp. maximum) value of the Green’s function on  $\partial A$  in terms of effective resistances.
It is of course much more useful to have an upper (resp. lower) bound for the maximum (resp. minimum) value of the Green’s function on  $\partial A$ .
Hence we need a Harnack-type estimate which allows us to compare the maximum and minimum values of the Green’s function on  $\partial A$ .
In this subsection we will prove such an estimate for the mated-CRT map  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  in the case when  $A$  is the set of vertices which intersect a Euclidean ball.
Throughout this subsection we assume the setup and notation of Section 2.3.
In particular we recall that for  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ ,  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  is chosen so that  $z$  is contained in the cell  $H_{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}$  and for  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$ ,  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  is the subgraph of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  induced by the vertex set  $\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}:z\in D\}$ .
We also recall that  $\rho\in(0,1)$  is fixed.
Proposition 3.8 (Harnack inequality on a circle).
