There exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that the following holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
Simultaneously for every  $z\in B_{\rho}$ , every  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]$ , and every function  $\mathfrak{f}:\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow[0,\infty)$  which is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{3s}(z))\setminus\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$ ,
$\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\mathfrak{f}(y)\leq C\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\mathfrak{f}(y).$
(3.20)
The reason why we do not require that  $\mathfrak{f}$  is discrete harmonic at the center point  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  is that we eventually want to apply Proposition 3.8 with  $\mathfrak{f}$  equal to the normalized Green’s function  $\operatorname{gr}_{U}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},\cdot)$  for  $B_{3s}(z)\subset U\subset B_{\rho}$  (recall Notation 3.3).
The key input in the proof of Proposition 3.8 is the following coupling lemma for random walks on a graph with different starting points, which follows from Wilson’s algorithm and is a variant of [GMS19, Lemma 3.12].
Lemma 3.9.
Let  $G$  be a connected graph and let  $A\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$  be a set such that the simple random walk started from any vertex of  $G$  a.s. hits  $A$  in finite time.
For  $x\in\mathcal{V}(G)$ , let  $X^{x}$  be the simple random walk started from  $x$  and let  $\tau^{x}$  be the first time  $X^{x}$  hits  $A$ .
For  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}(G)\setminus A$ , there is a coupling of  $X^{x}$  and  $X^{y}$  such that a.s.
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X^{x}_{\tau^{x}}=X^{y}_{\tau^{y}}\,\Big|\,X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}}}\right]\geq\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$X^{x}$ disconnects $y$ from $A$ before time $\tau^{x}$}}}\right].$
(3.21)
Proof.
The lemma is a consequence of Wilson’s algorithm.
Let  $T$  be the uniform spanning tree of  $G$  with all of the vertices of  $A$  wired to a single point. For  $x\in\mathcal{V}(G)$ , let  $L^{x}$  be the unique path in  $T$  from  $x$  to  $A$ .
For a path  $P$  in  $G$ , write  $\operatorname{LE}(P)$  for its chronological loop erasure.
By Wilson’s algorithm [Wil96], we can generate the union  $L^{x}\cup L^{y}$  in the following manner.
1.
Run  $X^{y}$  until time  $\tau^{y}$  and generate the loop erasure  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})$ .
2.
Conditional on  $X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}$ , run  $X^{x}$  until the first time  $\widetilde{\tau}^{x}$  that it hits either  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})$  or  $A$ .
3.
Set  $L^{x}\cup L^{y}=\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})\cup\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\widetilde{\tau}^{x}]})$ .
Note that  $L^{y}=\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})$  in the above procedure.
Applying the above procedure with the roles of  $x$  and  $y$  interchanged shows that  $L^{x}\overset{d}{=}\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\tau^{x}]})$ .
When we construct  $L^{x}\cup L^{y}$  as above, the points where  $L^{x}$  and  $L^{y}$  hit  $A$  coincide provided  $X^{x}$  hits  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})$  before  $A$ .
The conditional probability given  $X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}$  that  $X^{x}$  hits  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})$  before  $A$  is at least the unconditional probability that  $X^{x}$  disconnects  $y$  from  $A$  before time  $\tau^{x}$ . We thus obtain a coupling of  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\tau^{x}]})$  and  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]})$  such that the conditional probability given  $X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]}$  that these two loop erasures hit  $A$  at the same point is at least  $\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$X^{x}$ disconnects $y$ from $A$ before time $\tau^{x}$}}}\right]$ . We now obtain (3.21) by observing that  $X^{x}_{\tau^{x}}$  is the same as the point where  $\operatorname{LE}(X^{x}|_{[0,\tau^{x}]})$  first hits  $A$ , and similarly with  $y$  in place of  $x$ .
∎
In light of Lemma 3.9, to prove Proposition 3.8 we need a lower bound for the probability that the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  disconnects a circle from  $\partial B_{\rho}$  before exiting  $B_{\rho}$ .
Lemma 3.10.
There exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $p=p(\rho,\gamma)\in(0,1)$  such that the following is true.
Let  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and let  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ .
With polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , uniformly in the choices of  $z$  and  $s$ ,
$\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}\setminus B_{s/2})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\bigg[\text{$X$ disconnects $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbbm{A}_{s/2,s}(z))$ from $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial\mathbbm{A}_{s/4,2s}(z))$}$
$\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{before hitting $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial\mathbbm{A}_{s/4,2s}(z))$}\bigg]\geq p.$
(3.22)
Proof.
This follows from [GMS19, Proposition 3.6].
∎
We now upgrade Lemma 3.10 to a statement which holds simultaneously for all choices of  $z$  and  $s$  via a union bound argument.
Lemma 3.11.
There exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $p=p(\rho,\gamma)\in(0,1)$  such that the following is true.
With polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for every  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and every  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$  that
$\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\bigg[\text{$X$ disconnects $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))$ from $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{3s}(z))}}\right)\cup\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$}$
$\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{before hitting $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{3s}(z))}}\right)\cup\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$}\bigg]\geq p.$
(3.23)
Proof.
By Lemma 3.10, there exists  $\beta_{0}=\beta_{0}(\gamma)>0$ ,  $\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{0}(\gamma)>0$ , and  $p=p(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and each  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta_{0}},\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ , the estimate (3.22) holds with probability  $1-O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{\alpha_{0}})$ , uniformly in the choices of  $z$  and  $s$ .
Let  $\beta:=\frac{1}{100}\min\{\beta_{0},\alpha_{0}\}$ .
We can find a collection  $\mathcal{Z}$  of at most  $O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{-4\beta})$  points  $z\in B_{\rho}$  such that each point of  $B_{\rho}$  lies within Euclidean distance  $\varepsilon^{2\beta}$  of some  $z\in\mathcal{Z}$ .
Due to our choice of  $\beta$ , we can take a union bound over all  $z\in\mathcal{Z}$  and all  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]\cap\{2^{-n/2}\}$  to find that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , (3.22) holds simultaneously for every such  $z$  and  $s$ .
Due to our choice of  $\mathcal{Z}$ , if  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\rho/2]$  with  $B_{3s}(z)\subset B_{\rho}$ , then there exists  $z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}$  and  $s^{\prime}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]\cap\{2^{-n/2}\}$  such that
$\partial B_{s}(z)\subset\mathbbm{A}_{s^{\prime}/2,s^{\prime}}(z^{\prime})\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbbm{A}_{s^{\prime}/4,2s^{\prime}}(z)\subset B_{3s}(z)\setminus\{z\}.$
The estimate (3.23) for  $(z,s)$  therefore follows from (3.22) for  $(z^{\prime},s^{\prime})$ .
∎
Proof of Proposition 3.8.
By Lemma 3.11, it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that (3.23) holds simultaneously for every  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ .
We henceforth assume that this is the case and work under the conditional law given  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Fix  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ .
For  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , we let  $X^{x}$  be the simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  and we let  $\tau^{x}$  be the first time that  $X^{x}$  either exits  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{3s}(z))$  or hits  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$ .
It follows from (3.23) that the conditional probability given  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  that  $X^{x}$  disconnects  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))$  from  $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{3s}(z))}}\right)\cup\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$  before time  $\tau^{x}$  is at least  $p$ .
By this and Lemma 3.9, if  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))$  we can couple the random walks  $X^{x}$  and  $X^{y}$  in such a way that a.s.
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{\tau^{x}}^{x}=X^{y}_{\tau^{y}}\,|\,X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]},\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq p.$
(3.24)
If  $\mathfrak{f}:\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow[0,\infty)$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{3s}(z))\setminus\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$ , then
$\displaystyle\mathfrak{f}(x)=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathfrak{f}(X_{\tau^{x}})\,|\,\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathfrak{f}(X_{\tau^{x}})\,|\,X^{y}|_{[0,\tau^{y}]},\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\,|\,\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq p\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathfrak{f}(X_{\tau^{y}})\,|\,\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]=p\mathfrak{f}(y).$
(3.25)
Choosing  $x$  (resp.  $y$ ) so that  $\mathfrak{f}$  attains its minimum (resp. maximum) value on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))$  at  $x$  (resp.  $y$ ) now gives (3.20) with  $C=1/p$ .
∎
4 Lower bound for exit times
In this subsection we prove a lower bound for the quenched expected exit time of the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from a Euclidean ball.
We continue to work in the setting of Section 2.3.
We recall in particular the notation  $\tau_{D}^{\varepsilon}$  from (2.7) for (roughly speaking) the exit time of random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$ .
Proposition 4.1.
There exists  $\omega=\omega(\gamma)>0$  and  $c=c(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (at a rate depending on  $\rho,\gamma$ ), the following is true.
Simultaneously for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\varepsilon^{\omega}})$  and each  $r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\omega},\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ ,
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq\varepsilon^{-1}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{cr}(\eta(x))}}\right).$
(4.1)
Note that
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(\eta(x))}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$
(4.2)
where  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}$  is the Green’s function as in Notation 3.3.
Hence to prove Proposition 4.1 we need a lower bound for this Green’s function.
We will obtain such a lower bound using Lemma 3.4 and Proposition 3.8.
We first establish a lower bound for the effective resistance in  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  across a Euclidean annulus in Section 4.1 using Dirichlet’s principle (3.4) and bounds for the Dirichlet energies of discrete harmonic functions on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from [GMS19].
Due to Lemma 3.4, this gives us a lower bound for the maximum value of  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}(x,\cdot)$  over all vertices  $y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  whose corresponding cells intersects a specified Euclidean circle centered at  $\eta(x)$ .
We will then use Proposition 3.8 to upgrade this to a uniform lower bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}(x,\cdot)$ .
4.1 Lower bound for effective resistance
Let  $\omega>0$  be an exponent to be chosen later, in a manner depending only on  $\gamma$ . To lighten notation, for  $\varepsilon>0$  we let  $\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}=\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}(\omega,\rho)$  be the set of triples  $(z,r,s)\in\mathbbm{C}\times[0,\infty)\times[0,\infty)$  such that
$z\in B_{\rho-\varepsilon^{\omega}},\quad r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\omega},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right],\quad\text{and}\quad s\in[0,r/3].$
(4.3)
We also let  $\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}$  denote the effective resistance on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Lemma 4.2.
There exists  $\omega=\omega(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (at a rate depending on  $\rho,\gamma$ ),
$\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{r}(z)}}\right)\geq\frac{1}{C}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left((r/s)\wedge\varepsilon^{-1}}}\right),\quad\forall(z,r,s)\in\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}.$
(4.4)
Due to Dirichlet’s principle, Lemma 4.2 will follow from the following upper bound for the Dirichlet energy of certain harmonic functions on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Lemma 4.3.
There exists  $\omega=\omega(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (at a rate depending on  $\rho,\gamma$ ) that the following is true.
For each  $(z,r,s)\in\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}$ ,
let  $\mathfrak{f}^{\varepsilon}_{z,r,s}:\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow[0,1]$  be the function which is equal to 1 on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$ , is equal to zero outside of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))$ , and is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$ .
Then (in the notation of Definition 3.1)
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}^{\varepsilon}_{z,r,s};\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\frac{C}{\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left((r/s)\wedge\varepsilon^{-1}}}\right)},\quad\forall(z,r,s)\in\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}.$
(4.5)
Proof.
The main input in the proof is [GMS21, Proposition 4.4], which allows us to upper-bound the discrete Dirichlet energy of a discrete harmonic function on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  in terms of the Dirichlet energy of the continuum harmonic function on  $\mathbbm{C}$  with the same boundary data.
This estimate is applied in Step 1. The rest of the proof consists of union bound arguments which are needed to make (4.5) hold for all  $(z,r,s)\in\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}$  simultaneously.
Step 1: comparing discrete and continuum Dirichlet energy.
Let  $\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{\varepsilon}$  be defined as in (4.3) except with  $\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{\omega}$  in place of  $\varepsilon^{\omega}$  and  $r/2$  in place of  $r/3$ .
We first prove an estimate for a fixed choice of  $(z,r,s)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{\varepsilon}$ .
The reason for working with  $\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{\varepsilon}$  instead of  $\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}$  initially is that we will have to increase the parameters slightly in the union bound argument.
Let  $\mathfrak{g}_{z,r,s}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow[0,1]$  be the function which is equal to 1 on  $B_{s}(z)$ , is equal to 0 outside of  $B_{r}(z)$ , and is harmonic on the interior of  $B_{r}(z)\setminus B_{s}(z)$ .
That is,
$\mathfrak{g}_{z,r,s}(w)=\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\frac{\log(|w-z|/r)}{\log(s/r)},0}}\right\}.$
(4.6)
A direct calculation shows that the continuum Dirichlet energy of  $\mathfrak{g}_{z,r,s}$
is
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{g}_{z,r,s};B_{r}(z)\setminus B_{s}(z)}}\right)=\int_{B_{r}(z)\setminus B_{s}(z)}|\nabla\mathfrak{g}_{z,r,s}|^{2}=\frac{4\pi}{\log(r/s)}.$
Furthermore, the modulus of each of  $\mathfrak{g}_{z,r,s}$  and each of its first and second order partial derivatives is bounded above by a universal constant times  $s^{-2}(\log(r/s))^{-1}\leq s^{-2}(\log 2)^{-1}$  on  $B_{r}(z)\setminus B_{s}(z)$ .
Consequently, we can apply [GMS19, Theorem 3.2] to find that there exists  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0$ ,  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$ , and  $C_{1}=C_{1}(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that the following is true. If we take  $\omega\leq\beta/2$ , say, then for each fixed choice of  $(z,r,s)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{\varepsilon}$  such that  $s\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}$ , it holds with probability at least  $1-O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{\alpha})$  that
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,s}^{\varepsilon};\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\frac{C_{1}}{\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r/s}}\right)}.$
(4.7)
Note that we absorbed the  $\varepsilon^{\alpha}$  error in [GMS19, Theorem 3.2] into the main term  $C_{1}/\log(r/s)$ , which we can do since  $r/s\leq\varepsilon^{-\beta}$  and hence  $1/\log(r/s)\geq\beta/(\log\varepsilon^{-1})$ .
Step 2: transferring to a bound for all choices of  $z,r,s$  simultaneously.
Let  $\omega:=\frac{1}{100}\min\{\alpha,\beta\}$ . By a union bound over  $O_{\varepsilon}(\varepsilon^{8\omega}(\log\varepsilon^{-1})^{2})$  choices of  $(z,r,s)$ , we get that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the estimate (4.7) holds simultaneously for each
$(z,r,s)\in\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}^{\varepsilon}\quad\text{such that}\quad z\in B_{\rho}\cap(\varepsilon^{4\omega}\mathbbm{Z}^{2}),\quad r,s\in\{2^{-n}\}_{n\in\mathbbm{N}},\quad s\geq\varepsilon^{2\omega}/2.$
(4.8)
Henceforth assume that this is the case.
Let  $(z,r,s)\in\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}$  with  $s\geq\varepsilon^{2\omega}$ . Since  $r\geq\varepsilon^{\omega}$  by (4.3), if  $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$  is small enough (how small depends only on  $\rho,\gamma$ ) we can find  $(z^{\prime},r^{\prime},s^{\prime})$  satisfying the conditions in (4.8) such that
$B_{r^{\prime}}(z^{\prime})\subset B_{r}(z),\quad B_{s}(z)\subset B_{s^{\prime}}(z^{\prime}),\quad r^{\prime}\in[r/2,2r],\quad\text{and}\quad s^{\prime}\in[s/2,2s].$
(4.9)
By (4.9), the function  $\mathfrak{f}^{\varepsilon}_{z^{\prime},r^{\prime},s^{\prime}}$  is equal to zero on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$  and vanishes outside of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))$ .
Since the discrete harmonic function  $\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,s}^{\varepsilon}$  minimizes discrete Dirichlet energy subject to these conditions, it follows from (4.7) for  $z^{\prime},r^{\prime},s^{\prime}$  that
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,s}^{\varepsilon};\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}^{\varepsilon}_{z^{\prime},r^{\prime},s^{\prime}};\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\frac{C_{1}}{\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r^{\prime}/s^{\prime}}}\right)}\leq\frac{C_{2}}{\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r/s}}\right)},$
(4.10)
where  $C_{2}=100C_{1}$ , say.
Step 3: the case when  $s$  is small.
We have only proven (4.10) in the case when  $s\geq\varepsilon^{2\omega}$ . We now need to remove this constraint.
To this end, we observe that for each  $(z,r,s)\in\mathcal{Z}^{\varepsilon}$  with  $s\leq\varepsilon^{2\omega}$ , the function  $\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,\varepsilon^{2\omega}}^{\varepsilon}$  is equal to 1 on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$  and is equal to zero outside of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))$ .
Since  $\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,s}^{\varepsilon}$  minimizes discrete Dirichlet energy subject to these conditions, we infer from (4.10) with  $\varepsilon^{2\omega}$  in place of  $s$  that
$\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,s}^{\varepsilon};\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\operatorname{Energy}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,\varepsilon^{2\omega}};\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\frac{(2\omega)^{-1}C_{2}}{\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\varepsilon^{-1}}}\right)}.$
(4.11)
Combining (4.10) and (4.11) gives (4.5) with  $C=(2\omega)^{-1}C_{2}$ .
∎
Proof of Lemma 4.2.
By Dirichlet’s principle (3.4), the discrete Dirichlet energy of the function  $\mathfrak{f}_{z,r,s}^{\varepsilon}$  of Lemma 4.3 equals  $\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{r}(z)}}\right)^{-1}$ . Hence Lemma 4.2 follows from Lemma 4.3.
∎
4.2 Lower bound for the Green’s function
We now use Lemma 4.3 together with the results of Section 3 to prove a lower bound for the Green’s function on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Lemma 4.4.
There exists  $\omega=\omega(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that the following holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (at a rate depending on  $\rho,\gamma$ ).
For each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\varepsilon^{\omega}})$  and each  $r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\omega},\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ ,
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq C^{-1}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{r}{|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|}\wedge\varepsilon^{-1}}}\right)-1,\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r/3}(\eta(x)).$
(4.12)
Proof.
Let  $\omega_{0}=\omega_{0}(\gamma)>0$  be the exponent  $\omega$  from Lemma 4.2, let  $\beta$  be as in Proposition 3.8, and let  $\omega:=\frac{1}{2}\min\{\omega_{0},\beta\}$ .
The function  $y\mapsto\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(z)}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))\setminus\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$ .
We can therefore apply Proposition 3.8 to find that there exists  $C_{1}=C_{1}(\rho,\gamma)>1$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho-\varepsilon^{\omega}}$ , each  $r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\omega},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]$ , and each  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},r/3}}\right]$  that
$\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(z)}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)\leq C_{1}\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(z)}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y).$
(4.13)
By Lemma 3.4 (applied with  $A=\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$  and  $B=\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))$ ) and Lemma 3.7 (to say that the error term  $\delta$  from Lemma 3.4 is at most 1), a.s. for every such  $z$ ,  $r$ , and  $s$ ,44
4
We note that  $\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$ , in the notation (3.6), is contained in  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))$  but the inclusion could be strict since there could be cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which intersect  $\partial B_{s}(z)$  but which do not intersect any cells which are contained in  $\mathbbm{C}\setminus B_{s}(z)$ . However, all we need is that the maximum of  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(z)}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)$  over  $y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))$  is bounded below by the maximum over  $\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$ .
$\displaystyle\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(z)}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)\geq\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{r}(z)}}\right)-1.$
(4.14)
By Lemma 4.2, there exists  $C_{2}=C_{2}(\rho,\gamma)>1$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds for each  $z$ ,  $r$ , and  $s$  as above that
$\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{r}(z)}}\right)\geq C_{2}^{-1}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(r/s}}\right).$
(4.15)
We now apply (4.15) to lower-bound the right side of (4.14), then use this to lower-bound the left side of (4.13). This shows that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds for each  $z\in B_{\rho-\varepsilon^{\omega}}$ , each  $r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\omega},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]$ , and each  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},r/3}}\right]$  that
$\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(z)}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)\geq C_{1}^{-1}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C_{2}^{-1}\log(r/s)-1}}\right)\geq(C_{1}C_{2})^{-1}\log(r/s)-1.$
(4.16)
Setting  $z=\eta(x)$  and  $s=|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|$  in (4.16) gives (4.12) with  $C=C_{1}C_{2}$  in the special case when  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}$ .
In the case when  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|<\varepsilon^{\beta}$ , we use the maximum principle for the discrete harmonic function  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,\cdot)$ , followed by (4.16), to get
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq\min_{y^{\prime}:|\eta(x)-\eta(y^{\prime})|=\varepsilon^{\beta}}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y^{\prime})\geq(C_{1}C_{2})^{-1}\log\varepsilon^{\omega-\beta}-1.$
(4.17)
We thus obtain (4.12) with  $C=(C_{1}C_{2})^{-1}(\beta-\omega)$ .
∎
Proof of Proposition 4.1.
By Lemma 4.4, there exists  $\omega=\omega(\gamma)>0$  and  $C_{0}=C_{0}(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds for each  $x$  and  $r$  as in the proposition statement that
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq C_{0}^{-1}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{r}{|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|}\wedge\varepsilon^{-1}}}\right)-1,\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r/3}(\eta(x))).$
(4.18)
We now choose  $c:=\min\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{e^{-2C_{0}},1/3}}\right\}$ .
Then if  $\varepsilon<e^{-2C_{0}}$ , the first term on the right of the inequality in (4.18) is at least 2 whenever  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\leq cr$ .
Hence (4.12) implies that for each  $x$  and  $r$  as in the lemma statement,
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq 1\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{cr}(\eta(x)).$
(4.19)
Recall from Definition 3.2 that
$\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)=\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(y)\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq\operatorname{gr}_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}(x,y).$
If (4.19) holds, then for any  $x$  and  $r$  as in the lemma statement,
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(\eta(x))}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq\#\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{cr}(\eta(x))).$
(4.20)
Since each cell of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  has  $\mu_{h}$ -mass  $\varepsilon$ , we have  $\#\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{cr}(\eta(x))\geq\varepsilon^{-1}\mu_{h}(B_{cr}(\eta(x))$ .
Plugging this into (4.20) gives (4.1).
∎
5 Upper bound for exit times
In this section we will prove an upper bound for exit times from Euclidean balls for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
We will eventually use the  $L^{q}$  version of the Payley-Zygmund inequality for  $q=q(\gamma)\rightarrow\infty$  as  $\gamma\rightarrow 2$ , so we need a bound for moments of all orders.
Proposition 5.1.
There exists  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for every Borel set  $D\subset B_{\rho}$  with  $\mu_{h}(D)\geq\varepsilon^{\alpha}$  and every  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  that
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{D}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]\leq N!C^{N}\varepsilon^{-N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sup_{z\in D}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)}}\right)^{N},\quad\forall N\in\mathbbm{N}.$
(5.1)
We note that Proposition 5.1 together with a basic estimate for the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure (deferred to the appendix) implies the following simpler but less precise estimate.
Corollary 5.2.
For each  $q\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,(2-\gamma)^{2}/2}}\right)$ , it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that for every  $N\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(z))}\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{B_{\delta}(z)}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]\leq N!\varepsilon^{-N}\delta^{Nq}.$
(5.2)
Proof.
By Proposition 5.1, it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , at a rate depending on  $\delta$ , that (5.1) holds simultaneously with  $D=B_{\delta}(z)$  for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(z))$ . Note that we can apply Proposition 5.1 with  $\rho$  replaced by  $\rho^{\prime}\in(\rho,1)$  to deal with the possibility that  $B_{\delta}(z)\not\subset B_{\rho}$ .
For small enough  $\varepsilon$  (depending on  $\delta$ ) we have  $\delta+\varepsilon^{\alpha}\leq 2\delta$ , so we can bound the integral over  $B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(B_{\delta}(z))=B_{\delta+\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(z)$  in (5.1) by the integral over  $B_{2\delta}(z)$ .
Upon absorbing the factor of  $C^{N}$  in (5.1) into a small power of  $\delta$ , we have reduced our problem to showing that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\sup_{u\in B_{\delta}(z)}\int_{B_{2\delta}(z)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|u-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)\leq\delta^{q}.$
(5.3)
By Lemma A.3 (applied with  $A=(q/c_{1})\log\delta^{-1}$ ) it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that the left side of (5.3) is bounded above by a  $q,\rho,\gamma$ -dependent constant times  $(\log\delta^{-1})\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\mu_{h}(B_{2\delta}(z))+\delta^{q}$ . We now conclude (5.3) by applying Lemma A.1.
∎
The proof of Proposition 5.1 uses the same basic ideas as the proof of Proposition 4.1 except that all of the bounds go in the opposite direction.
Since  $\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{D}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]$  can be expressed in terms of the Green’s function  $\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}$  (see Lemma 5.9), we need to establish an upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}$ . In fact, we have  $\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}\leq\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}$  so we only need an upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}$ .
To prove such an upper bound, we first establish an upper bound for the effective resistance in  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from a Euclidean ball  $B_{s}(z)\subset B_{\rho}$  to  $\partial B_{\rho}$  in Section 5.1.
This is done by constructing a unit flow (via the method of random paths) and applying Thomson’s principle (3.5).
As explained in Section 5.2, this estimate together with Lemma 5.3 and Proposition 3.8 leads to an upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  in the case when  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|$  is not too small (at least some fixed small positive power of  $\varepsilon$ ).
In Section 5.3, we will establish a crude upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  which holds uniformly over all  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ , including pairs for which  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|$  is small or even  $x=y$ . This bound will be sufficient for our purposes since we will eventually sum over all  $x,y$  so the pairs for which  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|$  is small will not contribute significantly to the sum.
The proof is again based on Thomson’s principle but different estimates are involved.
In Section 5.4 we use our upper bounds for the Green’s function to establish Proposition 5.1.
5.1 Upper bound for effective resistance across an annulus
We have the following upper bound for the effective resistance from  $\partial B_{s}(z)$  to  $\partial B_{\rho}$ .
Together with Lemma 3.4 and Proposition 3.8 this will lead to an upper bound for the off-diagonal Green’s function on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Lemma 5.3.
There exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for every  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and every  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$  that
$\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)\leq C\log s^{-1}.$
(5.4)
Proof.
We will prove the lemma by constructing a unit flow  $\theta^{\varepsilon}$  from the vertex  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  to  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})$  and applying Thompson’s principle to the restriction of  $\theta^{\varepsilon}$  to  $\overline{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}$ .
The proof is similar to arguments in [GM21, Section 3.3].
We will first prove an estimate for a fixed choice of  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and  $s\in[0,\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$ , then transfer to an estimate which holds for all such  $(z,s)$  simultaneously via a union bound argument in Step 4 at the end of the proof.
Step 1: defining a unit flow.
We use the method of random paths; see, e.g., [LP16, Section 2.5, page 42] for a general discussion of this method.
For a fixed choice of  $z$ , let  $\mathbbm{u}$  be sampled uniformly from Lebesgue measure on  $\partial B_{1}(z)$ , independently from everything else.
Consider the infinite ray from  $z$  which passes though  $\mathbbm{u}$  and let  $S$  be the segment of this ray from  $z$  to a point of  $\partial B_{\rho}$ . For  $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ , choose (in some measurable manner) a simple path  $P^{\varepsilon}$  in  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(S)$  from  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  to a vertex whose corresponding cell contains the single point in  $S\cap\partial B_{\rho}$ . For an oriented edge  $e$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ , let  $\theta^{\varepsilon}(e)$  be the probability that the path  $P^{\varepsilon}$  traverses  $e$  in the forward direction, minus the probability that  $P^{\varepsilon}$  traverses  $e$  in the reverse direction.
It is easily seen that  $\theta^{\varepsilon}$  is a unit flow from  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  to  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})$  (this follows from general theory, and is checked carefully in our particular case in [GM21, Lemma 3.5]).
By Lemma 3.5, for each  $s\in[0,\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$ , the restriction of  $\theta^{\varepsilon}$  to the set of oriented edges of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  with at least one endpoint in  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$  is a unit flow from  $\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$  to  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})$  (here the boundary of a vertex set is defined as in (3.6)).
Note that each edge in this set also belongs to  $\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\mathbbm{C}\setminus B_{s}(z))$ .
By Thomson’s principle (3.5), we therefore have
$\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)\leq\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{s}(z))}[\theta^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2},\quad\forall s\in[0,\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})].$
(5.5)
Step 2: bounding the energy in terms of a sum over cells.
We now bound the right side of (5.5).
The argument is essentially the same as that of [GM21, Lemma 3.6], but we give the details for the sake of completeness.
We will bound the energy of  $\theta^{\varepsilon}$  in terms of a sum over cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which intersect  $B_{\rho}\setminus B_{s}(z)$ , which can in turn be bounded using [GMS19, Lemma 3.1].
Throughout the proof, we require all implicit constants in the symbol  $\preceq$  and the rates of all “polynomially high probability” statements to be deterministic and depend only on  $\rho$  and  $\gamma$  (not on  $z$  or  $s$ ).
By the definition of  $S$ , for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus\{x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\}$ , the conditional probability given  $(h,\eta)$  that the segment  $S$  intersects the cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  is at most a universal constant times  $\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\times\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{-1}$ , where here  $\operatorname{diam}$  and  $\operatorname{dist}$  denote Euclidean diameter and distance, respectively. By the definition of  $\theta^{\varepsilon}$ , this implies that for any edge  $\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  with  $x\not=x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$ ,
$|\theta^{\varepsilon}(x,y)|\leq\min\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\frac{\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)}{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)},\frac{\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)}{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)}}}\right\}.$
(5.6)
Now fix  $q\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,\tfrac{2}{(2+\gamma)^{2}}}}\right)$ , chosen in a manner depending only on  $\gamma$ .
By Lemma 2.4, it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that each cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  has diameter at most  $\varepsilon^{q}$ , so
$\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon},z}}\right)^{-1}\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(|\eta(x)-z|-\varepsilon^{q}}}\right)^{-1}\preceq|\eta(x)-z|^{-1},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{2\varepsilon^{q}}(z)}}\right).$
Plugging this into (5.6) shows that
$|\theta^{\varepsilon}(x,y)|\preceq|\eta(x)-z|^{-1}\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right),\quad\forall\{x,y\}\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{2\varepsilon^{q}}(z)}}\right)$
By summing this last estimate, we get that if  $\beta\in(0,q)$  and  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$  then whenever (5.6) holds and  $\varepsilon$  is sufficiently small (depending on  $\beta$  and  $q$ ),
$\displaystyle\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{s}(z))}[\theta^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}\preceq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{s}(z))}|\eta(x)-z|^{-2}\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{2}\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x).$
(5.7)
Step 3: bounding the sum over cells.
By [GMS19, Lemma 3.1], applied with  $f(w)=|w-z|^{-2}$ , there exists  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0$  and  $C_{0}=C_{0}(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that if  $\beta\in(0,q)$  is chosen sufficiently small, in a manner depending only on  $\gamma$ , then the following is true. For each  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$ , it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that the right side of (5.7) is bounded above by
$C_{0}\int_{B_{\rho}\setminus B_{s}(z)}|w-z|^{-2}\,dw+\varepsilon^{\alpha}\preceq\log s^{-1}.$
(5.8)
Since (5.7) holds simultaneously for all  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$  with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , by plugging (5.8) into (5.7) and then into (5.5), we get that the following is true. There exists  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that for each fixed  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$ , the bound (5.4) holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
Step 4: transferring to a bound for all  $(z,s)$  simultaneously.
We observe that if  $B_{s}(z)\subset B_{s^{\prime}}(z^{\prime})\subset B_{\rho}$ , then
$\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s^{\prime}}(z^{\prime})\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)\leq\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right).$
(5.9)
After possibly shrinking  $\beta$  so that it is much smaller than the exponent in the “polynomially high probability” statement at the end of the last step, we can take a union bound over all  $z\in B_{\rho}\cap(\varepsilon^{2\beta}\mathbbm{Z}^{2})$  and all  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,B_{\rho})]\cap\{2^{-n}\}_{n\in\mathbbm{Z}}$  to get that the following is true. With polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the bound (5.4) holds simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho}\cap(\varepsilon^{2\beta}\mathbbm{Z}^{2})$  and all  $s\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\operatorname{dist}(z,B_{\rho})]\cap\{2^{-n}\}_{n\in\mathbbm{Z}}$ .
Due to (5.9), this implies that (5.4) holds simultaneously for all  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and  $s\in[0,\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})]$  with  $2C$ , say, in place of  $C$ .
∎
5.2 Upper bound for off-diagonal Green’s function
We now use Lemma 3.4, Proposition 3.8, and Lemma 5.3 to prove the following upper bound for the Green’s function.
Lemma 5.4.
There exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|}}}\right)+C$
(5.10)
simultaneously for all  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  with  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}$ .
We first prove a variant of Lemma 5.4 where we also impose an upper bound for  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|$ .
The proof is basically the same as that of Lemma 4.4, but with the inequalities going in the opposite direction.
Lemma 5.5.
There exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|}}}\right).$
(5.11)
simultaneously for all  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  with  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]$ .
Proof.
Since the function  $y\mapsto\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus(\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})\cup\{x\})$ , we can apply Proposition 3.8 to find that there exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $C_{1}=C_{1}(\rho,\gamma)>1$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and each  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(z,\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]$  that
$\max_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)\leq C_{1}\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y).$
(5.12)
By Lemma 3.4 (applied with  $A=\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))$  and  $B=\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ ) and Lemma 3.7 (to say that the error term  $\delta$  from Lemma 3.4 is at most 1), a.s. for every such  $z$  and  $s$ ,
$\displaystyle\frac{a}{1+1/a}=\frac{a^{2}}{a+1}\leq\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right),\quad\text{for}\quad a=\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y).$
(5.13)
Re-arranging the inequality (5.13) gives
$\displaystyle\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1+\frac{1}{\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)}}}\right)\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right).$
(5.14)
By Lemma 5.3, after possibly shrinking  $\beta$  we can find  $C_{2}=C_{2}(\rho,\gamma)>1$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and each  $s\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho})}}\right]$  that
$\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{s}(z)\leftrightarrow\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)\leq C_{2}\log s^{-1}.$
(5.15)
We now use (5.15) to upper-bound the left side of (5.14), but some care is needed due to the term  $\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s})}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)$  on the right side.
This is dealt with as follows.
If  $\min_{y\in\partial\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s}(z))}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)$  were larger than  $2C_{2}\log s^{-1}\geq 1$ , then the right side of (5.14) would be at most  $C_{2}\log s^{-1}+1\leq 2C_{2}\log(s^{-1})$ , so either way we must in fact have
$\min_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{s})}\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x_{z}^{\varepsilon},y)\leq 2C_{2}\log s^{-1}.$
(5.16)
Combining (5.12) and (5.16), each applied with  $z=\eta(x)$  and  $s=|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|$ , now gives (5.11) with  $C=2C_{1}C_{2}$ .
∎
Proof of Lemma 5.4.
We need to remove the constraint that  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\leq\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho})$ .
Set  $\rho^{\prime}:=(1+\rho)/2$ .
Obviously,  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho^{\prime}}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\geq\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  for each  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ , so it suffices to prove (5.10) with  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho^{\prime}}}^{\varepsilon}$  in place of  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}$ .
This will allow us to avoid dealing with boundary effects (which are manifested in the requirement that  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\leq\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho})$  in Lemma 5.5).
By Lemma 5.5 with  $\rho^{\prime}$  in place of  $\rho$ , there exists  $\beta$  and  $C$  as in the lemma statement such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho^{\prime}}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|}}}\right)$
(5.17)
for all  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho^{\prime}})$  with  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho^{\prime}})}}\right]$ .
By Lemma 2.4, there exists  $q=q(\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , we have  $\eta(x)\in B_{\rho+\varepsilon^{q}}$  for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ .
If this is the case, then for small enough  $\varepsilon>0$  (how small depends only on  $\rho,\gamma$ ),
$\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{dist}(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho^{\prime}})\geq\frac{\rho^{\prime}-\rho-\varepsilon^{q}}{3}\geq\frac{\rho^{\prime}-\rho}{6}.$
(5.18)
Therefore, with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the bound (5.17) holds for all  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho^{\prime}})$  with  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\beta},(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)/6}}\right]$ .
Henceforth assume that this is the case.
Since  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho^{\prime}}}^{\varepsilon}(x,\cdot)$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho^{\prime}})\setminus\{x\}$  and vanishes on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho^{\prime}})$ , we can apply (5.17) and the maximum principle to get that for  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  with  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|>(\rho^{\prime}-\rho)/6$ ,
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{6}{\rho^{\prime}-\rho}}}\right).$
(5.19)
Combining this with (5.17) gives (5.10) with  $C\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{6}{\rho^{\prime}-\rho}}}\right)$  in place of  $C$ .
∎
5.3 Upper bound for on-diagonal Green’s function
Lemma 5.4 only provides an upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  in the case when  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}$ .
The purpose of this subsection is to prove a crude upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  which will deal with the case when  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\leq\varepsilon^{\beta}$ .
Lemma 5.6.
For each  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ , it holds polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\max_{x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta}.$
(5.20)
Since  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$  attains its maximum value when  $x=y$ , to prove Lemma 5.6, we only need to prove an upper bound for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,x)$ . Since degrees in  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  are easy to control, this amounts to proving an upper bound for the effective resistance from  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  to  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})$ .
The proof of this upper bound is based on Thomson’s principle applied to the same unit flow used in the proof of Lemma 5.3.
However, the estimates involved are somewhat more delicate.
The following lemma is one of the key ingredients of the proof.
Lemma 5.7.
For each  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ , it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that the following is true.
Simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$ , the number of vertices  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  whose corresponding cell satisfies
$\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)$
(5.21)
is at most  $\varepsilon^{-\zeta}$ .
Proof.
By Lemma 2.4, there are constants  $0<q<p<\infty$  depending only on  $\gamma$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\varepsilon^{p}\leq\operatorname{diam}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon^{q},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(5.22)
By (5.22) together with [GHM20, Proposition 3.4 and Remark 3.9], it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\text{$H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ contains a Euclidean ball of radius at least $\varepsilon^{\zeta/4}\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)$},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(5.23)
Henceforth assume that the estimates (5.22) and (5.23) hold.
We will show that the event in the lemma statement occurs.
To this end, fix  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  let  $\mathcal{C}_{k}$  be the set of  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  such that  $\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)$  and  $\operatorname{diam}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})\in[2^{-k-1},2^{-k}]$ .
By (5.22),  $\mathcal{C}_{k}=\emptyset$  for  $k\notin[\log_{2}\varepsilon^{-q},\log_{2}\varepsilon^{-p}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$ .
Therefore, we only need to show that
$\sum_{k=\lfloor\log_{2}\varepsilon^{-q}\rfloor}^{\lceil\log_{2}\varepsilon^{-p}\rceil}\#\mathcal{C}_{k}\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta}.$
(5.24)
For each  $x\in\mathcal{C}_{k}$ , the cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  is contained in  $B_{2^{-k+1}}(z)$ .
Since the cells  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  intersect only along their boundaries, the Euclidean balls of (5.23) for different choices of  $x$  are disjoint.
Therefore,
$\pi 2^{-2k+2}=\operatorname{area}B_{2^{-k+1}}(z)\geq\pi\sum_{x\in\mathcal{C}_{k}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\varepsilon^{\zeta/4}\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)}}\right]^{2}\geq\pi\varepsilon^{\zeta/2}2^{-2k-2}\#\mathcal{C}_{k},$
(5.25)
where in the last inequality we used that  $\operatorname{diam}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})^{2}\geq 2^{-k-1}$  for each  $x\in\mathcal{C}_{k}$ .
By re-arranging (5.25) we get  $\#\mathcal{C}_{k}\leq 16\varepsilon^{-\zeta/2}$ .
Summing this estimate over the logarithmically many values of  $k\in[\log_{2}\varepsilon^{-q},\log_{2}\varepsilon^{-p}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$  now shows that (5.24) holds provided  $\varepsilon$  is at most some  $\zeta$ -dependent constant.
∎
Proof of Lemma 5.6.
Step 1: regularity events.
We first define a high-probability regularity event which we will truncate on throughout the proof.
After this step, all of the arguments are entirely deterministic.
As explained at the beginning of the proof of Lemma 5.7, it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that the bounds (5.22) and (5.23) both hold.
By [GMS19, Lemma 2.6], it holds with superpolynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(5.26)
By Lemma 5.7, it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\#\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}):\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(z,H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)}}\right\}\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in B_{\rho}.$
(5.27)
Henceforth assume that (5.22), (5.23), (5.26), and (5.27) all hold, which happens with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
Step 2: bounding the effective resistance in terms of a unit flow.
For  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , we let  $\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)$  be a point of the cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  chosen in such a way that  $\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)$  lies at maximal Euclidean distance from  $\partial H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ , so that by (5.23),
$\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),\partial H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\geq\varepsilon^{\zeta/4}\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right).$
(5.28)
For  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ , let  $\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  be the flow defined in the proof of Lemma 5.3 with  $z=\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)$ .
As explained in that lemma,  $\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  is a unit flow from  $x$  to  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})$  and hence by Thomson’s principle (3.5),
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,x)=\mathcal{R}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(x\leftrightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})}}\right)\leq\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}[\theta^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}.$
(5.29)
Furthermore, by (5.6), for each oriented edge  $(y,y^{\prime})$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  with  $y\not=x$ , we have
$|\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(y,y^{\prime})|\preceq\frac{\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)}{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)},$
(5.30)
with a universal implicit constant.
We want to bound the sum on the right side of (5.29) using (5.30).
We define the set of “good” vertices  $\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  to be the set of  $y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  such that  $\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)>\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)$ .
We write  $\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  to be the set of edges  $e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  which have at least one endpoint in  $\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ .
We will bound the sum of  $[\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}$  over the set of “bad” edges  $\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  and the set of “good” edges  $\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  separately.
The idea is that (5.30) gives a useful bound for the sum over good edges, whereas (5.27) tells us that there cannot be too many bad edges.
Step 3: bounding the sum over the bad edges.
By (5.27) with  $z=\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)$ , the total number of “bad” vertices satisfies  $\#(\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta}$ .
By combining this with (5.26), we have  $\#(\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon^{-2\zeta}$ .
By the definition of  $\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ , we have  $|\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)|\leq 1$  for each  $e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ .
Therefore,
$\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}[\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}\leq\varepsilon^{-2\zeta}.$
(5.31)
Step 4: bounding the sum over the good edges.
We eventually want to compare  $\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}[\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}$  to a deterministic integral using (5.30).
We start by summing (5.30) over all edges in  $\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  to get
$\displaystyle\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}[\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}$
$\displaystyle\leq\sum_{y\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}\frac{\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{2}\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(y)}{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{2}}\quad\text{by~\eqref{eqn-diag-flow-prob}}$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-3\zeta/2}\sum_{y\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(y),\partial H_{y}^{\varepsilon})}}\right)^{2}}{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{2}}\quad\text{by \eqref{eqn-comp-inrad} and~\eqref{eqn-diag-max-deg}}.$
(5.32)
If  $y\in\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ , then by definition  $\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)>\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)$ , so for each  $w\in H_{y}^{\varepsilon}$ ,
$|w-\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)|\leq\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)+\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq 2\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right).$
(5.33)
By applying (5.33) to lower-bound the denominator, then averaging over all  $w\in H_{y}^{\varepsilon}$ , we see that each term in the sum on the right side of (5.32) satisfies
$\displaystyle\frac{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(y),\partial H_{y}^{\varepsilon})}}\right)^{2}}{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)^{2}}\leq 4\int_{H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}\frac{\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(y),\partial H_{y}^{\varepsilon})}}\right)^{2}}{\operatorname{area}(H_{y}^{\varepsilon})|w-\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)|^{2}}\,dw\leq\frac{4}{\pi}\int_{H_{y}^{\varepsilon}}\frac{1}{|w-\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)|^{2}}\,dw$
(5.34)
where in the last inequality we used that  $\operatorname{area}(H_{y}^{\varepsilon})\geq\pi\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(y),\partial H_{y}^{\varepsilon})}}\right)^{2}$ .
By plugging the inequality (5.34) into the right side of (5.32), we get
$\displaystyle\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}[\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}\preceq\varepsilon^{-3\zeta/2}\int_{\mathbbm{D}\setminus H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}\frac{1}{|w-\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)|^{2}}\,dw,$
(5.35)
with a universal implicit constant.
By the lower bound in (5.22) and the definition of  $\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)$ ,
$\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x),\partial H_{x}^{\varepsilon})}}\right)\geq\varepsilon^{p+\zeta/4}\quad\text{which implies}\quad B_{\varepsilon^{p+\zeta/4}}(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x))\subset H_{x}^{\varepsilon},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(5.36)
Combining (5.35) and (5.36) shows that
$\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}\mathcal{S}_{x}^{\varepsilon}}[\theta_{x}^{\varepsilon}(e)]^{2}\preceq\varepsilon^{-3\zeta/2}\int_{\mathbbm{D}\setminus B_{\varepsilon^{p+\zeta/4}}(\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x))}\frac{1}{|w-\mathfrak{u}^{\varepsilon}(x)|^{2}}\,dw\preceq\varepsilon^{-3\zeta/2}\log\varepsilon^{-1},$
(5.37)
with the implicit constant depending only on  $\rho,\gamma$ .
Step 5: conclusion.
Plugging (5.31) and (5.37) into (5.29) gives  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,x)\preceq\varepsilon^{-3\zeta/2}\log\varepsilon^{-1}$  with the implicit constant depending only on  $\gamma$ .
Since  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,\cdot)$  is discrete harmonic on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\setminus(\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})\cup\{x\})$  and vanishes on  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\rho})$ , the maximum principle implies that for any  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(x)$ , we have  $\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,x)\preceq\varepsilon^{-3\zeta/2}\log\varepsilon^{-1}$ .
Since  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)=\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\operatorname{gr}^{\varepsilon}_{B_{\rho}}(x,y)$ , we see from this and and (5.26) that  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\preceq\varepsilon^{-5\zeta/2}\log\varepsilon^{-1}$  for all  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ .
Since  $\zeta\in(0,1)$  is arbitrary, this concludes the proof.
∎
5.4 Proof of Proposition 5.1
The following estimate is the main input in the proof of Proposition 5.1.
Lemma 5.8.
There are constants  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0$  and  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for every Borel set  $D\subset B_{\rho}$  and every  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  that
$\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}.$
(5.38)
Proof.
Note that the Green’s function is increasing in the domain, so for any  $D\subset B_{\rho}$ ,
$\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y),\quad\forall x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D).$
(5.39)
Hence our upper bounds for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}$  automatically give upper bounds for  $\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Fix  $\beta,\zeta>0$ , to be chosen later in a manner depending only on  $\gamma$ .
For a Borel set  $D\subset B_{\rho}$  and  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$ , we break the sum on the left side of (5.38) into two pieces:
$\displaystyle Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}$
$\displaystyle:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D):|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|<\varepsilon^{\beta}}}\right\}$
$\displaystyle Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{typical}}$
$\displaystyle:=\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)\setminus Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}.$
Let us first bound the sum over  $Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}$ .
By Lemma 5.6, it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\max_{x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon^{-\zeta}.$
(5.40)
Since the cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  have  $\mu_{h}$ -mass  $\varepsilon$ , it is easily seen from Lemmas A.1 and 2.4 that there exists  $\alpha_{0}=\alpha_{0}(\beta,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , we have  $\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\#\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\varepsilon^{\beta}}(z))\leq\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{0}}$ , which implies that
$\#Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}\leq\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{0}},\quad\forall D\subset B_{\rho},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(5.41)
By (5.40) and (5.41) we get that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\sum_{y\in Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{near}}}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}(x,y)\leq\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{0}-\zeta},\quad\forall D\subset B_{\rho},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D).$
(5.42)
Henceforth assume that  $\zeta<\alpha_{0}$ .
We now turn our attention to  $Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{typical}}$ .
By Lemma 5.4, there exists  $C_{0}=C_{0}(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that if  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  is chosen to be sufficiently small, then with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\displaystyle\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq C_{0}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|}}}\right)+C_{0},\quad\forall x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})\quad\text{with}\quad|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}.$
(5.43)
For  $y\in Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{typical}}$ , we have  $|\eta(x)-\eta(y)|\geq\varepsilon^{\beta}$  by definition, so (5.43) implies that
$\operatorname{gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)\leq f_{x}(\eta(y)),\quad\forall y\in Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{typical}},\quad\text{where}\quad f_{x}(w):=\frac{C_{0}}{\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(|\eta(x)-w|^{-1}\wedge\varepsilon^{-\beta}}}\right)}+C_{0}.$
(5.44)
The absolute value of  $f_{x}$  is bounded above by  $C\log(\varepsilon^{-\beta})$  on  $B_{\rho}$ .
Furthermore, it is easily seen by differentiating that  $f_{x}$  is Lipschitz continuous on  $B_{\rho}$  with Lipschitz constant at most a  $C$ -dependent constant times  $\varepsilon^{-\beta}$ .
Therefore, Lemma A.5 implies that there exists  $\alpha_{1}=\alpha_{1}(\gamma)>0$  such that if  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  is chosen to be sufficiently small, then with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for every Borel set  $D\subset B_{\rho}$  and every  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  that
$\displaystyle\sum_{y\in Y_{D,x}^{\operatorname{typical}}}\operatorname{Gr}_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$
$\displaystyle\leq\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(y)f_{x}(\eta(y))\quad\text{by~\eqref{eqn-gr-upper-typical} and~\eqref{eqn-green-deg}}$
$\displaystyle\leq 6\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha_{1}}}(D)}f_{x}(w)\,d\mu_{h}(w)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{1}}\quad\text{by Lemma~\ref{lem-cell-sum-deg}}$
$\displaystyle\leq 6C_{0}\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha_{1}}}(D)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha_{1}}\quad\text{by~\eqref{eqn-gr-upper-typical}}.$
(5.45)
Combining (5.42) and (5.45) and recalling (5.39) gives the statement of the lemma with  $C=6C_{0}$  and  $\alpha:=\min\{\alpha_{0}-\zeta,\alpha_{1}\}$ .
∎
We now prove an elementary lemma for general graphs which will allow us to deduce moment bounds for exit times of the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from Lemma 5.8.
Lemma 5.9.
Let  $G$  be a graph, let  $B\subset\mathcal{V}(G)$ , and let  $x\in B$ .
Let  $\tau_{B}$  be the exit time from  $B$  of the simple random walk on  $G$  started from  $x$ .
Then for each  $N\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B}^{N}}}\right]\leq N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\operatorname{Gr}_{B}(x,y_{1})\prod_{n=2}^{N}\operatorname{Gr}_{B}(y_{n-1},y_{n}).$
(5.46)
Proof.
We have
$\tau_{B}=\sum_{y\in B}\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\mathbbm{1}_{(j<\tau_{B},\,X_{j}=y)}.$
By expanding out the sum, we get
$\displaystyle\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B}^{N}}}\right]$
$\displaystyle=\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\sum_{j_{1},\dots,j_{N}\in\mathbbm{N}_{0}}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{N}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1},\dots,X_{j_{N}}=y_{N}}}\right]$
$\displaystyle\leq N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\sum_{0\leq j_{1}\leq\dots\leq j_{N}<\infty}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{N}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1},\dots,X_{j_{N}}=y_{N}}}\right].$
(5.47)
For  $y\in B$ , let  $X^{y}$  denote the simple random walk on  $G$  started from  $y$  and let  $\tau_{B}^{y}$  be its exit time from  $B$  (so that  $X=X^{x}$  and  $\tau_{B}=\tau_{B}^{x}$ ).
By  $N$  applications of the strong Markov property, we obtain
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{N}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1},\dots,X_{j_{N}}=y_{N}}}\right]=\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{1}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1}}}\right]\prod_{n=2}^{N}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{n}-j_{n-1}<\tau_{B}^{y_{n-1}},X^{y_{n-1}}_{j_{n}-j_{n-1}}=y_{j}}}\right].$
(5.48)
Note that we allow  $j_{n}=j_{n-1}$  for some  $n\in[1,N]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$ , in which case the  $n$ th factor in the product on the right side of (5.48) is either zero or one according to whether  $y_{n}=y_{n-1}$ .
By (5.48), the right side of (5.47) equals
$\displaystyle N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in B}\sum_{0\leq j_{1}\leq\dots\leq j_{N}<\infty}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{1}<\tau_{B},\,X_{j_{1}}=y_{1}}}\right]\prod_{n=2}^{N}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[j_{n}-j_{n-1}<\tau_{B}^{y_{n-1}},X^{y_{n-1}}_{j_{n}-j_{n-1}}=y_{n}}}\right].$
(5.49)
Summing over  $j_{N}$ , then over  $j_{N-1}$ ,  $\dots$ , then over  $j_{1}$  gives (5.46).
∎
Proof of Proposition 5.1.
Let  $\alpha$  and  $C$  be as in Lemma 5.8.
That lemma tells us that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for every Borel set  $D\subset B_{\rho}$  with  $\mu_{h}(D)\geq\varepsilon^{\alpha}$  and every  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  that
$\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(x,y)$
$\displaystyle\leq C\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}$
$\displaystyle\leq(C+1)\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|\eta(x)-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w).$
(5.50)
Note that we have used the hypothesis that  $\mu_{h}(D)\geq\varepsilon^{\alpha}$  to absorb the  $\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}$  error into the first term.
By Lemma 5.9, for each such  $D$  and  $x$ ,
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{D}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]\leq N!\sum_{y_{1},\dots,y_{N}\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(x,y_{1})\prod_{n=2}^{N}\operatorname{Gr}_{D}^{\varepsilon}(y_{n-1},y_{n}).$
(5.51)
The estimate (5.1) (with  $C+1$  in place of  $C$ ) follows by applying (5.50) to bound the sum over  $y_{N}$ , then the sum over  $y_{N-1}$ ,  $\dots$ , then the sum over  $y_{1}$  on the right side of (5.51).
∎
6 Tightness
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , let  $X^{z,\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{N}_{0}\rightarrow\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  denote the simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from the vertex  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Let  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  be the process  $t\mapsto\eta(X_{t/\varepsilon}^{z,\varepsilon})$ , extended from  $\varepsilon\mathbbm{N}_{0}$  to  $[0,\infty)$  by piecewise linear interpolation.
We want to establish a tightness result for the random functions
$P^{\varepsilon}:z\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\text{Conditional law of $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t}$ given $(h,\eta)$}}}\right\}$
(6.1)
from  $\mathbbm{C}$  to the space of probability measures on continuous paths  $[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$ .
To state our tightness result we need to specify metrics on various spaces.
•
The space  $C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})$  of continuous paths  $X:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\overline{B}_{\rho}$  is equipped with the local uniform metric
$\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Unif}}(X,X^{\prime})=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-T}\wedge\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\sup_{t\in[0,T]}|X_{t}-X_{t}^{\prime}|}}\right\}\,dT,$
(6.2)
so that  $X^{n}\rightarrow X$  if and only if  $X^{n}\rightarrow X$  uniformly on each compact subset of  $[0,\infty)$ .
•
The space  $\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$  of probability measures on  $C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})$  is equipped with the Prokhorov metric  $\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Prok}}$  induced by the metric  $\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Unif}}$  on  $C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})$ .
•
The space of functions  $P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$  is equipped with the  $L^{\infty}$  metric
$\mathbbm{d}_{\infty}(P,P^{\prime})=\sup_{z\in\mathbbm{C}}\mathbbm{d}_{\operatorname{Prok}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(P_{z},P^{\prime}_{z}}}\right),$
(6.3)
so that  $P^{n}\rightarrow P$  if and only if  $P^{n}_{z}\rightarrow P_{z}$  uniformly on each compact subset of  $\mathbbm{C}$  with respect to the above Prokhorov topology on  $\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$ .
The main result of this subsection is the following proposition.
Proposition 6.1.
The laws of the random functions (6.1) for  $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$  are tight with respect to the topology specified just above.
If  $P$  is any subsequential limit in law of these functions, then a.s.  $P$  is continuous and the following is true.
If  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is a path with the law  $P_{z}$ , then a.s.  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time.
Fix  $\rho\in(0,1)$ .
Since most of our estimates only apply for cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which intersect  $B_{\rho}$ , we will first prove a tightness statement when we stop our walks upon exiting  $B_{\rho}$ .
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ , let  $\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}$  be the first time that  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  hits a point  $\eta(x)\in\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$  whose corresponding cell  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  is disjoint from  $B_{\rho}$ .
We define
$P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}:z\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\text{Conditional law of $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}$ given $(h,\eta)$}}}\right\}.$
(6.4)
Note that  $P_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon}$  assigns probability 1 to the constant path at  $x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  if  $z$  is not contained in a cell of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which intersects  $B_{\rho}$ .
Proposition 6.2.
The laws of the random functions (6.4) for  $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$  are tight with respect to the topology specified just above Proposition 6.1.
If  $P_{\rho,\cdot}$  is any subsequential limit in law of these functions, then a.s.  $P$  is continuous and the following is true.
If  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is a path with the law  $P_{\rho,z}$ , then a.s.  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time before it exits  $B_{\rho}$ .
Most of this section is devoted to the proof of Proposition 6.2. We will deduce Proposition 6.1 from Proposition 6.2 and a scaling argument in Section 6.4.
For proving tightness results, it is convenient to work with the space
$\mathcal{C}:=C\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{C},\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)}}\right]$
(6.5)
of continuous functions  $\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$ , rather than the space of all functions  $\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$  (e.g., so that we can use the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem).
So, we will approximate the function  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$  of (6.4) by a continuous function  $\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{C}$  which satisfies  $\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}=P_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}$  for each  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ . One way to do this is as follows.
For each  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ , choose  $r_{x}^{\varepsilon}>0$  such that the Euclidean neighborhood of the cell  $B_{r_{x}^{\varepsilon}}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})$  does not contain  $\eta(y)$  for any  $y\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\setminus\{x\}$ .
Choose a partition of unity  $\{\phi_{x}^{\varepsilon}\}_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}}$  subordinate to the open cover  $\{B_{r_{x}^{\varepsilon}}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})\}_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}}$  of  $\mathbbm{C}$ .
Then set  $\widetilde{P}_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon}=\sum_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}}P_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}\phi_{x}^{\varepsilon}(z)$ .
To prove Proposition 6.2, we need a compactness criterion, which follows easily from the Prokhorov theorem and the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem.
Lemma 6.3.
Let  $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathcal{C}$ .
Then  $\mathcal{K}$  is pre-compact (i.e., the closure of  $\mathcal{K}$  is compact) if the following conditions are satisfied.
1.
