(Equicontinuity of laws) For each  $L>1$ , there exists  $\delta=\delta(L)>0$  such that for each  $P=(P_{z})_{z\in\mathbbm{C}}\in\mathcal{K}$  and each  $z,w\in B_{L}(0)$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$ , the Prokhorov distance between the laws  $P_{z}$  and  $P_{w}$  is at most  $1/L$ .
2.
(Equicontinuity of paths) For each  $L>0$  and each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , there exists  $\delta=\delta(z,L)>0$  such that
for each  $P=(P_{w})_{w\in\mathbbm{C}}\in\mathcal{K}$ , the following is true.
If  $X:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  is sampled from the law  $P_{z}$ , then with probability at least  $1-1/L$ ,
$|X_{s}-X_{t}|\leq 1/L,\quad\forall s,t\in[0,L]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta.$
Proof.
By the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem for continuous functions into the complete metric space
$\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$ ,  $\mathcal{K}$  is pre-compact provided condition 1 holds and for
each fixed  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , the set  $\{P_{z}\}_{P\in\mathcal{K}}$  is a pre-compact subset of  $\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$ .
By the Prokhorov theorem,  $\{P_{z}\}_{P\in\mathcal{K}}$  is pre-compact provided that for each
$\zeta\in(0,1)$ , there is a pre-compact subset  $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}=\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}(z)$  of  $C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})$
such that for each  $P\in\mathcal{K}$ , we have  $P_{z}[\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}]\geq 1-\zeta$ .
By the Arzéla-Ascoli theorem,  $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}$  is pre-compact provided there is a uniform modulus of continuity for all of the functions in  $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}$ .
We now assume condition 2 and check that  $\{P_{z}\}_{P\in\mathcal{K}}$  is pre-compact using the criterion of the preceding paragraph.
To this end, fix  $\zeta\in(0,1)$  and for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  let  $\delta_{k}$  be as in condition 2 for  $L=2^{k}/\zeta$ .
By a union bound over all  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$ , we get that if  $P\in\ \mathcal{K}$  and  $X$  is sampled from  $P_{z}$  then it holds with probability at least  $1-\zeta$  that
$|X_{s}-X_{t}|\leq\zeta/2^{k},\quad\forall s,t\in[0,2^{k}/\zeta]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta_{k},\quad\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}.$
(6.6)
The set  $\mathcal{K}^{\prime}_{\zeta}$  of  $X\in C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})$  for which (6.6) holds and  $X_{0}=z$  is a pre-compact subset of  $C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})$ , which verifies the condition of the preceding paragraph.
∎
The proof of the tightness part of Proposition 6.2 is divided into two steps, based on the two conditions of Lemma 6.3.
First we prove equicontinuity of paths in Section 6.1, then we prove equicontinuity of laws in Section 6.2.
In Section 6.3, we prove an estimate for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which will help us verify the last part of Proposition 6.1 (i.e., that the subsequential limiting path does not stay at a point for a positive time interval).
In Section 6.4 we deduce Proposition 6.1 from Proposition 6.2 via a scaling argument.
Throughout this section, we will use the following terminology.
Definition 6.4.
We say that  $\psi:[0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty)$  is a superpolynomial function if  $\psi(0)=0$  and  $\lim_{\delta\rightarrow 0}\delta^{-p}\psi(\delta)=0$  for every  $p>0$ .
We do not require the superpolynomial functions appearing in different proposition / lemma statements to be the same.
6.1 Equicontinuity of paths
The main result of this subsection is the following estimate.
Proposition 6.5 (Equicontinuity of paths).
Let  $\chi>\frac{2(2+\gamma)}{2-\gamma}$ .
There is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$ , depending only on  $\rho,\chi,\gamma$ , such that probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , it holds simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  that the following is true.
With conditional probability at least  $1-\psi(\delta)$  given  $(h,\eta)$ ,
$|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t}|\leq 2\delta,\quad\forall s,t\in[0,\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta^{\chi}.$
(6.7)
Once Theorem 1.2 is established, Proposition 6.5 implies that a.s. Liouville Brownian motion is locally Hölder continuous with any exponent less than  $\frac{2-\gamma}{2(2+\gamma)}$ . This bound is not optimal: indeed, it follows from [GRV16, Corollary 2.14] that Liouville Brownian motion is Hölder continuous with any exponent less than  $\frac{1}{2(1+\gamma/2)^{2}}$ .
Note in particular that this exponent does not degenerate as  $\gamma$  approaches 2. The proof in [GRV16]
relies on the study of negative moments for the exit time from a ball, which in turn relies on the a priori knowledge of
the multifractal spectrum of Liouville Brownian motion. Such tools are not directly available here and we instead use a “worst-case scenario” approach
which leads to a suboptimal (but still finite) exponent.
To prove Proposition 6.5 we want to use our lower bound for the exit times of the walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  from Euclidean balls (Proposition 4.1) to say that  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  is very unlikely to travel a long Euclidean distance in a short amount of time.
The main difficulty is that Proposition 6.5 only gives a lower bound for the conditional expectation of the exit time given  $(h,\eta)$ .
This by itself is far from good enough to get a modulus of continuity estimate for  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ , so we need to use additional arguments to get a better lower bound for exit times.
The first step of the proof, carried out in Lemma 6.6, is to use Proposition 4.1 together with our upper bound for moments of exit times from Euclidean balls (Proposition 5.1) and the Payley-Zygmund inequality to say the following.
Let  $c>0$  be the constant from Proposition 4.1.
If  $\delta\in(0,1)$  is fixed and  $\varepsilon>0$  is small, then with high probability it holds uniformly over all  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  and all  $r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\delta,\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$  that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{Exit time of $\widehat{X}^{\eta(x),\varepsilon}$ from $B_{r}(\eta(x))$}\geq\frac{1}{2}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{cr}(\eta(x))}}\right)\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]$
(6.8)
is bounded below by an explicit quantity depending on  $\mu_{h}|_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}$ .
Using basic “worst-case” estimates for the LQG measure, the above bound can be made more explicit.
In particular, fix a large constant  $\ell>1$  to be chosen later. Then when  $\varepsilon$  and  $\delta$  are small, it holds with high probability
over  $(h,\eta)$  that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{Exit time of $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ from $B_{\delta^{\ell}}(z)$}\gtrsim\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]\gtrsim\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2}$
(6.9)
uniformly over all  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta^{\ell}})$ , where here  $\gtrsim$  denotes inequality up to a multiplicative error of order  $\delta^{\zeta}$ , where  $\zeta>0$  can be made as small as we like (see Lemma 6.7).
At first glance, the bound (6.9) still seems to be far from a modulus of continuity estimate for  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  since it only gives a lower bound for exit times which holds with probability at least  $\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2}$ , not with probability close to 1.
To get around this difficulty, we exploit the (quenched) convergence of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization, which was proven in [GMS21].
Indeed, using a basic Brownian motion estimate (Lemma 6.8) and the aforementioned convergence, we can show that when  $\varepsilon$  and  $\delta$  are small the following is true with extremely high conditional probability given  $(h,\eta)$ .
If  $z\in B_{\rho}$ , then the walk  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  has to travel Euclidean distance  $\delta^{\ell}$  at least  $N\approx\delta^{-2(\ell-1)}$  times before exiting the ball of radius  $\delta$  centered at its starting point.
More precisely, if  $T$  is the exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\delta}$  from  $B_{\delta}(z)$ , then typically there are of order  $N\approx\delta^{-2(\ell-1)}$  times  $0=\tau_{0}<\tau_{1}<\dots<\tau_{N}<T$  such that  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\tau_{n}}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\tau_{n-1}}\geq\delta^{\ell}$  for each  $n=1,\dots,N$  (Lemma 6.9).
This is related to the fact that Brownian motion has linear quadratic variation.
The estimate (6.9) tells us that (ignoring small multiplicative errors) under the conditional law given  $(h,\eta)$ , each of the time intervals  $[\tau_{n-1},\tau_{n}]$  has probability at least  $\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2}$  to have length at least  $\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}$ .
Since there are of order  $\delta^{-2(\ell-1)}$  such intervals, and using the Markov property of the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , we get that the probability that at least one of these intervals has length at least  $\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}$  is at least
$1-\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2}}}\right)^{\delta^{-2(\ell-1)}}.$
(6.10)
If we choose  $\ell>4/(4-\gamma^{2})$ , so that  $2(\ell-1)>\ell\gamma^{2}/2$ , then (6.10) is of the form  $1-\psi(\delta)$  for a superpolynomial function  $\psi$ .
We therefore get that when  $\varepsilon>0$  is small, it holds uniformly over all  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})$  that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{Exit time of $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ from $B_{\delta}(z)$}\gtrsim\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2}\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]\geq 1-\psi(\delta);$
(6.11)
see Lemma 6.11.
Once (6.11) is established, it is a simple matter to conclude the proof of Proposition 6.5 using the Markov property and a union bound.
We remind the reader that this only holds with high probability over  $(h,\eta)$  because the bound (6.9) only holds with high probability.
We now proceed with the details of the above argument.
For convenience we will mostly phrase our estimates in terms of the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  instead of in terms of the embedded, linearly interpolated walk  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  as in the outline above.
We start with the Payley-Zygmund argument mentioned above.
Lemma 6.6.
Fix  $p>1$  and let  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)$  be as in Proposition 5.1.
There are constants  $a=a(p,\rho,\gamma)>0$  and  $c=c(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that for each  $\delta\in(0,1)$ , it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that simultaneously for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})$  and each  $r\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\delta,\operatorname{dist}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta(x),\partial B_{\rho}}}\right)}}\right]$ ,
$\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}\geq\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{-1}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{cr}(\eta(x))}}\right)}}\right]\geq a\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{\mu_{h}(B_{cr}(\eta(x))}{\sup_{z\in B_{r}(\eta(x))}\int_{B_{r+\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(\eta(x))}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)}}}\right)^{p}.$
(6.12)
Proof.
Let  $q:=p/(p-1)$  be the Hölder conjugate exponent to  $p$  and let  $N:=\lceil q\rceil$ .
By Proposition 5.1, there exists  $C=C(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that for each  $\delta\in(0,1)$ , it holds with with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that simultaneously for each  $x$  and  $r$  as in the lemma statement,
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]\leq N!C^{N}\varepsilon^{-N}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sup_{z\in B_{r}(\eta(x))}\int_{B_{r+\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(\eta(x))}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)}}\right)^{N}.$
(6.13)
Since  $N>q$ , the function  $x\mapsto x^{N/q}$  is convex so Jensen’s inequality together with (6.13) gives
$\displaystyle\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon})^{q}}}\right]$
$\displaystyle\leq\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]^{q/N}$
$\displaystyle\leq(N!)^{q/N}C^{q}\varepsilon^{-q}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sup_{z\in B_{r}(\eta(x))}\int_{B_{r+\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(\eta(x))}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)}}\right)^{q}.$
(6.14)
By Proposition 4.1, there exists  $c=c(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that for each  $x$  and  $r$  as in the lemma statement,
$\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{r}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq\varepsilon^{-1}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{cr}(\eta(x))}}\right)$
(6.15)
The bound (6.12) for an appropriate choice of  $a$  now follows from (6.14), (6.13), and the  $L^{q}$  variant of the Payley-Zygmund inequality.
∎
We now make the bound in Lemma 6.6 more explicit (so that it is in terms of  $\delta$  rather than in terms of  $\mu_{h}$ ).
This is done using basic uniform estimates for the LQG measure from Appendix A.
Lemma 6.7.
Let  $\ell>1$  and  $\zeta>0$ .
It holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that
$\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta^{\ell}})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{\delta^{\ell}}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}\geq\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2+\zeta}}}\right]\geq\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2+o_{\zeta}(1)},$
(6.16)
where the  $o_{\zeta}(1)$  is deterministic and depends only on  $\zeta,\ell,\gamma$ .
As discussed in the outline above, we eventually want to choose  $\ell$  to be sufficiently large depending on  $\gamma$ .
The parameter  $\zeta$  represents a small error in the exponent and will eventually be sent to zero.
Proof of Lemma 6.7.
By Lemma A.3 applied with  $A=\delta^{\zeta}/100$  together with Lemma A.1 applied with  $e^{-\operatorname{const}/\delta^{\zeta/2}}$  in place of  $\delta$ , it holds except on an event of probability decaying faster than any positive power of  $\delta$  that
$\sup_{z\in B_{\delta^{\ell}}(z)}\int_{B_{2\delta^{\ell}}(z)}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)+1\,d\mu_{h}(w)\leq\delta^{\zeta}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{2\delta^{\ell}}(z)}}\right),\quad\forall z\in B_{\rho}.$
(6.17)
Note that Lemma A.1 is applied to absorb the additive error term  $e^{-\operatorname{const}/\delta^{\zeta}}$  from Lemma A.3 into the main term  $\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{2\delta^{\ell}}(z)}}\right)$ .
Let  $c>0$  be the constant from Lemma 6.6. We emphasize that  $c$  does not depend on  $p$ .
By Lemma A.2 applied with  $2\delta^{\ell}$  in place of  $\delta$ , it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that
$\frac{\mu_{h}(B_{c\delta^{\ell}}(z))}{\mu_{h}(B_{2\delta^{\ell}}(z))}\geq\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2+\zeta},\quad\forall z\in B_{\rho}.$
(6.18)
We now apply (6.17) followed by (6.18) to lower-bound the right side of the inequality of Lemma 6.6 with  $r=\delta^{\ell}$  and with  $p=1+\zeta$ .
Note that  $\delta^{\ell}+\varepsilon^{\alpha}\leq 2\delta^{\ell}$  for each small enough  $\varepsilon>0$ , so we can bound the integral over  $B_{\delta^{\ell}+\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(z)$  by the integral over  $B_{2\delta^{\ell}}(z)$ .
We find that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta^{\ell}})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{\delta^{\ell}}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}\geq\frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{-1}\mu_{h}(B_{c\delta^{\ell}}(\eta(x))}}\right]\geq\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2+o_{\zeta}(1)}.$
(6.19)
By Lemma A.1, it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that
$\inf_{z\in B_{\rho}}\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{c\delta^{\ell}}(z)}}\right)\geq 2\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2+\zeta}.$
(6.20)
Combining (6.19) and (6.20) gives (6.16).
∎
Continuing with the outline above, we now want to use the convergence of random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  to Brownian motion modulo time parametrization to argue that the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  has to have at least  $\delta^{-2(\ell-1)}$  increments during which it travels Euclidean distance  $\delta^{\ell}$  before it can travel Euclidean distance  $\delta$ .
We start with the desired Brownian motion estimate.
Lemma 6.8.
Let  $\mathcal{B}$  be a standard planar Brownian motion started from 0.
For  $r\in(0,1)$ , let  $\sigma_{0}(r):=0$  and inductively let  $\sigma_{k}(r)$  for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  be the first time  $t\geq\sigma_{k-1}(r)$  for which  $|\mathcal{B}_{t}-\mathcal{B}_{\sigma_{k-1}(r)}|\geq r$ .
For each  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ , there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$  such that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\mathcal{B}$ first exits $B_{1}(0)$ before time $\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)$}}}\right]\leq\psi(r)\quad\text{and}$
(6.21)
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\mathcal{B}$ first exits $B_{1}(0)$ after time $\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2+\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)$}}}\right]\leq\psi(r).$
(6.22)
Proof.
By Brownian scaling, the rescaled increments  $r^{-2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\sigma_{k}(r)-\sigma_{k-1}(r)}}\right)$  are i.i.d., and each has the same law as the exit time  $\sigma_{1}(1)$  of  $\mathcal{B}$  from  $B_{1}(0)$ .
Using the strong Markov property of Brownian motion, it is easily seen that there are universal constants  $c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}>0$  such that or each  $A>1$ , each  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$ , and each  $r>0$ ,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{k}(r)-\sigma_{k-1}(r)>Ar^{2}}}\right]=\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{1}(1)>A}}\right]\leq c_{0}e^{-c_{1}A}\quad\text{and}$
(6.23)
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{k}(r)-\sigma_{k-1}(r)\geq r^{2}}}\right]\geq c_{2}.$
(6.24)
Proof of (6.21).
By expanding  $\sigma_{K}(r)^{N}$  as a sum over  $K^{N}$  products of  $N$  increments and applying (6.23), we get that for each  $K\in\mathbbm{N}$  and each  $N\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{K}(r)^{N}}}\right]\preceq r^{2N}K^{N},$
(6.25)
with the implicit constant depending only on  $N$ .
By setting  $K=\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor$  in (6.25) and applying the Chebyshev inequality, we get
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)>r^{\zeta/2}}}\right]\preceq r^{\zeta N/2},\quad\forall N\in\mathbbm{N}.$
(6.26)
On the other hand, by a Gaussian tail bound, Brownian scaling, and the reflection principle,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{1}(1)<r^{\zeta/2}}}\right]\preceq e^{-1/(2r^{\zeta/2})},$
(6.27)
with a universal implicit constant.
Combining (6.26) and (6.27) and sending  $N\rightarrow\infty$  gives (6.21) for an appropriate choice of  $\psi$ .
Proof of (6.22).
By (6.24),  $r^{-2}\sigma_{k}(r)$  stochastically dominates a binomial random variable with  $k$  trials and success probability  $c_{2}$ .
By a standard binomial concentration inequality,  $\mathbbm{P}[\sigma_{\lfloor r^{-(2-\zeta)}\rfloor}(r)<r^{-\zeta/2}]$  decays faster than any positive power of  $r$  as  $r\rightarrow 0$ .
By the upper bound for  $\sigma_{1}(1)$  in (6.23) we also have that  $\mathbbm{P}[\sigma_{1}(1)>r^{-\zeta/2}]$  decays faster than any positive power of  $r$  as  $r\rightarrow 0$ . Combining the two preceding sentences gives (6.22).
∎
The events considered in Lemma 6.8 do not depend on the time parametrization of the Brownian motion  $\mathcal{B}$ , so we can transfer the conclusion of Lemma 6.8 to a statement for random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  using the convergence modulo time parametrization established in [GMS21].
Lemma 6.9.
Fix  $\ell>1$ .
For  $\delta\in(0,1)$  and a random walk  $X^{\varepsilon}$  on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  (with some choice of starting point), let  $\tau_{0}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})=0$  and for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  inductively let  $\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})$  be the first time  $j$  after  $\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})$  for which  $X_{j}^{\varepsilon}\notin\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta^{\ell}}(X^{\varepsilon}_{\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})}))$ .
For each  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ , there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$ , depending only on  $\zeta,\ell,\gamma$ , such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (at a rate which depends on  $\delta$ ), it holds for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})$
that
$\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$X^{\varepsilon}$ exits $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{\delta}(\eta(x))}}\right)$ before time $\tau_{\lfloor\delta^{-(2-\zeta)(\ell-1)}\rfloor}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})$}}}\right]\leq\psi(\delta).$
(6.28)
Proof.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , let  $\mathcal{B}^{z}$  be a standard planar Brownian motion started from  $z$ .
Let  $\sigma_{0}^{z}(\delta^{\ell})=0$  and inductively let  $\sigma_{k}^{z}(\delta^{\ell})$  for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  be the first time  $t\geq\sigma_{k-1}^{z}(\delta^{\ell})$  for which  $|\mathcal{B}^{z}_{t}-\mathcal{B}^{z}_{\sigma_{k-1}^{z}(\delta^{\ell})}|\geq\delta^{\ell}$ .
By (6.21) of Lemma 6.8 (applied with  $r=\delta^{\ell-1}$ )
and Brownian scaling, there exists a superpolynomial function  $\psi$  as in the lemma statement such that for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ ,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\mathcal{B}^{z}$ exits $B_{\delta}(z)$ before time $\sigma_{\lfloor\delta^{-(2-\zeta)(\ell-1)}\rfloor}^{z}(\delta^{\ell})$}}}\right]\leq\psi(\delta).$
(6.29)
Now let  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  be the embedded, linearly interpolated random walk as described at the beginning of this section.
By [GMS21, Theorem 3.4], the supremum over all  $z\in\mathbbm{D}$  of the Prokhorov distance between the law of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and the law of  $\mathcal{B}^{z}$ , each stopped at its exit time from  $\mathbbm{D}$ , with respect to the topology on curves modulo time parametrization, tends to zero in probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
By combining this with (6.29) we obtain (6.28) (with  $2\psi$  in place of  $\psi$ , say).
∎
The estimate (6.22) of Lemma 6.9 also yields a useful estimate for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Lemma 6.10.
For  $\delta\in(0,1)$  and a random walk  $X^{\varepsilon}$  on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  (with some choice of starting point), let  $\sigma_{0}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)=0$  and for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  inductively let  $\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$  be the first time  $j$  after  $\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$  for which  $X_{j}^{\varepsilon}\notin\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(X^{\varepsilon}_{\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)}))$ .
For each  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ , there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$ , depending only on  $\zeta,\gamma$ , such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  (at a rate which depends on  $\delta$ ), it holds for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  that
$\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$X^{\varepsilon}$ first exits $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{\rho}}}\right)$ before time $\sigma_{\lfloor\delta^{-(2+\zeta)}\rfloor}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$}}}\right]\leq\psi(\delta).$
(6.30)
Proof.
This follows from (6.22) of Lemma 6.9 and [GMS21, Theorem 3.4] via exactly the same argument used in the proof of Lemma 6.9.
∎
We now get a lower bound for exit times which holds with extremely high probability, which is the main input in the proof of Proposition 6.1.
Lemma 6.11.
Let  $\chi>\frac{2(2+\gamma)}{2-\gamma}$ . There is a superpolynomial function  $\psi:(0,\infty)\rightarrow(0,\infty)$  such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{\delta}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}<\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{\chi}}}\right]\leq\psi(\delta).$
(6.31)
Proof.
Fix  $\ell>1$  and  $\zeta>0$ .
Define the stopping times  $\{\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})\}_{k\in\mathbbm{N}_{0}}$  for  $X$  as in Lemma 6.9.
By Lemma 6.9, there exists a superpolynomial function  $\psi_{0}$ , depending only on  $\zeta,\ell,\gamma$ , such that for each  $\delta\in(0,1)$ , it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{\delta}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon}<\tau_{\lfloor\delta^{-(2-\zeta)(\ell-1)}\rfloor}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})}}\right]\leq\psi_{0}(\delta).$
(6.32)
By the strong Markov property of the walk  $X^{\varepsilon}$  under  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ , the  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ -conditional law of
$X^{\varepsilon}$  given  $X^{\varepsilon}|_{[0,\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})]}$  is that of a simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from
$X^{\varepsilon}_{\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})}$ .
The time  $\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})-\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})$  is the exit time of this walk from  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta^{\ell}}(\eta(X_{\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})})))$ .
By Lemma 6.7, we infer that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})}\max_{k\in\mathbbm{N}}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})<\tau_{B_{\delta}(x)}^{\varepsilon},\,\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})-\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})<\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2+\zeta}\,\big|\,X|_{[0,\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})]}}}\right]\leq 1-\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2+o_{\zeta}(1)}.$
(6.33)
By multiplying (6.33) over all  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  and using (6.32), we get that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\displaystyle\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})-\tau_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})<\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2+\zeta},\,\text{$\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}$ with $\tau_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta^{\ell})<\tau_{B_{\delta}(x)}^{\varepsilon}$}}}\right]$
$\displaystyle\qquad\leq\psi_{0}(\delta)+\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\delta^{\ell\gamma^{2}/2+o_{\zeta}(1)}}}\right)^{\delta^{-(2-\zeta)(\ell-1)}}.$
(6.34)
If we choose  $\ell>4/(4-\gamma^{2})$ , then for a small enough choice of  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ , the term  $\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-\delta^{\ell p\gamma^{2}/2+o_{\zeta}(1)}}}\right)^{\delta^{-(2-\zeta)(\ell-1)}}$  in (6.34) decays faster than any positive power of  $\delta$  as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ .
From this, we infer that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho-\delta})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{B_{\delta}(x)}^{\varepsilon}<\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2+\zeta}}}\right]\leq\psi(\delta),$
(6.35)
for some superpolynomial function  $\psi$  depending only on  $\zeta,\ell,\gamma$ .
If we choose  $\ell$  sufficiently close to  $4/(4-\gamma^{2})$  and  $\zeta$  sufficiently close to zero, then we can make  $(2+\gamma)^{2}\ell/2+\zeta$  as close as we like to  $\frac{2(2+\gamma)}{2-\gamma}$ . This gives (6.31).
∎
Proof of Proposition 6.5.
For  $\delta>0$ , let  $\widehat{\sigma}_{0}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)=0$  and for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  inductively let  $\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)$  be the first time  $t\geq\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)$  for which  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t}=\eta(x)$  for some  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)}))$  (basically,  $\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)$  is a slight modification of the exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  from  $B_{\delta}(\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)})$ ).
Recall that  $\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}$  denotes the exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  from  $B_{\rho}$ .
By Lemma 6.10, there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi_{0}$  depending only on  $\rho,\gamma$  such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}\leq\widehat{\sigma}_{\lfloor\delta^{-3}\rfloor}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]\geq 1-\psi_{0}(\delta).$
(6.36)
Each  $\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)$  is a stopping time for the conditional law of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  given  $(h,\eta)$  satisfying  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)}\in\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$ .
By the strong Markov property of the conditional law of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ , the conditional law of  $\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)-\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)$  given  $(h,\eta)$  and  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}|_{[0,\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)]}$  is the same as the conditional law given  $(h,\eta)$  of (a slight modification of) the exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  from  $B_{\delta}(w)$  for  $w=\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)}$ .
Let  $\psi_{1}$  be the superpolynomial function as in Lemma 6.11.
By applying Lemma 6.11 to bound each of the exit times in the preceding paragraph, taking a union bound over all  $k\in[1,\delta^{-3}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$ , and recalling (6.36), we find that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ , the following is true.
Simultaneously for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$ , it holds with conditional probability at least  $1-\delta^{-3}\psi_{1}(\delta)-\psi_{0}(\delta)$  given  $(h,\eta)$  that
$\widehat{\sigma}_{k}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)-\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)\geq\delta^{\chi},\quad\text{$\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}$ such that $\widehat{\sigma}_{k-1}^{z,\varepsilon}(\delta)\leq\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}$}.$
(6.37)
The bound (6.37) implies that  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  cannot travel Euclidean distance more than  $2\delta$  in less than  $\delta^{\chi}$  units of time (recall that  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  is constant after time  $\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}$ ).
We therefore obtain (6.7) with  $\psi(\delta)=\psi_{0}(\delta)+\delta^{-3}\psi_{1}(\delta)$ .
∎
6.2 Equicontinuity of laws
In this section we establish the other part of the compactness criterion of Lemma 6.3 for the function  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$  of (6.4).
Proposition 6.12 (Equicontinuity of laws).
There exists  $\xi=\xi(\rho,\gamma)>0$ , and  $A=A(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that the following is true with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ .
For each  $z,w\in B_{\rho}$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$ , the Prokhorov distance (w.r.t. the local Skorokhod metric) between the conditional laws given  $(h,\eta)$  of the stopped processes  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}$  and  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}$  is at most  $A\delta^{\xi}$ .
Unlike for the exponent  $\chi$  of Proposition 6.5, our proof of Proposition 6.12
does not give an explicit expression for the exponent  $\xi$ . We note that a similar continuity result is obtained for Liouville Brownian motion in [GRV16, Proposition 2.19] which allows
the authors to a.s. start Liouville Brownian motion from any given point.
The basic idea of the proof of Proposition 6.5 (which differs somewhat from [GRV16]) is that if  $|z-w|<\delta$  then the embedded, linearly interpolated walk  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  is likely to disconnect  $w$  from  $\partial B_{\rho}$  before leaving  $B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$  (similar estimates are proven in Section 3).
We can then use Lemma 3.9 to couple  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  in such a way that they agree after their exit times from  $B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$  with high probability (see Lemma 6.13).
Both of these exit times are likely to be small (Corollary 5.2), so the uniform modulus of continuity estimate of Proposition 6.5 tells us that under such a coupling, the uniform distance between  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}$  and  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}$  is small.
Lemma 6.13.
There exists  $\xi=\xi(\rho,\gamma)>0$ , and  $A=A(\rho,\gamma)>0$  such that for each  $\delta\in(0,1)$ , it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that the following is true.
For each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and each  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(z))$ , the total variation distance between the conditional laws given  $(h,\eta)$  of the following two random variables is at most  $A\delta^{\xi}$ :
•
The first vertex of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$  hit by a random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from  $x$ .
•
The first vertex of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$  hit by a random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from  $y$ .
Furthermore, if  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-\delta})$ , then it holds with probability at least
$1-A\delta^{\xi}$  that the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from  $x$  exits  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  before hitting  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(\eta(x)))$ .
Proof.
Let  $\rho^{\prime}=(1+\rho)/2\in(\rho,1)$ .
By [GMS19, Lemma 3.11] (which is a variant of Lemma 3.11), there exists  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  and  $p=p(\rho,\gamma)\in(0,1)$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the following is true.
For each  $z\in B_{\rho^{\prime}}$  and each  $r\in[\varepsilon^{\beta},\rho]$  such that  $B_{2r}(z)\subset B_{\rho}$ , we have
$\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{r}(z))}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\big[\text{$X^{\varepsilon}$ disconnects $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{r/2}(z))$ from $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{2r}(z))$}$
$\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\text{before hitting $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{2r}(z))$}\big]\geq p.$
(6.38)
Henceforth assume that this is the case and that  $\varepsilon$  is small enough (depending on  $\delta$ ) so that  $\varepsilon^{\beta}<\delta/100$ .
We also assume that  $\delta$  is small enough that  $\rho+2\sqrt{\delta}<\rho^{\prime}$ , so that  $B_{2\sqrt{\delta}}(z)\subset B_{\rho^{\prime}}$  for each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  (larger values of  $\delta$  can be dealt with by increasing  $A$ ).
We will show that the condition in the lemma statement is satisfied.
We now consider  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and a random walk  $X^{\varepsilon}$  on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  started from  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ .
We apply the strong Markov property of the conditional law of  $X^{\varepsilon}$  given  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  at the exit time of  $X^{\varepsilon}$  from  $B_{2^{-k}}(\eta(x))$  for each  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  such that  $2^{-k}\in[2\delta,\sqrt{\delta}/2]$ . This together with our above constraints on  $\varepsilon$  and  $\delta$  allows us to apply estimate (6.38) with  $z=\eta(x)$  and  $r=2^{-k}$ , then multiply over all  $k$  for which  $2^{-k}\in[2\delta,\sqrt{\delta}/2]$ , to get
$\displaystyle\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{2\delta}(z)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\big[\text{$X^{\varepsilon}$ disconnects $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\delta}(z))$ from $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$
before hitting $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$}\big]$
$\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\geq 1-(1-p)^{\lfloor\log_{2}\delta^{-1}\rfloor-2}\geq 1-A\delta^{\xi}$
(6.39)
for constants  $\xi,A>0$  as in the lemma statement.
If  $x,y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(z))$ , then by (6.39), it holds with  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ -probability at least  $1-A\delta^{\xi}$  that  $X^{\varepsilon}$  disconnects  $y$  from  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$  before hitting  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$ . By Lemma 3.9, this implies the total variation condition in the lemma statement.
To get the last statement, we observe that if  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-\delta})$  and the random walk started from  $x$  disconnects  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\delta}(\eta(x)))$  from  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(\eta(x)))$  before hitting  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(\eta(x)))$ , then this walk must exit  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  before hitting  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(\eta(x)))$ . The last statement of the lemma therefore follows from (6.39).
∎
Proof of Proposition 6.12.
Step 1: coupling walks so that they agree after exiting a ball of radius  $\sqrt{\delta}$ .
By Lemma 6.13, there exists  $\xi_{0},A_{0}>0$  depending only on  $\rho,\gamma$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the following is true.
For each  $z,w\in B_{\rho}$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$ , the total variation distance between the conditional laws given  $(h,\eta)$  of the first vertex of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$  hit by  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and the first vertex of  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$  hit by  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  is at most  $A_{0}\delta^{\xi_{0}}$ .
Due to the strong Markov property of the conditional law of random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ , it follows that on this event we can couple the conditional laws given  $(h,\eta)$  of  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  in such a way that the following is true.
If we let  $T^{z}=T^{z,\varepsilon}_{\delta}$  (resp.  $T^{w}=T^{w,z,\varepsilon}_{\delta}$ ) be the exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  (resp.  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$ ) from55
5
We use  $B_{2\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$  instead of  $B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$  here since the points  $\eta(x)$  for  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(\partial B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z))$  are not necessarily contained in  $B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$ . However, the cell  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  for each such  $x$  must intersect  $B_{\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$  so by Lemma 2.4 it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that  $\eta(x)$  for each such  $x$  is contained in  $B_{2\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$ .
$B_{2\sqrt{\delta}}(z)$ , then
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t+T^{z}}=\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t+T^{w}},\>\forall t\geq 0\,\big|h,\eta}}\right]\geq 1-A_{0}\delta^{\xi_{0}}.$
(6.40)
If  $z,w\in B_{\rho-2\sqrt{\delta}}$ , then necessarily  $T^{z}\leq\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $T^{w}\leq\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}$  so it follows from (6.40) that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{(t+T^{z})\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}=\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{(t+T^{w})\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}},\quad\forall t\geq 0\,\big|h,\eta}}\right]\geq 1-A_{0}\delta^{\xi_{0}}.$
(6.41)
Step 2: the effect of the initial time increment.
For most of the rest of the proof we assume that  $z,w\in B_{\rho-2\sqrt{\delta}}$ , hence we can couple  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  so that (6.41) holds. We will treat the case when either  $z$  or  $w$  belongs to  $B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-2\sqrt{\delta}}$  at the very end of the proof.
To deduce the proposition statement from (6.41) we need to show that the behavior of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  before time  $T^{z}$  and  $T^{w}$ , respectively, has a negligible effect on the uniform distance between  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}$  and  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}$  with high probability when  $\delta$  is small.
We first show that the times  $T^{z}$  and  $T^{w}$  are typically small.
To this end, let  $0<q<q^{\prime}<(2-\gamma)^{2}/2$ .
By Corollary 5.2 and Markov’s inequality, it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that the following is true.
For each  $z,w\in B_{\rho}$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$ ,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[T^{z}\leq\delta^{q/4}\,|\,(h,\eta)}}\right]\geq 1-\delta^{q/4}\quad\text{and}\quad\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[T^{w}\leq\delta^{q/4}\,|\,(h,\eta)}}\right]\geq 1-\delta^{q/4}.$
(6.42)
We next use Proposition 6.5 to bound the effect on the walk from shifting time by at most  $\delta^{q/4}$ .
Let  $\chi>{\frac{2(2+\gamma)}{2-\gamma}}$ , as in Proposition 6.5.
By Proposition 6.5 (applied with  $\delta^{q/(4\chi)}$  in place of  $\delta$ ), there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$  depending only on  $\rho,\chi$  such that the following is true with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ .
For each  $z\in B_{\rho}$ ,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}|\leq 2\delta^{q/(4\chi)},\>\forall s,t\in[0,\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}]\>\text{with}\>|s-t|\leq\delta^{q/4}\,|\,h,\eta}}\right]\geq 1-\psi(\delta).$
(6.43)
Let us now condition on  $(h,\eta)$  and assume that (6.41) and (6.42) hold for every  $z,w\in B_{\rho}$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$  and (6.43) holds for every  $z\in B_{\rho}$ , which happens with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ .
Fix  $z,w\in B_{\rho-2\sqrt{\delta}}$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$  and suppose we have coupled  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  as in (6.41).
Except on an event whose conditional probability given  $(h,\eta)$  is bounded above by  $A\delta^{\xi}$  for  $A,\xi$  as in the lemma statement, the events in (6.41) and (6.42) occur and also the event in (6.43) occurs for each of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$ .
If this is the case, then we can bound the uniform distance between  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}$  and  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}$  as follows.
If  $s\in[0,T^{z}\vee T^{w}]$ , then by the event in (6.42) we have  $s\leq\delta^{q/4}$  so by (6.43) (applied once to each of  $z$  and  $w$ ),
$|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}-\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{s}|\leq 4\delta^{q/(4\chi)}+|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{0}-\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{0}|\leq 4\delta^{q/(4\chi)}+\delta\leq 5\delta^{q/(4\chi)}.$
(6.44)
Alternatively, if  $s>T^{z}\vee T^{w}$ , then we can find  $t^{z},t^{w}\geq 0$  such that  $s=t^{z}+T^{z}=t^{w}+T^{w}$ .
By the event in (6.42),  $|t^{z}-t^{w}|=|T^{z}-T^{w}|\leq\delta^{q/4}$ .
By the events in (6.41) and (6.43), we therefore have
$|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}-\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{s\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}|\leq|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{(t^{z}+T^{z})\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}-\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{(t^{z}+T^{w})\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}|+|\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{(t^{z}+T^{w})\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}-\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}_{(t^{w}+T^{w})\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{w,\varepsilon}}|\leq 2\delta^{q/(4\chi)}.$
(6.45)
By (6.44) and (6.45), the uniform distance between  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{w,\varepsilon}$  is at most  $5\delta^{q/(4\chi)}$ .
By possibly increasing  $A$  and/or decreasing  $\xi$ , we now obtain the proposition statement in the case when  $z,w\in B_{\rho-2\sqrt{\delta}}$ .
Step 3: points close to the boundary.
If  $|z-w|\leq\delta$  and either  $z$  or  $w$  belongs to  $B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-2\sqrt{\delta}}$ , then  $z,w\in B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-3\sqrt{\delta}}$ .
By the last assertion of Lemma 6.13 applied with  $3\sqrt{\delta}$  in place of  $\delta$ , if  $z\in B_{\rho-3\sqrt{\delta}}$  then holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ stays in $B_{\sqrt{3}\delta^{1/4}}(z)$ until time $\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}$}}}\right]\geq 1-3^{\xi}A_{0}\delta^{\xi_{0}/2}.$
(6.46)
If the event in (6.46) occurs then  $|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}}-z|\leq\sqrt{3}\delta^{1/4}$  for all  $t\geq 0$ .
Hence we obtain the proposition statement in the case when either  $z$  or  $w$  belongs to  $B_{\rho}\setminus B_{\rho-3\sqrt{\delta}}$  after possibly increasing  $A$  and/or decreasing  $\xi$ .
∎
6.3 The walk does not get stuck
In this subsection we will prove a proposition which will eventually imply the last statement of Proposition 6.2, which asserts that  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  does not remain at a single point for a positive interval of times.
We will then conclude the proof of Proposition 6.2.
Proposition 6.14.
Fix  $q\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,(2-\gamma)^{2}/2}}\right)$ .
There is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$  depending only on  $\zeta,\gamma$  such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ , it holds for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$  that
$\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\min_{j\in[0,\tau_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}}\max_{i_{1},i_{2}\in[j,j+2\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{q}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}}|\eta(X_{i_{1}}^{\varepsilon})-\eta(X_{i_{2}}^{\varepsilon})|\geq\delta}}\right]\geq 1-\psi(\delta).$
(6.47)
Proof.
Fix  $q^{\prime}\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(q,(2-\gamma)^{2}/2}}\right)$ .
By Corollary 5.2 applied with  $q^{\prime}$  in place of  $q$ , it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that for every  $N\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\overline{\mathbbm{E}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[(\tau_{B_{\delta}(\eta(x))}^{\varepsilon})^{N}}}\right]\leq N!\varepsilon^{-N}\delta^{Nq^{\prime}}.$
(6.48)
Basically, the proposition follows by applying (6.48), the Chebyshev inequality, and a union bound in the appropriate manner.
To be precise, define the times  $\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$  for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}_{0}$  as in Lemma 6.10: that is, let  $\sigma_{0}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)=0$  and for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  inductively let  $\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$  be the first time  $j\geq\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$  for which  $X_{j}^{\varepsilon}\notin\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(\eta(X_{\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)})))$ .
By the Markov property of  $X^{\varepsilon}$  under  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ , the  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ -conditional law of  $\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)-\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)$  given  $X^{\varepsilon}|_{[0,\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)]}$  is the same as the  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{X_{\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)}}$ -law of the exit time of  $X^{\varepsilon}$  from  $\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\delta}(\eta(X_{\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)})))$ .
Using (6.48), the Chebyshev inequality, and a union bound over all  $k\in[0,\delta^{-3}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$ , we find that for any fixed  $\zeta\in(0,1)$  and  $N\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)-\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{q},\>\forall k\in[0,\delta^{-3}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}\>\text{with}\>\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)\leq\tau_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq 1-N!\delta^{N(q^{\prime}-q)-3}.$
(6.49)
On the other hand, it follows from Lemma 6.10 (applied with  $\zeta=1$ ) that there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi_{0}$  such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}\leq\sigma_{\lfloor\delta^{-3}\rfloor}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)}}\right]\geq 1-\psi_{0}(\delta).$
(6.50)
By sending  $N\rightarrow\infty$  in (6.49) and combining with (6.50), we find that there is a superpolynomial function  $\psi$  such that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\min_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)-\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{q},\>\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}\>\text{with}\>\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)\leq\tau_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq 1-\psi(\delta).$
(6.51)
If the event in (6.51) occurs for some  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ , then every interval of times of the form  $[a,b]\subset[0,\tau_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}]$  with  $b-a\geq 2\varepsilon^{-1}\delta^{q}$  must contain  $[\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta),\sigma_{k}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)]$  for some  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$  with  $\sigma_{k-1}^{\varepsilon}(\delta)\leq\tau_{B_{\rho}}^{\varepsilon}$ .
By definition,  $\eta(X^{\varepsilon})$  travels Euclidean distance at least  $\delta$  during each such time interval, so we get (6.47).
∎
Proof of Proposition 6.2.
Define  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  as in (6.4) and let  $\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$  be a continuous approximation of  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$  as in the discussion just after (6.5).
Since  $P_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}=\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\eta(x)}^{\varepsilon}$  for each  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  it is easily seen that if  $\varepsilon_{n}\rightarrow 0$  is a sequence along which  $\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon_{n}}$  converges in law, then also  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon_{n}}$  converges in law to the same limit.
Therefore, to prove tightness for  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$  we only need to prove tightness for  $\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$ .
The subsequential limits will be continuous since continuity is preserved under uniform convergence.
By the Prokhorov theorem, we need to show that for each  $\zeta>0$ , there is a compact
subset  $\mathcal{K}_{\zeta}$  of the space  $\mathcal{C}$  of continuous functions  $\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  such that for each small enough  $\varepsilon>0$ , we have  $\mathbbm{P}[\widetilde{P}_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{K}_{\zeta}]\geq 1-\zeta$ .
As a consequence of Lemma 6.3,
it suffices to establish the following.
1.
(Equicontinuity of laws) For each  $L>1$ , there exists  $\delta>0$  such that for each small enough  $\varepsilon>0$ , it holds with (annealed) probability at least  $1-1/L$  that for each  $z,w\in B_{\rho}$  with  $|z-w|\leq\delta$ , the Prokhorov distance between the laws  $P_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon}$  and  $P_{\rho,w}^{\varepsilon}$  is at most  $1/L$ .
2.
(Equicontinuity of paths) For each  $z\in B_{\rho}$  and each  $L>1$ , there exists  $\delta=\delta(z,L)>0$  such that for each small enough  $\varepsilon>0$ , the following is true. With (annealed) probability at least  $1-1/L$ ,
$|\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}-\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{s}|\leq 1/L,\quad\forall s,t\in[0,\widehat{\tau}^{z,\varepsilon}]\quad\text{with}\quad|s-t|\leq\delta.$
While this seems very similar to the statement of Lemma 6.3,
there is in fact a difference: the compactness criterion of that lemma require us to check the
equicontinuity of laws and paths conditions with quenched probability at least  $1-\zeta$  (i.e.,
conditioned on  $h$  and  $\eta$ ), whereas we claim here it suffices to check these conditions with annealed
(i.e., unconditional) probability. That this is sufficient follows from a dyadic argument
similar to the one in the proof of Lemma 6.3: in particular, we apply the conditions with  $L=2^{k}/\zeta$  for  $k\in\mathbbm{N}$ , then take a union bound over  $k$ .
Recall that for  $z\notin B_{\rho}$ ,  $P_{\rho,z}^{\varepsilon}$  is simply the point mass at the constant  $t\mapsto x_{z}^{\varepsilon}$ , which is why we only need to consider  $z\in B_{\rho}$ .
Conditions 1 and 2 follow from Propositions 6.12 and 6.5, respectively.
Finally, the last assertion of the proposition (that  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time until after exiting  $B_{\rho}$ ) is immediate from Proposition 6.14.
∎
6.4 Proof of Proposition 6.1
We now deduce Proposition 6.1 from Proposition 6.2 and the scale invariance property of the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone.
For  $b>0$ , let  $R_{b}:=\sup\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{r>0:h_{r}(0)+Q\log r=\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b}}\right\}$  and  $h^{b}:=h(R_{b}\cdot)+Q\log R_{b}-\frac{1}{\gamma}\log b$ , as in Lemma 2.3.
Also let  $\eta^{b}:=R_{b}^{-1}\eta(b\cdot)$ .
By Lemma 2.3 and the scale invariance of the law of  $\eta$ , we have  $(h^{b},\eta^{b})\overset{d}{=}(h,\eta)$ .
Consequently,
$\{\eta([x-\varepsilon,x]):x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\}\overset{d}{=}\{\eta^{b}([x-\varepsilon,x])\}_{x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}}=\{R_{b}^{-1}\eta([y-b\varepsilon,y])\}_{y\in b\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}}.$
(6.52)
For  $u\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ , we define the linearly interpolated walk
$\widehat{X}^{b,u,\varepsilon}_{t}:=R_{b}^{-1}\widehat{X}^{R_{b}u,\varepsilon}_{t/b},$
(6.53)
which is related to  $(h^{b},\eta^{b})$  in the same manner that  $\widehat{X}^{u,\varepsilon}$  is related to  $(h,\eta)$ .
For  $u\in B_{\rho}$ , let  $\widehat{\tau}^{b,u,\varepsilon}$  be the first time that the walk  $\widehat{X}^{b,u,\varepsilon}_{t}$  hits a point of the form  $\eta(y)$  for  $y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho})$ .
Equivalently, for  $z\in B_{R_{b}\rho}$ , we have that  $b\widehat{\tau}^{b,z/R_{b},\varepsilon}$  is the first time that the walk  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  hits a point of the form  $\eta(x)$  for  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}\setminus\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{R_{b}\rho})$ .
Since  $(h^{b},\eta^{b})$  and  $(h,\eta)$  generate the same  $\sigma$ -algebra, it follows from (6.52) that the function
$P_{\rho,\cdot}^{b,\varepsilon}:u\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\text{Conditional law of $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{b,u,\varepsilon}_{t\wedge\widehat{\tau}^{b,u,\varepsilon}}$ given $(h,\eta)$}}}\right\}$
(6.54)
has the same law as  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Therefore, Proposition 6.2 implies that the laws of the functions (6.54) are tight and if  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{(b)}$  is a subsequential limit in law of these functions, then a.s.  $P_{\rho,\cdot}^{(b)}$  is continuous and the following is true.
If  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is a path with the law  $P_{\rho,z}^{(b)}$ , then a.s.  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time before it exits  $B_{\rho}$ .
Unpacking the definitions, we see that for any  $b>0$  the laws of the functions
$z\mapsto\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\text{Conditional law given $(h,\eta)$ of $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ stopped upon exiting $B_{\rho R_{b}}$}}}\right\}$
(6.55)
are tight. Moreover, if  $P^{(b)}$  is any subsequential limit in law of these functions, then a.s.  $P$  is continuous and the following is true.
If  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is a path with the law  $P^{(b)}_{z}$ , then a.s.  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  does not stay at a single point for a positive interval of time before it exits  $B_{\rho R_{b}}$ . Since  $R_{b}\rightarrow\infty$  a.s. as  $b\rightarrow\infty$ , the conclusion of Proposition 6.1 now follows.
∎
7 Identifying the subsequential limit
We equip the space of distributions on  $\mathbbm{C}$  with the usual weak topology (whereby convergence of distributions is equivalent to convergence of the integrals against all smooth compactly supported text functions).
We also equip the space of continuous curves  $\mathbbm{R}\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  with the local uniform topology.
We know from Proposition 6.1 that the laws of the functions  $P^{\varepsilon}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  of (6.1) are tight.
By the Prokhorov theorem also the joint laws of  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})$  as  $\varepsilon$  varies are tight.
Before we explain the main ideas behind the identification of  $(h,\eta,P)$ , we point out that a priori we do not even know that  $P$  is determined by  $(h,\eta)$ . To explain what is the issue, note first that if we used the known tightness of  $P^{\varepsilon}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ , then any subsequential limit  $P$  of the family of laws  $P^{\varepsilon}$  could only be random insofar as  $(h,\eta)$  is random: i.e.,  $P$  would necessarily be determined by  $(h,\eta)$ . However, this approach would force us to deal with possibly random subsequences  $\varepsilon$  along which the convergence to  $P$  occurs and would add a serious layer of complication to our arguments. Instead, we prefer to work with the law of the triplet  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})$  which is also tight and consider a subsequential limit  $(h,\eta,P)$ . The trade-off, however, is that we do not know a priori that  $P$ , viewed as a random variable in the space  $\mathcal{C}$  of continuous functions from  $\mathbbm{C}$  to  $\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$ , is measurable with respect to  $(h,\eta)$ : indeed, it is straightforward to construct examples of random variables  $(X,Y_{n})$  converging to  $(X,Y)$  in distribution with  $Y_{n}$  measurable with respect to  $X$ , but  $Y$  not measurable with respect to  $X$ . This lack of a priori measurability will require specific arguments in various places (especially in Section 7.3).
We want to show that if  $(h,\eta,P)$  is a subsequential limit of these joint laws, then  $P_{z}$  is the law of the  $\gamma$ -Liouville Brownian motion associated with  $h$  started from  $z$  for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , up to a linear time-change. To do this, we first establish some basic properties (such as the Markov property) of any subsequential limit in Section 7.1. These properties are easy consequences of basic properties of random walk on random planar maps.
We then prove a general uniqueness criterion for Markovian time-changed Brownian motions in Section 7.2 (using general theory of Markov processes).
This criterion will show that  $P_{z}$  for  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  is the law as that of Liouville Brownian motion pre-composed with the linear time change  $t\mapsto ct$  for some random  $c>0$  which does not depend on  $c$ , but which may depend on  $(h,\eta,P)$ . In Section 7.3 we will argue that  $c$  is a.s. equal to a deterministic constant.
Then, we will change the time scaling in order to eliminate the dependence of this constant on the choice of subsequence, as discussed at the end of Section 1.4.
This will complete the proof of Theorem 1.2.
Finally, in Section 7.4 we will explain how to deduce the disk version of the theorem statement, Theorem 1.4, from Theorem 1.2.
We now record some definitions which will play a fundamental role in this section.
In each definition, we let  $P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)\in\mathcal{C}$  be a function from  $\mathbbm{C}$  to the set of probability measures on continuous paths  $[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  such that  $P_{z}$  for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  is supported on paths started from  $z$ .
We recall that the topology on the space of such functions  $P$  is defined in Section 6.
Definition 7.1.
We say that  $P$  is Markovian if the following is true.
Let  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and let  $X^{z}$  be sampled from  $P_{z}$ . For each  $s\geq 0$ , the conditional law of  $X_{s+\cdot}^{z}$  given  $X^{z}|_{[0,s]}$  is a.s. equal to  $P_{X_{s}}$ .
Definition 7.2.
We say that  $P$  defines a time-changed Brownian motion if the following is true.
Let  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and let  $X^{z}$  be sampled from  $P_{z}$ .
Then there is a standard planar Brownian motion  $\mathcal{B}$  started from  $z$  and a continuous, strictly increasing process  $u\mapsto\tau_{u}$  with  $\tau_{0}=0$  such that a.s.  $X^{z}_{u}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau_{u}}$  for each  $u\geq 0$ .
We say that  $P$  defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion if also  $P$  is Markovian.
Definition 7.3.
We say that a measure  $\mu$  on  $\mathbbm{C}$  is invariant for  $P$  if for every Borel set  $A\subset\mathbbm{C}$ ,
$\int_{\mathbbm{C}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{t}\in A}}\right]d\mu(z)=\mu(A)$
(7.1)
We say that  $\mu$  is reversible for  $P$  if for every pair of Borel sets  $A,B\subset\mathbbm{C}$ ,
$\int_{B}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{t}\in A}}\right]d\mu(z)=\int_{A}P_{w}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{t}\in B}}\right]d\mu(w).$
(7.2)
We note that if  $\mu$  is reversible for  $P$ , then  $\mu$  is stationary for  $P$ : just take  $B=\mathbbm{C}$  in (7.2).
7.1 Properties of subsequential limits
Let  $(h,\eta,P)$  be distributed according to a subsequential scaling limit of the joint law of  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})$  as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
Note that  $P$  is a continuous function  $\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$ .
In this section we will establish some properties for  $P$  which are known to also hold for Liouville Brownian motion due to results in [GRV16]. The key behind these properties is the a priori continuity in the starting point  $z$  of the laws  $P_{z}$ . More precisely, we show that  $P$  defines a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion and the LQG measure  $\mu_{h}$  is reversible for  $P$ . The proof of the first statement uses only the Markov property for random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  and the fact that  $P^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P$  in law w.r.t. the local uniform (in  $z$ ) topology. The proof of the second statement uses the fact that the counting measure on vertices of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , weighted by their degree, is reversible for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ ; the fact that this measure converges weakly to  $\mu_{h}$  under the SLE/LQG embedding (Corollary A.6); and the aforementioned convergence  $P^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P$ .
Lemma 7.4.
Almost surely, the random function  $P$  defines a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion in the sense of Definition 7.2.
To check the Markov property for  $P$  in proof of Lemma 7.4, we will use the following criterion for the convergence of conditional laws (see, e.g., [GP20, Lemma 4.3]).
Lemma 7.5.
Let  $(X_{n},Y_{n})$  be a sequence of pairs of random variables taking values in a product of separable metric spaces  $\Omega_{X}\times\Omega_{Y}$  and let  $(X,Y)$  be another such pair of random variables such that  $(X_{n},Y_{n})\rightarrow(X,Y)$  in law. Suppose further that there is a family of probability measures  $\{P_{y}:y\in\Omega_{Y}\}$  on  $\Omega_{X}$ , indexed by  $\Omega_{Y}$ , such that for each bounded continuous function  $f:\Omega_{X}\rightarrow\mathbbm{R}$ ,  $y\mapsto\mathbbm{E}_{P_{y}}(f)$  is a measurable function of  $y\in\Omega_{Y}$  and
$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[f(X_{n})\,|\,Y_{n}}}\right],Y_{n}}}\right)\rightarrow\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathbbm{E}_{P_{Y}}(f),Y}}\right)\quad\text{in law}.$
(7.3)
Then  $P_{Y}$  is a regular conditional law of  $X$  given  $Y$ .
Proof.
This elementary lemma (stated and proved in [GP20, Lemma 4.3]) is a straightforward consequence of the uniqueness of the conditional distribution as a probability kernel (see [Kal02, Theorem 6.5] and preceding definitions) since the assumption that  $y\mapsto\mathbbm{E}_{P_{y}}(f)$  is measurable guarantees that  $(y,B)\mapsto P_{y}(B)$  for  $y\in\Omega_{Y}$  and  $B$  a Borel set in  $\Omega_{X}$  is a probability kernel.
∎
The proof of Lemma 7.4 also involves the topology on curves viewed modulo time parametrization, which we now briefly recall.
If  $\beta_{1}:[0,T_{\beta_{1}}]\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\beta_{2}:[0,T_{\beta_{2}}]\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  are continuous curves defined on possibly different time intervals, we set
$\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}}}\right):=\inf_{\phi}\sup_{t\in[0,T_{\beta_{1}}]}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|\beta_{1}(t)-\beta_{2}(\phi(t))}}\right|$
(7.4)
where the infimum is over all increasing homeomorphisms  $\phi:[0,T_{\beta_{1}}]\rightarrow[0,T_{\beta_{2}}]$  (the CMP stands for “curves modulo parameterization”). It is shown in [AB99, Lemma 2.1] that  $\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}$  induces a complete metric on the set of curves viewed modulo time parameterization.
Since we will be working with curves defined for infinite time, we will use a local variant of the metric  $\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}$ . Suppose  $\beta_{1}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\beta_{2}:[0,\infty)\rightarrow\mathbbm{C}$  are two curves. For  $r>0$ , let  $T_{1,r}$  (resp.  $T_{2,r}$ ) be the first exit time of  $\beta_{1}$  (resp.  $\beta_{2}$ ) from the ball  $B_{r}(0)$  (or 0 if the curve starts outside  $B_{r}(0)$ ).
We define
$\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}_{\operatorname{loc}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1},\beta_{2}}}\right):=\int_{1}^{\infty}e^{-r}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1\wedge\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1}|_{[0,T_{1,r}]},\beta_{2}|_{[0,T_{2,r}]}}}\right)}}\right)\,dr,$
(7.5)
so that  $\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}_{\operatorname{loc}}(\beta^{n},\beta)\rightarrow 0$  if and only if for Lebesgue a.e.  $r>0$ ,  $\beta^{n}$  stopped at its first exit time from  $B_{r}(0)$  converges to  $\beta$  stopped at its first exit time from  $B_{r}(0)$  with respect to the metric (7.4).
We note that the definition (7.4) of  $\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1}|_{[0,T_{1,r}]},\beta_{2}|_{[0,T_{2,r}]}}}\right)$  makes sense even if one or both of  $T_{1,r}$  or  $T_{2,r}$  is infinite, provided we allow  $\mathbbm{d}^{\operatorname{CMP}}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\beta_{1}|_{[0,T_{1,r}]},\beta_{2}|_{[0,T_{2,r}]}}}\right)=\infty$  (this doesn’t pose a problem due to the  $1\wedge$  in (7.5)).
Proof of Lemma 7.4.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , let  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  denote a random path whose conditional law given  $(h,\eta,P)$  is  $P_{z}$ .
Let  $\mathcal{E}$  be a sequence of  $\varepsilon$ ’s tending to zero along which  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$  in law as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
By [GMS21, Theorem 3.4], we know that for each fixed  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , the conditional law given  $(h,\eta)$  of the process  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  converges in distribution to Brownian motion w.r.t. the local topology on curves viewed modulo time parametrization, as defined in (7.5).
The conditional law given  $(h,\eta)$  of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ , viewed modulo time parametrization, is a continuous functional of the conditional law  $P_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ .
Since  $P_{z}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P_{z}$  in law along  $\mathcal{E}$ , we infer that  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is a continuous time change of Brownian motion.
The last part of Proposition 6.1 implies that the time change function is strictly increasing.
Therefore,  $P$  defines a time-changed Brownian motion in the sense of Definition 7.2.
Now we need to check the Markov property for  $\widehat{X}^{z}$ . In general, a limit of a Markov process need not be Markov, as is easily checked. Ultimately, we will obtain the Markov property as a result of
Lemma 7.5 and the uniformity (in  $z$ ) of the assumed convergence of  $P^{\varepsilon}_{z}$  to  $P_{z}$ . We explain the details more precisely now.
By the Markov property of random walk, for each  $\varepsilon>0$  the conditional law66
6
We look at time  $\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil$  instead of time  $t$  since by the definition of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ ,  $\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}^{z,\varepsilon}$  is of the form  $\eta(x)$  for some  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}=\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ . Otherwise, since  $\widehat{X}$  is defined by linear interpolation, the Markov property is not easily expressed.
of  $s\mapsto\widehat{X}_{s+\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}^{z,\varepsilon}$  given  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon},\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}|_{[0,{\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}]})$  is  $P^{\varepsilon}_{\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}^{z,\varepsilon}}$ .
Along  $\mathcal{E}$ , we have that the law of  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon},\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon})$  converges to that of  $(h,\eta,P,\widehat{X}^{z})$ .
Hence, since the topology for  $P$  is the local uniform topology, we also have that
this implies the convergence in law
$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon},\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}|_{[0,{\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}]},\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\cdot+\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil},P^{\varepsilon}_{\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}^{z,\varepsilon}}}}\right)\rightarrow\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(h,\eta,P,\widehat{X}^{z}|_{[0,t]},\widehat{X}^{z}_{\cdot+t},P_{\widehat{X}_{t}^{z}}}}\right).$
We now apply Lemma 7.5 with  $X_{n}=\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\cdot+\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil}$ ,  $Y_{n}=(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon},\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}|_{[0,\varepsilon\lceil t/\varepsilon\rceil]})$ ,  $X=\widehat{X}^{z}_{\cdot+t}$ ,  $Y=(h,\eta,P,\widehat{X}^{z}|_{[0,t]})$ , and  $P_{Y}=P_{\widehat{X}_{t}^{z}}$ .
This shows that  $P_{\widehat{X}_{t}^{z}}$  is the conditional law of  $\widehat{X}^{z}_{\cdot+t}$  given  $(h,\eta,P,\widehat{X}^{z}|_{[0,t]})$ , as required.
∎
Lemma 7.6.
Almost surely, the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure  $\mu_{h}$  is reversible for  $P$  (Definition 7.3).
The idea of the proof of Lemma 7.6 is as follows. The measure on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  which assigns mass  $\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)$  to each vertex  $x$  is reversible for the simple random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , and under the embedding  $x\mapsto\eta(x)$  this measure converges in law to  $\mu_{h}$  (see Corollary A.6).
We want to pass this through to the limit to get Lemma 7.6.
The next lemma is the main technical input in the proof of Lemma 7.6. It gives us the convergence statements necessary to pass the reversibility of random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  through to the limit.
For the statement of the lemma, we will use the following notation.
For a set  $A\subset\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ , let
$A^{\varepsilon}:=\bigcup_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(A)}H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$
(7.6)
be the union of the space-filling SLE cells which intersect  $A$ .
Lemma 7.7.
Let  $\mathcal{E}$  be a sequence of  $\varepsilon$ -values tending to zero along which  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$  in law.
There is a coupling of  $(h,\eta)$  with a sequence of field / curve pairs  $(h^{\varepsilon},\eta^{\varepsilon})\overset{d}{=}(h,\eta)$  for  $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{E}$  such that the following is true. Define  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  and  $\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  with  $(h^{\varepsilon},\eta^{\varepsilon})$  in place of  $(h,\eta)$ .
Let  $t>0$ , let  $U,V\subset\mathbbm{C}$  be bounded open sets, and define  $V^{\varepsilon}$  as in (7.6).
For each  $\delta>0$ , it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta^{\varepsilon}(X_{\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}^{\varepsilon})\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\leq 6\int_{\overline{U}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{V}}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)+\delta$
(7.7)
and
$\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta^{\varepsilon}(X_{\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}^{\varepsilon})\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\geq 6\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in V}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)-\delta.$
(7.8)
Proof.
Let  $\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}$  be the measure on  $\mathbbm{C}$  whose restriction to each cell  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  for  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  is equal to  $\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)$  times  $\mu_{h}|_{\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])}$ .
Then by the definition of  $\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}$ ,
$\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta(X_{\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}^{\varepsilon})\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)=\int_{U^{\varepsilon}}P_{z}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]d\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}(w),\quad\forall t\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{N}_{0}.$
(7.9)
Here we note that  $z\mapsto P_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  is constant on the interior of each cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ . Basically, (7.7) and (7.8) follow from the fact that the joint law of  $(\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon},P^{\varepsilon})$  converges to the joint law of  $(6\mu_{h},P)$  w.r.t. the local weak topology on the first coordinate and the topology of Section 6 on the second coordinate.
Let us now make this more precise.
By Corollary A.6, as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  the measure  $\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}$  converges in probability to  $6\mu_{h}$  w.r.t. the local Prokhorov topology. (The factor 6 in front of  $\mu_{h}$  is related to some fairly general topological properties of parabolic unimodular surfaces, see e.g. [AHNR16].)
Since  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$  in law and  $\mu_{h}$  is a measurable function of  $h$ , it follows that  $(h,\eta,\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon},P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,6\mu_{h},P)$  in law.
By the Skorokhod theorem, we can find a coupling of a sequence of field / curve pairs  $(h^{\varepsilon},\eta^{\varepsilon})\overset{d}{=}(h,\eta)$  for  $\varepsilon\in\mathcal{E}$  with  $(h,\eta)$  such that the following is true. If we construct  $\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}$  and  $P^{\varepsilon}$  with  $(h^{\varepsilon},\eta^{\varepsilon})$  in place of  $(h,\eta)$ , then a.s.
$\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow\mu_{h}\quad\text{and}\quad P^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P,\quad\text{as $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$}.$
(7.10)
Henceforth fix such a coupling and let all objects with a superscript  $\varepsilon$  be defined with  $(h^{\varepsilon},\eta^{\varepsilon})$  in place of  $(h,\eta)$ .
By the definition of the topology for  $P$  from Section 6, the Prokhorov distance between  $P_{z}^{\varepsilon}$  and  $P_{z}$  converges to zero uniformly on a neighborhood of  $\overline{U}$ . Furthermore, by Lemma 2.4 the maximal distance from any point in  $V^{\varepsilon}$  to  $V$  tends to zero in probability as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ . Consequently, for each  $\zeta>0$  it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$P_{z}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\leq P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}\in B_{\zeta}(V)}}\right]+\zeta,\quad\forall z\in U^{\varepsilon}.$
(7.11)
By the continuity of  $z\mapsto P_{z}$  and  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}_{t}$ , the Prokhorov distance between the  $P_{z}$ -laws of  $\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}$  and  $\widehat{X}_{t}$  converges in probability to zero as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , uniformly over all  $z$  in a neigborhood of  $\overline{U}$ . Hence, (7.11) holds with  $\widehat{X}_{t}$  in place of  $\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}$ .
By integrating this last variant of (7.11) over  $U^{\varepsilon}$  w.r.t.  $\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}$  and using (7.9), we get that with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta(X_{\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}^{\varepsilon})\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\leq\int_{U^{\varepsilon}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in B_{\zeta}(V)}}\right]d\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}(z)+\zeta\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}(U^{\varepsilon}).$
(7.12)
We know that  $\mu_{h^{\varepsilon}}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow\mu_{h}$  a.s. weakly as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  along  $\mathcal{E}$  and  $z\mapsto P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{B_{\zeta}(V)}}}\right]$  is upper semicontinuous (due to the Prokhorov continuity of  $z\mapsto P_{z}$ ).
It follows (using a consequence of the portmanteau theorem, see [Bil13, Exercice 2.6, Chapter I]) that with probability tending to 1 as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the right side of (7.12) is at most
$\int_{\overline{U}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{B_{\zeta}(V)}}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)+\zeta\mu_{h}(\overline{V})+\zeta.$
(7.13)
Recalling (7.12) and choosing  $\zeta$  to be sufficiently small, depending on  $\delta$ , gives (7.7).
To obtain (7.8), we first use the Prokhorov convergence  $P_{z}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P_{z}$  as in (7.11) to get that for each  $\zeta>0$  it holds with probability tending to 1 as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
