$P_{z}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\geq P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor}\in V\setminus B_{\zeta}(\partial V)}}\right]-\zeta,\quad\forall z\in U^{\varepsilon}.$
(7.14)
We then argue exactly as in the proof of (7.7) but with the inequality signs reversed.
∎
We can now prove the following weaker version of Lemma 7.6.
Lemma 7.8.
Let  $U,V\subset\mathbbm{C}$  be deterministic bounded open sets and let  $t>0$ . Almost surely,
$\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in V}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)\leq\int_{\overline{V}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{U}}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z).$
(7.15)
Proof.
We know that the uniform measure on vertices  $x$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  weighted by  $\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)$  is reversible for the random walk on  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ . That is, for any  $x\in\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  and any  $j\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{j}^{\varepsilon}=y}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)=\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{y}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[X_{j}^{\varepsilon}=x}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(y).$
(7.16)
Summing (7.16) over all  $x\in\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)$  and  $y\in\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(V)$  shows that for each  $j\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(U)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{x}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta(X_{j}^{\varepsilon})\in V^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(V)}\overline{\mathbbm{P}}_{y}^{\varepsilon}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\eta(X_{j}^{\varepsilon})\in U^{\varepsilon}}}\right]\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(y).$
(7.17)
We now take  $j=\varepsilon\lfloor t/\varepsilon\rfloor$  and apply Lemma 7.7 to get (7.15).
∎
The inequality of Lemma 7.8 could be converted into an equality if we knew that  $\mu_{h}(\partial V)=0$  and  $\int_{\overline{V}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\partial U}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)=0$ . This is achieved by means of the following lemma.
Lemma 7.9.
Let  $A,U\subset\mathbbm{C}$  be deterministic bounded sets such that  $A$  is closed with zero Lebesgue measure and  $U$  is open.
For each  $t>0$ , a.s.
$\mu_{h}(A)=0\quad\text{and}\quad\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in A}}\right]\,d\mu_{h}(z)=0.$
(7.18)
Proof.
It is immediate from the basic properties of the LQG area measure that  $\mu_{h}(A)=0$  a.s. Indeed, the analogous statement with  $h$  replaced by a zero-boundary GFF an any open domain in  $\mathbbm{C}$  follows from, e.g., [DS11, Proposition 1.2] or [Ber17, Theorem 1.1]. The statement that  $\mu_{h}(A)=0$  a.s. follows from this and straightforward absolute continuity considerations.
To get the second assertion in (7.18), fix  $\delta>0$  (which we will eventually send to zero). By Lemma 7.8 applied with  $V=B_{\delta}(A)$ , a.s.
$\displaystyle\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in A}}\right]\,d\mu_{h}(z)$
$\displaystyle\leq\int_{U}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in B_{\delta}(A)}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)$
$\displaystyle\leq\int_{\overline{B_{\delta}(A)}}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in\overline{U}}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)$
$\displaystyle\leq\mu_{h}(\overline{B_{\delta}(A)}).$
(7.19)
Since  $\mu_{h}(A)=0$  and  $\overline{B_{\delta}(A)}$  decreases to  $A$  as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  (since  $A$  is closed) we can send  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  in (7.19) to conclude the proof.
∎
Proof of Lemma 7.6.
Fix  $t>0$ . We need to show that a.s. for any two Borel sets  $A,B\subset\mathbbm{C}$ ,
$\int_{A}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in B}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z)=\int_{B}P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{X}_{t}\in A}}\right]d\mu_{h}(z).$
(7.20)
By Lemmas 7.8 and 7.9, (7.20) holds a.s. if  $A,B$  are fixed open sets whose boundaries have zero Lebesgue measure.
In fact, these lemmas (applied with  $U$  and  $V$  equal to the interiors of  $A$  and  $B$ ) imply that (7.20) holds a.s. if  $A,B$  are fixed Borel sets such that  $\partial A$  and  $\partial B$  have zero Lebesgue measure,  $\overline{A}$  is equal to closure of the interior of  $A$ , and  $\overline{B}$  is equal to closure of the interior of  $B$ .
We now fix  $R>0$  and show that a.s. (7.20) holds for all Borel sets  $A,B\subset B_{R}(0)$ .
We do this using the monotone class theorem.
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be the collection of subsets of  $B_{R}(0)$  which can be expressed in terms of finite unions and intersections of sets of the form  $B_{r}(z)$  or  $B_{R}(0)\setminus B_{r}(z)$  for  $r\in\mathbbm{Q}\cap(0,\infty)$  and  $z\in\mathbbm{Q}^{2}$ .
Then  $\mathcal{A}$  has the following properties. It is countable; it is closed under finite unions and intersections; it generates the Borel  $\sigma$ -algebra of  $B_{R}(0)$ ; we have  $B_{R}(0)\setminus A\in\mathcal{A}$  for each  $A\in\mathcal{A}$ ; the boundary of each  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  has zero Lebesgue measure; and for each  $A\in\mathcal{A}$  the closure  $\overline{A}$  is also equal to the closure of the interior of  $A$ .
From this, we infer that a.s. (7.20) holds simultaneously for each  $A,B\in\mathcal{A}$ .
Due to the monotone convergence theorem, for each fixed  $A$  the set of Borel sets  $B$  for which (7.20) holds is closed under increasing unions and intersections.
By two applications of the monotone class theorem (one for each of  $A$  and  $B$ ), we get that a.s. (7.20) holds for all Borel sets  $A,B\subset B_{R}(0)$ . Sending  $R\rightarrow\infty$  now concludes the proof.
∎
7.2 Time-changed Brownian motions are determined by invariant measures
We now have two random functions  $\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$  which each define a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion, namely the subsequential limit  $P$  above and the function which takes  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  to the law of Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t.  $h$  started from  $z$ . These functions have a common reversible measure, namely the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure.
We want to show that these two functions are a.s. the same up to a global linear time change.
Proposition 7.10.
Let  $P^{1},P^{2}$  be two continuous mappings  $\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C})}}\right)$  which each define a Markovian time changed Brownian motion.
Assume that there is a non-zero measure  $\mu$  which is invariant for both  $P^{1}$  and  $P^{2}$ .
There is a determinsitic constant  $c>0$  such that the following is true.
For each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , a process with the law  $P_{z}^{1}$  can be obtained by composing a process with the law  $P_{z}^{2}$  by the linear time change  $t\mapsto ct$ .
We note that Proposition 7.10, applied under the conditional law given  $h$ , immediately implies Theorem 1.5 since the conditional law of LBM given  $h$  is a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion which leaves the LQG measure  $\mu_{h}$  invariant [GRV16].
Proposition 7.10 is a consequence of results in the general theory of positive continuous additive functionals of Brownian motion.
To explain how the proposition is proven, we will need to review some of this theory.
In what follows, for  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  we let  $\mathbbm{P}_{z}$  be the law of standard planar Brownian motion  $\mathcal{B}$  started from  $z$ .
Definition 7.11.
A positive continuous additive functional (PCAF) of  $\mathcal{B}$  is a process  $t\mapsto\mathcal{A}_{t}$ , defined for all possible choices of starting points for  $\mathcal{B}$ , which is adapted to the filtration generated by  $\mathcal{B}$  (completed by null events), such that the following is true.
Almost surely,  $\mathcal{A}_{0}=0$  and  $\mathcal{A}_{t}$  is continuous and non-decreasing in  $t$ .
Furthermore, for each  $s,t\geq 0$ , a.s.
$\mathcal{A}_{s+t}=\mathcal{A}_{t}+\mathcal{A}_{s}\circ\theta_{t}$
(7.21)
where  $\theta_{t}$  is the shift operator on the state space for  $\mathcal{B}$  defined by  $\theta_{t}(\mathcal{B})=\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$ .
Definition 7.11 is related to Proposition 7.10 by the following lemma.
Lemma 7.12.
Suppose that  $P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  is continuous and defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion as in Definition 7.1.
Write  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$  for a process with the law  $P_{z}$  for some starting point  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ .
Let  $u\mapsto\tau_{u}$  be the time change used to get from standard Brownian motion to  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ , as in Definition 7.2, and for  $t\geq 0$  let  $\mathcal{A}_{t}=\tau^{-1}(t):=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{u\geq 0:\tau_{u}=t}}\right\}$ .
Then  $\mathcal{A}$  is a PCAF for the Brownian motion  $\mathcal{B}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}$ .
For the proof of Lemma 7.12, we need the following elementary fact.
Lemma 7.13.
Suppose that  $P:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  is continuous and defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion.
Then  $P$  is strongly Markovian, i.e., if  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}$  is sampled from  $P_{z}$  then for each stopping time  $\sigma$  for  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}$ , the conditional law of  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\sigma+\cdot}^{z}$  given  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}|_{[0,\sigma]}$  is  $P_{\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{\sigma}}$ .
Proof.
If  $\sigma$  takes on only countably many possible values, the Markov property at time  $\sigma$  is immediate from the case of a deterministic time.
Due to the continuity of  $z\mapsto P_{z}$  and the a.s. continuity of a process with the law  $P$ , we can approximate a general stopping time by a sequence of stopping times which take on only countably many possible values to get the result in general.
∎
Proof of Lemma 7.12.
Since  $u\mapsto\tau_{u}$  is continuous, strictly increasing, and satisfies  $\tau_{0}=0$ , the same is also true for  $\mathcal{A}$ , and furthermore  $\tau_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}=\mathcal{A}_{\tau_{t}}=t$ , whence  $\mathcal{B}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}$  for any  $t\geq 0$ .
The time  $\mathcal{A}_{t}$  is the smallest  $u\geq 0$  for which the quadratic variation of  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}|_{[0,u]}$  is  $t$ .
This implies in particular that  $\mathcal{A}_{t}$  is a stopping time for  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ .
Before arguing that  $\mathcal{A}$  is adapted, we will first check that for  $0\leq a<b\leq\infty$ ,
$\sigma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\{\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}\}_{u\in[0,\mathcal{A}_{b}-\mathcal{A}_{a}]}}}\right)=\sigma\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathcal{B}|_{[a,b]},\{\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{A}_{a}\}_{t\in[a,b]}}}\right).$
(7.22)
Indeed, for any  $t\in[a,b]$  we have that  $\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{A}_{a}$  is the first time that the quadratic variation of the process  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+\cdot}$  reaches  $t-a$ , and  $\mathcal{B}_{t}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}$ .
This shows that the left  $\sigma$ -algebra in (7.22) contains the right  $\sigma$ -algebra.
For the reverse inclusion, we now observe that for each  $u\in[0,\mathcal{A}_{b}-\mathcal{A}_{a}]$  we have  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}}$  and  $\tau_{\mathcal{A}_{a}+u}=\inf\{t\geq a:\mathcal{A}_{t}-\mathcal{A}_{a}=u\}$ .
By (7.22) (applied with  $(a,b)=(0,t)$  and with  $(a,b)=(t,\infty)$ ) and Lemma 7.13 (applied with  $\sigma=\mathcal{A}_{t}$ ), we get that the pairs  $(\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot},\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t})$  and  $(\mathcal{B}|_{[0,t]},\mathcal{A}|_{[0,t]})$  are conditionally independent given  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}}$ , equivalently, given  $\mathcal{B}_{t}$ .
We will now argue that  $\mathcal{A}$  is a.s. determined by  $\mathcal{B}$ .
Indeed, it follows from the above that if we condition on  $\mathcal{B}$  then the process  $\mathcal{A}$  is continuous with conditionally independent increments.
It follows that the conditional law of  $\mathcal{A}$  given  $\mathcal{B}$  is that of a Gaussian process: indeed, it is easy to see from the independence of the increments that the centered process is a continuous martingale with deterministic quadratic variation, conditionally on  $\mathcal{B}$ .
But,  $\mathcal{A}$  is non-negative, so the conditional law of  $\mathcal{A}$  given  $\mathcal{B}$  must be a point mass at some  $\mathcal{B}$ -measurable continuous increasing function.
That is,  $\mathcal{A}$  is a.s. determined by  $\mathcal{B}$  (which implies that also  $\tau=\mathcal{A}^{-1}$  and  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\cdot}=\mathcal{B}_{\tau(\cdot)}$  are a.s. determined by  $\mathcal{B}$ ) .
Since  $(\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot},\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t})$  and  $(\mathcal{B}|_{[0,t]},\mathcal{A}|_{[0,t]})$  are conditionally independent given  $\mathcal{B}_{t}$ , it follows that  $\mathcal{A}|_{[0,t]}$  is a.s. determined by  $\mathcal{B}|_{[0,t]}$  and that  $\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}$  is a.s. determined by  $\mathcal{B}|_{[t,\infty)}$ . In particular,  $\mathcal{A}$  is adapted to the natural filtration of  $\mathcal{B}$  completed by null events and  $\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}$  is a.s. given by a functional of the shifted process  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$ .
Hence for each  $t,s\geq 0$  there is a measurable function  $F_{t,s}$  from continuous paths in  $\mathbbm{C}$  to  $[0,\infty)$  such that a.s.  $F_{t,s}(\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot})=\mathcal{A}_{t+s}-\mathcal{A}_{t}$ , i.e.,
$\mathcal{A}_{t+s}=\mathcal{A}_{t}+F_{t,s}\circ\theta_{t}.$
(7.23)
We need to check that the functional  $F_{t,s}$  does not depend on  $t$ .
The process  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  is obtained by parameterizing  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}$  by its quadratic variation, so the functional which takes in  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}$  and outputs  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  does not depend on  $t$ .
Since  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  a.s. determines  $\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}$ , it follows that  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  a.s. determines  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}$ , i.e., there is a measurable functional which takes in  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  and a.s. outputs  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}$ .
Since the functional which takes in  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}$  and outputs  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  does not depend on  $t$ , it follows that the functional which goes in the opposite direction can be taken to not depend on  $t$  either.
Since  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{\mathcal{A}_{t}+\cdot}$  determines  $\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}$  in a manner which does not depend on  $t$ , we get that  $\mathcal{B}_{t+\cdot}$  a.s. determines  $\mathcal{A}_{t+\cdot}-\mathcal{A}_{t}$  in a manner which does not depend on  $t$ , i.e.,  $F_{t,s}$  does not depend on  $t$ . In particular,  $F_{t,s}=F_{0,s}$  is the functional which a.s. takes  $\mathcal{B}$  to  $\mathcal{A}_{s}$ . By (7.23),  $\mathcal{A}$  is a PCAF.
∎
PCAFs are in bijective correspondence with so-called Revuz measures, defined as follows.
Definition 7.14.
A Revuz measure is a measure  $\mu$  on  $\mathbbm{C}$  such that  $\mu(A)=0$  for each set  $A$  which is polar for the Brownian motion  $\mathcal{B}$  (i.e., it is a.s. never hit by  $\mathcal{B}$ ).
From [FOT11, Theorem 5.1.3] (here the Hunt process in the theorem statement is planar Brownian motion), we know that there is a bijective correspondence between PCAFs and Revuz measures.
For each PCAF  $\mathcal{A}$  there exists a unique Revuz measure  $\mu$  such that for any two bounded continuous functions  $f,g:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow[0,\infty)$ ,
$\int_{\mathbbm{C}}\mathbbm{E}_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\int_{0}^{t}f(B_{s})\,d\mathcal{A}_{s}}}\right]g(z)\,dz=\int_{0}^{t}\int_{\mathbbm{C}}\int_{\mathbbm{C}}p_{s}(z,w)f(w)g(z)\,d\mu(w)\,dz\,ds$
(7.24)
and for every Revuz measure  $\mu$  there exists a unique PCAF  $\mathcal{A}$  for which (7.24) holds.
Here,  $d\mathcal{A}_{s}$  is interpreted as a Lebesgue-Stieljes measure.
We call  $\mu$  the Revuz measure of  $\mathcal{A}$ .
For a PCAF  $\mathcal{A}$ , we can define the time-changed process
$\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{u}:=\mathcal{B}_{\tau_{u}},\quad\text{where}\quad\tau_{u}:=\inf\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{t\geq 0:\mathcal{A}_{t}=u}}\right\}.$
(7.25)
Then the law of  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$  for varying choices of starting points defines a Markovian time changed Brownian motion in the sense of Definition 7.1.
By [FOT11, Theorem 6.2.1(i)], the Revuz measure of  $\mathcal{A}$  is reversible (hence invariant) for  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ .
In fact, the Revuz measure of  $\mathcal{A}$  is the only invariant measure for  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ , up to multiplication by a deterministic constant, as shown by the following lemma.
Lemma 7.15.
Let  $P$  define a Markovian time changed Brownian motion and assume that  $z\mapsto P_{z}$  is continuous.
Let  $\mathcal{A}$  be the corresponding PCAF as in Lemma 7.12 and let  $\mu$  be the Revuz measure of  $\mathcal{A}$ .
Then any other invariant measure for  $P$  is a deterministic constant multiple of  $\mu$ .
To prove Lemma 7.15, we will use a general criterion for the uniqueness of invariant measures for Markov processes; see, e.g., [RY99, Chapter X, Section 3]. One of the hypotheses of this criterion involves the resolvent associated with  $P$ , which is the operator  $R^{\lambda}:L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C})\rightarrow L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C})$  defined by
$\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}E_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}_{t})}}\right]\,dt,$
(7.26)
where  $E_{z}$  denotes expectation w.r.t.  $P_{z}$ .
Lemma 7.16.
Let  $P$  define a Markovian time changed Brownian motion and assume that  $z\mapsto P_{z}$  is continuous. If  $f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C})$ , then  $\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f$  is continuous.
That is,  $P$  is strongly Feller.
Proof.
The proof is based on the fact that hitting distributions of Brownian motion (i.e., harmonic measure) depend continuously on the starting point in the total variation sense. This allows us to show that if  $|z-w|$  is small then we can couple processes sampled from  $P_{z}$  and  $P_{w}$  so that they agree after leaving a small ball centered at  $z$ . When the processes are coupled together in this way, it is not hard to check that for a fixed choice of  $f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C})$ , it holds that  $|\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)-\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(w)|$  is small. A similar argument is used to prove the strong Feller property for Liouville Brownian motion in [GRV14, Theorem 2.4].
Step 1: defining the coupling.
Fix  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  and  $\varepsilon>0$ .
A path sampled from the law  $P_{z}$  a.s. does not stay constant for any non-trivial interval of time, so we can find  $\delta_{0}\in(0,1)$  such that
$P_{z}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ exits $B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$ before time $\varepsilon$}}}\right]\geq 1-\varepsilon.$
(7.27)
Since  $P_{w}$  depends continuously on  $w$  in the Prokhorov distance, there exists  $\delta_{1}\in(0,\delta_{0}]$  such that
$P_{w}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\text{$\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ exits $B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$ before time $2\varepsilon$}}}\right]\geq 1-2\varepsilon,\quad\forall w\in B_{\delta_{1}}(z).$
(7.28)
The harmonic measure on  $\partial B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$  as viewed from  $w\in B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$  (which is the same as that of Brownian motion and is therefore known explicitly) depends continuously on  $w$  in the total variation sense.
Therefore, we can find  $\delta_{2}\in(0,\delta_{0}]$  such that for any  $w\in B_{\delta_{2}}(z)$ , we can find a coupling of  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}\sim P_{z}$  and  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}\sim P_{w}$  such that with probability at least  $1-\varepsilon$ ,  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}$  and  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}$  exit  $B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$  at the same point.
Let  $T_{z}$  and  $T_{w}$  denote the exit times of  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}$  and  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}$  from  $B_{\delta_{0}}(z)$ , respectively.
Then our coupling is such that  $\mathbbm{P}[\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{T_{z}}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{T_{w}}]\geq 1-\varepsilon$ . By the strong Markov property (Lemma 7.13) we can re-couple so that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{T_{z}+s}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{T_{w}+s},\>\forall s\geq 0}}\right]\geq 1-\varepsilon.$
(7.29)
Henceforth fix such a coupling and let
$E:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{T_{z}+s}=\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{T_{w}+s},\>\forall s\geq 0}}\right\}\cap\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{T_{z}\vee T_{w}\leq 2\varepsilon}}\right\},$
(7.30)
so that by (7.28) and (7.29) we have  $\mathbbm{P}[E]\geq 1-5\varepsilon$ .
Step 2: bounding the resolvent.
Now fix  $f\in L^{\infty}(\mathbbm{C})$ .
By considering the positive and negative parts of  $f$  separately, we can assume without loss of generality that  $f\geq 0$ .
We have
$\displaystyle\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)$
$\displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]$
$\displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E^{c}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]$
$\displaystyle=\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{T_{z}}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda(s+T_{z})}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})\,ds}}\right]+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E^{c}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt}}\right]$
and similarly with  $w$  in place of  $z$ .
By subtracting the formulas for  $z$  and  $w$  and using the triangle inequality, we get
$\displaystyle|\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)-\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(w)|$
$\displaystyle\leq\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\int_{0}^{T_{z}}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})\,dt+\int_{0}^{T_{w}}e^{-\lambda t}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{t})\,dt}}\right)}}\right]$
$\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|e^{-\lambda(s+T_{z})}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})-e^{-\lambda(s+T_{w})}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{s+T_{w}})}}\right|\,ds}}\right]$
$\displaystyle\qquad\qquad+\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E^{c}}\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda t}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{t})+f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{t})}}\right)\,dt}}\right]$
(7.31)
On  $E$ , we have  $T_{z}\vee T_{w}\leq 2\varepsilon$ , which implies that the first expectation on the right side of (7.31) is at most  $4\varepsilon\|f\|_{\infty}$ .
Furthermore, on  $E$  we have  $f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})=f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{w}_{s+T_{w}})$  for each  $s\geq 0$ , so the second expectation on the right side of (7.31) is equal to
$\mathbbm{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathbbm{1}_{E}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left|e^{-\lambda T_{z}}-e^{-\lambda T_{w}}}}\right|\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-\lambda s}f(\widehat{\mathcal{B}}^{z}_{s+T_{z}})\,ds}}\right],$
(7.32)
which in turn is at most  $(1-e^{-2\lambda\varepsilon})\lambda^{-1}\|f\|_{\infty}$  since  $T_{z}\vee T_{w}\leq 2\varepsilon$  on  $E$ .
Finally, since  $\mathbbm{P}[E^{c}]\leq 4\varepsilon$  the last term on the right side of (7.31) is at most  $8\varepsilon\lambda^{-1}\|f\|_{\infty}$ .
Plugging the above estimates into (7.31) gives
$|\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(z)-\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f(w)|\leq o_{\varepsilon}(1)\|f\|_{\infty}$
(7.33)
where the  $o_{\varepsilon}(1)$  tends to zero as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  at a rate depending only on  $\lambda$ . Since  $\varepsilon>0$  was arbitrary we infer that  $\mathcal{R}^{\lambda}f$  is continuous at  $z$ .
∎
Proof of Lemma 7.15.
As discussed just after (7.25), the measure  $\mu$  is reversible, hence invariant, for  $P$ .
If  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$  is sampled from  $P_{z}$  for some  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ , then  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$  is a time change of Brownian motion, so every open subset of  $\mathbbm{C}$  is recurrent for  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ . Moreover, Lemma 7.16 says that  $P$  is strongly Feller.
By [RY99, Chapter X, Proposition 3.9], the process  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$  is Harris recurrent w.r.t. the measure  $\mu$ , i.e., each open set  $A\subset\mathbbm{C}$  with  $\mu(A)>0$  is recurrent for  $\widehat{\mathcal{B}}$ .
From this and the ergodic theorem for additive functionals of Brownian motion [RY99, Chapter X, Theorem 3.12] (see also [RY99, Chapter X, Exercise 3.14]) one obtains the uniqueness of the invariant measure for  $P$  up to multiplication by a deterministic constant factor.
∎
Proof of Proposition 7.10.
Let  $\mathcal{A}^{1}$  and  $\mathcal{A}^{2}$  be the PCAFs associated with  $P^{1}$  and  $P^{2}$ , as in Lemma 7.12.
Let  $\mu^{1}$  and  $\mu^{2}$  be the Revuz measures associated with these PCAFs.
By the discussion just after (7.25), we know that  $\mu^{1}$  (resp.  $\mu^{2}$ ) is invariant for  $P^{1}$  (resp.  $P^{2}$ ).
By Lemma 7.15, we know that each of  $P^{1}$  and  $P^{2}$  has a unique invariant measure, up to multiplication by a deterministic constant factor.
Therefore, there are deterministic constants  $c_{1},c_{2}>0$  such that a.s.  $\mu^{1}=c_{1}\mu$  and  $\mu^{2}=c_{2}\mu$ .
Since the Revuz measure uniquely determines the PCAF, we get that  $\mathcal{A}^{1}=(c_{1}/c_{2})\mathcal{A}^{2}$ .
By the definitions of  $\mathcal{A}^{1}$  and  $\mathcal{A}^{2}$ , this implies Proposition 7.10.
∎
7.3 Proof of Theorem 1.2
As above, let  $(h,\eta,P)$  be a subsequential limit of the joint laws of  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})$  as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
Let us first record what we get from Proposition 7.10.
Lemma 7.17.
There is a random variable  $c>0$ , which is measurable with respect to the  $\sigma$ -algebra generated by  $(h,\eta,P)$  (completed by null sets), such that a.s. for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  the law  $P_{z}$  is the same as the conditional law given  $h$  of the Liouville Brownian motion started from  $z$  pre-composed with the time change  $t\mapsto ct$ .
Proof.
By Lemma 7.4,  $P$  defines a Markovian time-changed Brownian motion and by Lemma 7.6 the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure  $\mu_{h}$  is reversible, hence invariant, for  $P$ .
It is shown in [GRV16] that the same properties are a.s. true for the function  $P^{\operatorname{LBM}}:\mathbbm{C}\rightarrow\operatorname{Prob}(C([0,\infty),\mathbbm{C}))$  which maps  $z$  to the conditional law of LBM started from  $z$  given  $h$ .
The lemma therefore follows from Proposition 7.10 applied under the conditional law given  $(h,\eta,P)$ .
∎
We claim the following.
Lemma 7.18.
The random variable  $c>0$  from Lemma 7.17 is a.s. equal to a deterministic constant.
We will prove Lemma 7.18 just below. We first assume the lemma and conclude the proof of Theorem 1.2.
Proof of Theorem 1.2, assuming Lemma 7.18.
Let  $\mathcal{E}$  be a sequence of  $\varepsilon$ -values tending to zero along which  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$  in law.
Lemmas 7.17 and 7.18 together imply that there is a deterministic constant  $c>0$  such that a.s.  $P_{z}$  for each  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  is the law of Liouville Brownian motion started from  $z$  pre-composed with the time change  $t\mapsto ct$ .
The constant  $c$  may depend on the choice of subsequence  $\mathcal{E}$  (equivalently,  $c$  may depend on the law of  $(h,\eta,P)$ ).
We do not know how to rule this out so we get around the issue as follows.
Recall that, in the notation used in Section 6 and in the theorem statement,  $P^{\varepsilon}$  is the conditional law of  $(\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{\cdot/\varepsilon}))_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ .
On the other hand, the theorem asserts that the conditional law of  $(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$  converges to the conditional law of LBM given  $h$ , where  $m_{\varepsilon}$  is as in (1.7).
Equivalently,  $\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}$  is the annealed median exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{0,\varepsilon}$  from  $B_{1/2}$ .
Since  $\widehat{X}^{0,\varepsilon}$  converges in law as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  along  $\mathcal{E}$ , it follows that  $\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}$  converges to a constant  $\mathfrak{m}>0$  as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  along  $\mathcal{E}$ .
Let  $\widehat{P}^{\varepsilon}$  be the conditional law of  $(\eta(X^{z,\varepsilon}_{m_{\varepsilon}t}))_{t\geq 0}=(\widehat{X}^{z,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}t})_{t\geq 0}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ .
From the convergence  $\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}\rightarrow\mathfrak{m}$  along  $\mathcal{E}$ , we infer that along  $\mathcal{E}$  the joint law of  $(h,\eta,\widehat{P}^{\varepsilon})$  converges to the joint law of  $(h,\eta,\widehat{P})$ , where  $\widehat{P}$  is defined as follows.
For  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$ ,  $\widehat{P}_{z}$  is the law of the path  $t\mapsto\widehat{X}^{z}_{\mathfrak{m}t}$  where  $\widehat{X}^{z}$  is sampled from  $P_{z}$ .
Equivalently,  $\widehat{P}_{z}$  is the law of Liouville Brownian motion started from  $z$  pre-composed with the time change  $t\mapsto c\mathfrak{m}t$ .
By the definition of  $m_{\varepsilon}$ , the annealed median exit time of  $\widehat{X}^{0,\varepsilon}_{\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}t}$  from  $B_{1/2}$  is 1, hence the annealed median exit time of a path with the law  $\widehat{P}_{0}$  from  $B_{1/2}$  is 1.
This fixes the value of the constant  $c\mathfrak{m}$  independently of the choice of subsequence.
We therefore get that  $(h,\eta,\widehat{P}^{\varepsilon})$  converges in law to  $(h,\eta,P^{\operatorname{LBM}})$  as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , not just subsequentially, where here  $P^{\operatorname{LBM}}_{z}$  for  $z\in\mathbbm{C}$  is the conditional law given  $h$  of (1.6), i.e., LBM with respect to  $h$  started from  $z$  pre-composed with the time-change  $t\mapsto m_{0}t$ , where  $m_{0}$  is the median of the exit time of the  $B_{1/2}$  of this LBM.
Since  $P^{\operatorname{LBM}}$  is a.s. determined by  $h$ , it follows from an elementary fact in probability theory (analogous to the fact that convergence in distribution to a constant implies convergence in probability, see, e.g., [SS13, Lemma 4.5]) that in fact  $P^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow P^{\operatorname{LBM}}$  in probability.
The bounds (1.8) for  $m_{\varepsilon}$  follow since we have show that for every sequence of  $\varepsilon$ ’s tending to zero, there is a further subsequence along which  $\varepsilon m_{\varepsilon}$  converges to a positive number.
∎
It remains to prove Lemma 7.18.
Our argument will use the following minor generalization of Definition 2.1.
Definition 7.19.
A curve-decorated quantum surface is an equivalence class of triples  $(D,h,\eta)$  where  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$  is open,  $h$  is a distribution on  $D$ , and  $\eta$  is a curve in  $\overline{D}$ , under the equivalence relation whereby two such triples  $(D,h,\eta)$  and  $(\widetilde{D},\widetilde{h},\widetilde{\eta})$  are equivalent if there is a conformal map  $\phi:\widetilde{D}\rightarrow\widetilde{h}$  which extends to a homeomorphism  $\widetilde{D}\cup\partial\widetilde{D}\rightarrow D\cup\partial D$  (with  $\partial\widetilde{D}$  and  $\partial D$  viewed as collections of prime ends) such that  $h$  and  $\widetilde{h}$  are related as in (2.1) and  $\phi\circ\widetilde{\eta}=\eta$ .
We similarly define a curve-decorated quantum surface with more than one curve.
The idea of the proof of Lemma 7.18 is as follows.
Let  $a<u<b$  and let  $\widehat{X}$  be a random curve sampled from the law  $P_{\eta(u)}$  and stopped upon exiting  $\eta([a,b])$ . It is easily seen that the constant  $c$  is a.s. determined by the triple  $(\eta([a,b]),h|_{\eta([a,b])},\widehat{X})$ .
Indeed, since the time parametrization of LBM is locally determined by the GFF, from this data we can see how we need to scale the time parametrization of  $\widehat{X}$  in order to get LBM w.r.t.  $h$  (see Lemma 7.22).
In fact,  $c$  is a.s. determined by  $(\eta([a,b]),h|_{\eta([a,b])},\widehat{X})$  viewed as a curve-decorated quantum surface since both LBM and the adjacency graph of cells obey the LQG coordinate change formula (by [Ber15, Theorem 1.4]).
If  $a<b<\widetilde{a}<\widetilde{b}$ , then [DMS21, Theorem 1.9] tells us that the curve-decorated quantum surfaces corresponding to  $(\eta([a,b]),h|_{\eta([a,b])})$  and  $(\eta([\widetilde{a},\widetilde{b}]),h|_{\eta([\widetilde{a},\widetilde{b}])})$  are independent.
If we knew that  $P$  were in some sense locally determined by  $(h,\eta)$ , then we would be done: indeed, if we knew this then the preceding paragraph would tell us that  $c$  is a.s. determined by each of two different independent random variables, which means that  $c$  is independent from itself and hence a.s. constant.
However, we do not know that  $P$  is locally determined or even determined at all by  $(h,\eta)$ , even though  $P^{\varepsilon}$  is a.s. determined by  $(h,\eta)$ .
This is because the property of one random variable being a.s. determined by another is not in general preserved under convergence in law.
However, we know that  $P^{\varepsilon}$  is a.s. determined by  $(h,\eta)$  and moreover independence is preserved under convergence in law.
So, we can make the above argument precise by appealing to the subsequential convergence in law  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$ .
Figure 4:
Illustration of the setup used to prove Lemma 7.18.
The figure shows the case when  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$ . For  $\gamma\in(0,\sqrt{2})$ , the interior of  $\eta([a,b])$  is connected and is equal to  $U$ .
We now describe the framework in which we will prove the independence property needed to get Lemma 7.18.
See Figure 4 for an illustration.
Fix finite times  $a<u<b$ .
Let  $U$  be the connected component of the interior of  $\eta([a,b])$  which contains  $\eta(u)$  (such a component exists a.s. since a.s.  $\eta(u)\notin\partial\eta([a,b])$ ).
Due to the difference in topology for space-filling SLEκ in the phases  $\kappa\geq 8$  and  $\kappa\in(4,8)$ ,
when  $\gamma\in(0,\sqrt{2}]$  the set  $U$  is the entire interior of  $\eta([a,b])$  but for  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$  a.s.  $U$  is a proper subset of the interior of  $\eta([a,b])$ .
The domain  $U$  is homeomorphic to the unit disk and there is a unique time interval  $[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]$  for which  $\eta([a^{\prime},b^{\prime}])=\overline{U}$ .
Again, for  $\gamma\in(0,\sqrt{2}]$  we have  $[a,b]=[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]$  but this is a.s. not the case for  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$ .
Also let  $\widehat{X}$  be sampled from the law  $P_{\eta(u)}$  and let  $T$  be the first exit time of  $\widehat{X}$  from  $U$ .
We are interested in the curve(s)-decorated quantum surfaces  $(U,h,\eta|_{[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]},\widehat{X}|_{[0,T]})$ . We could just work directly with this curve-decorated quantum surface, but we find it more clear to instead specify a particular parametrization which depends only on the curve-decorated quantum surface (not on the original choice of equivalence class representative).
Let  $\phi:\mathbbm{D}\rightarrow U$  be the unique conformal map such that  $\phi(0)=\eta(u)$  and  $\phi(a^{\prime})=1$ .
Recalling (2.1), we define
$h^{\mathbbm{D}}:=h\circ\phi+Q\log|\phi^{\prime}|,\quad\eta^{\mathbbm{D}}:=\phi^{-1}\circ\eta|_{[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]},\quad\text{and}\quad\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D}}:=\phi^{-1}\circ\widehat{X}|_{[0,T]}.$
Then  $(\mathbbm{D},h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D}})=(U,h,\eta|_{[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]},\widehat{X}|_{[0,T]})$  as curve-decorated quantum surfaces.
We define
$P^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\text{$P_{\eta(u)}$-law of $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D}}$}}}\right),$
(7.34)
so  $P^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0}$  is a random probability measure on curves in  $\mathbbm{D}$  started from 0 and stopped upon hitting  $\partial\mathbbm{D}$ .
Our proof of Lemma 7.18 is based on the following three lemmas.
Lemma 7.20.
Let  $c$  be the random variable from Lemma 7.17.
In the setting described just above, a.s.  $P^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0}$  is the law of LBM with respect to  $h$  started from 0 and stopped upon hitting  $\partial\mathbbm{D}$ , pre-composed with the time change  $t\mapsto ct$ .
Proof.
This is immediate from the  $\gamma$ -LQG coordinate change formula for LBM [Ber15, Theorem 1.3] and for the adjacency graph of cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  (which follows from the coordinate change formula for the LQG area measure plus the conformal invariance of space-filling SLE).
∎
Lemma 7.21.
Let  $a<u<b$  and  $\widetilde{a}<\widetilde{u}<\widetilde{b}$  be two triples of times and assume that  $b<\widetilde{a}$ .
Define  $h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},$  and  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  as above for  $a,u,b$  and define  $\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},$  and  $\widetilde{P}^{\mathbbm{D}}_{0}$  as above with  $\widetilde{a},\widetilde{u},\widetilde{b}$  in place of  $a,u,b$ .
Then the triples  $(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}})$  and  $(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}})$  are independent.
Proof.
Fix a time  $\mathbbm{s}\in(b,\widetilde{a})$ .
By [DMS21, Theorem 1.9], the past / future curve-decorated quantum surfaces
$\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta((-\infty,\mathbbm{s}]),h|_{\eta((-\infty,\mathbbm{s}])},\eta|_{(-\infty,\mathbbm{s}]}}}\right)\quad\text{and}\quad\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\eta([\mathbbm{s},\infty)),h|_{\eta([\mathbbm{s},\infty))},\eta|_{[\mathbbm{s},\infty)}}}\right)$
(7.35)
are independent.
By definition,  $(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}})$  (resp.  $(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}})$  is determined by the first (resp. second) quantum surface in (7.35).
Hence  $(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}})$  and  $(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}})$  are independent.
We need to show that the independence continues to hold if we also include the random laws  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  and  $\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$ .
The basic idea of the proof is that for each  $\varepsilon>0$ , the discrete analogs of the laws  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  and  $\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  in the  $\varepsilon$ -mated-CRT map setting are determined by the first and second curve-decorated quantum surfaces in (7.35), respectively, so one has the desired independence statement with these discrete laws used in place of  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  and  $\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$ .
This will allow us to later use the fact that independence (unlike the condition that one random variable determines another) is preserved under taking limits in law.
Let us now define the discrete analogs of the laws  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  and  $\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}}$  which we will work with. Recalling the times  $a^{\prime},b^{\prime}\in[a,b]$  defined above, for  $\varepsilon>0$  let  $\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$  be the subgraph of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  induced by the vertex set  $[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$ .
Let  $\partial\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$  be the set of vertices  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$  which are joined by an edge of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  to a vertex which is not in  $\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$ .
By the Brownian motion definition of the mated-CRT map (1.2), for small enough  $\varepsilon>0$  both  $\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$  and  $\partial\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$  are determined by the left/right boundary length process  $(L-L_{\mathbbm{s}},R-R_{\mathbbm{s}})|_{(-\infty,\mathbbm{s}]}$ , which in turn is a.s. determined by the first curve-decorated quantum surface (7.35).
Let  $u^{\varepsilon}:=\varepsilon\lceil u/\varepsilon\rceil$ , so that  $u^{\varepsilon}\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ .
Conditional on  $(h,\eta)$ , let  $X^{\varepsilon}$  be a simple random walk on  $\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$  stopped at the first time  $J^{\varepsilon}$  that it hits  $\partial\mathcal{T}^{\varepsilon}$ .
Recalling the conformal map  $\phi:\mathbbm{D}\rightarrow U$  above, for  $t\in[0,\varepsilon J^{\varepsilon}]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$ , let  $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}_{t}:=\phi^{-1}(\eta(t/\varepsilon))$ .
We extend the definition of  $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  to all of  $[0,\varepsilon J^{\varepsilon}]$  by piecewise linear interpolation at constant speed.
Let  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  be the conditional law of  $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}_{t}$  given  $(h,\eta)$ .
By the preceding paragraph and the definition of  $\phi$ , the law  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  is a.s. determined by the first quantum surface in (7.35).
If we define  $\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  similarly but with  $\widetilde{a},\widetilde{u},\widetilde{b}$  in place of  $a,u,b$ , then  $\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  is a.s. determined by the second quantum surface in (7.35).
As a consequence, the triples  $(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon})$  and  $(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon})$  are independent.
We now argue that if  $\mathcal{E}$  is a subsequence along which  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$  in law, then we also have
$(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon},\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}})$
(7.36)
in law as  $\mathcal{E}\ni\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , which concludes the proof since indepenendence is preserved under convergence of joint laws.
To get (7.36), we note that a process  $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  sampled from  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  is almost the same as the process  $\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon})$ , where  $\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon}$  is sampled from  $P_{\eta(u^{\varepsilon})}^{\varepsilon}$  and stopped at the first time it hits a point in  $\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}\setminus[a^{\prime},b^{\prime}])$ , except for the following minor difference.
The process  $\widehat{X}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  travels along straight line segments between the times when it hits points of  $\phi^{-1}(\eta(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}))$ , whereas the path  $\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon})$  instead travels along paths whose images under  $\phi$  are straight line segments.
It is easily seen that the conformal map  $\phi$  can be extended to a homeomorphism  $\overline{U}\rightarrow\overline{\mathbbm{D}}$ : indeed, by the flow line construction of space-filling SLE [MS17, Section 1.2.3],  $\partial U$  is a finite union of SLEκ-type curves which intersect only at their endpoints.
In particular,  $\partial U$  is a Jordan curve so the desired extension of  $\phi$  follows from [Pom92, Theorem 2.6].
By the above continuity and the preceding paragraph (note that  $\phi$  does not depend on  $\varepsilon$ ), the Prokhorov distance between the law  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  and the  $P_{\eta(h^{\varepsilon})}^{\varepsilon}$ -law of  $\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon})$  tends to zero in probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ .
On the other hand, it is easily seen from the convergence  $(h,\eta,P^{\varepsilon})\rightarrow(h,\eta,P)$  in law that (7.36) holds if we replace  $P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}$  by the  $P_{\eta(u^{\varepsilon})}^{\varepsilon}$ -law of  $\phi^{-1}(\widehat{X}^{\varepsilon})$ , and we make the analogous replacement made for  $\widetilde{P}^{\mathbbm{D},\varepsilon}_{0}$ . Thus (7.36) holds.
∎
Lemma 7.22.
Let  $h$  be a random distribution on a domain  $D\subset\mathbbm{C}$  whose law is locally absolutely continuous w.r.t. the law of the GFF on  $D$ .
Let  $z\in D$  and let  $X$  be the Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t.  $h$ , stopped at the first time that it exists  $D$ .
For any  $c_{1},c_{2}>0$  with  $c_{1}\not=c_{2}$ , the laws of  $(h,(X_{c_{1}t})_{t\geq 0})$  and  $(h,(X_{c_{2}t})_{t\geq 0})$  are mutually singular.
Proof.
Let  $B$  be a standard planar Brownian motion started from  $z$  and stopped when it exits  $D$ , sampled independently from  $h$ .
By the definition of Liouville Brownian motion, there is a random  $\sigma(h,B)$ -measurable function  $\phi:[0,\infty)\rightarrow[0,\infty)$  such that  $(h,(X_{t})_{t\geq 0})\overset{d}{=}(h,B_{\phi^{-1}(t)})_{t\geq 0}$ .
We have the following trivial elementary probability fact: if  $Y$  is a random variable and  $f$  and  $g$  are measurable functions such that  $\mathbbm{P}[f(Y)\not=g(Y)]=1$ , then the laws of  $(Y,f(Y))$  and  $(Y,g(Y))$  are mutually singular.
To get the lemma, we apply this fact with  $Y=(h,B)$  and  $f$  and  $g$  given by the functionals which take  $(h,B)$  to  $B_{\phi^{-1}(c_{1}t)}$  and  $B_{\phi^{-1}(c_{2}t)}$ , respectively.
∎
Remark 7.23.
The proof of Lemma 7.22 relies crucially on the fact that we are looking at the joint law of  $h$  and the Liouville Brownian motion.
At least for some choices of  $h$ , the marginal laws of  $(X_{c_{1}t})_{t\geq 0}$  and  $(X_{c_{2}t})_{t\geq 0}$  are mutually absolutely continuous.
Indeed, if  $h$  is the restriction to  $D$  of a zero-boundary GFF on a larger domain  $D^{\prime}$  with  $\overline{D}\subset D^{\prime}$ , then the laws of  $h+\log c_{1}$  and  $h+\log c_{2}$ , hence also the laws of  $(h+\log c_{1},(X_{c_{1}t})_{t\geq 0})$  and  $(h+\log c_{2},(X_{c_{2}t})_{t\geq 0})$  are mutually absolutely continuous (see, e.g., [MS16a, Proposition 3.4]).
Proof of Lemma 7.18.
Let  $c>0$  be as in Lemma 7.17 and assume the setup of Lemma 7.21. Due to Lemma 7.20 (applied to each of the triples  $a,u,b$  and  $\widetilde{a},\widetilde{u},\widetilde{b}$ ) followed by Lemma 7.22, we know that  $c$  can a.s. be expressed as a measurable function of either of the two triples  $(h^{\mathbbm{D}},\eta^{\mathbbm{D}},P_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}})$  or  $(\widetilde{h}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{\eta}^{\mathbbm{D}},\widetilde{P}_{0}^{\mathbbm{D}})$ .
However, by Lemma 7.21 these two triples are independent from each other.
Hence  $c$  is independent from itself so  $c$  must be a.s. equal to a deterministic constant.
∎
7.4 From whole plane to disk
In this short section we explain why Theorem 1.2 (convergence to Liouville Brownian motion in the whole plane case with the LQG embedding) implies Theorem 1.4 (convergence to Liouville Brownian motion in the disk case, under the Tutte embedding). The arguments in this section are quite close to (but more detailed than) [GMS21, Section 3.3], see in particular [GMS21, Lemma 3.6].
As recalled in Section 2.2, let  $(\mathbbm{C},h,0,\infty)$  denote a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone (corresponding to a weight  $W=4-\gamma^{2}$ , in the terminology of [DMS21]), and let  $\eta$  be an independent space-filling SLEκ, with  $\kappa=16/\gamma^{2}$ , reparametrised by  $\gamma$ -quantum area, i.e.,  $\mu_{h}(\eta([s,t]))=t-s$  for any  $s<t$ . Then by [DMS21, Theorem 1.9],
the quantum surface  $\mathcal{W}$  obtained by restricting  $h$  to the interior  $D$  of  $\eta([0,\infty))$ , that is,  $\mathcal{W}=(D,h|_{D},0,\infty)$  has the distribution of a quantum wedge with weight  $W=2-\gamma^{2}/2$ . Note that this corresponds to an  $\alpha$ -quantum wedge where  $\alpha=3\gamma/2$  (see Table 1.1 in [DMS21]), where  $\alpha$  denotes the strength of the logarithmic singularity near 0 in a half-plane embedding. In particular, since  $\alpha$ -quantum wedges are thick (have the topology of a half-plane) for  $\alpha\leq Q$ , and are thin (given by a Poissonian chain of so-called “beads”) if  $\alpha\in(Q,Q+\gamma/2)$ , this means that  $\mathcal{W}$  is thick for  $\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}$  and thin if  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$ . Furthermore, given  $D$ , in the thick case  $\eta$  is simply an independent chordal space-filling SLEκ in  $D$  from 0 to  $\infty$ , reparametrised by its area, while in the thin case it is a concatenation of space-filling chordal SLEκ in each bead of  $\mathcal{W}$ .
Basically, the idea of the proof is to use the absolute continuity of the law of the quantum disk w.r.t. the law of  $\mathcal{W}$  (or a single bead of  $\mathcal{W}$  if  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$ ) away from their respective marked points.
Consider first the case  $\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}$  so that  $\mathcal{W}$  is a thick quantum wedge.
Fix a large constant  $C>1$ .
We apply a conformal map  $D\rightarrow\mathbbm{H}$  to get a new parametrization  $(\mathbbm{H},h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C},-C,\infty)$  of the quantum surface  $\mathcal{W}$ , chosen so that the two marked points are  $-C$  and  $\infty$  and the  $\nu_{h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}}$ -length of  $[-C,0]$  is 1 (this last choice of normalization is somewhat arbitrary — 1 can be replaced by any number larger than  $1/2$ ).
Let  $\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}$  be the image of  $\eta|_{[0,\infty)}$  under this conformal map, so that  $\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}$  is a chordal SLEκ from  $-C$  to  $\infty$  in  $\mathbbm{H}$  parameterized by  $\gamma$ -LQG mass w.r.t.  $h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}$ .
Recall that Liouville Brownian motion satisfies the quantum surface change of coordinates (2.1) by Theorem 1.4 in [Ber15].
From this and Theorem 1.2, we deduce the analog of Theorem 1.2 for  $(h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C},\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C})$ : if we condition on  $(h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C},\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C})$ , then the conditional law of the random walk on the adjacency graph of cells  $\eta^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}([x-\varepsilon,x])$  for  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{N}$ , stopped at the first time it hits a cell which intersects  $\partial\mathbbm{H}$ , linearly interpolated and time changed appropriately, converges as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  to the law of Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t  $h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}$  stopped upon hitting  $\partial\mathbbm{H}$ . Moreover, the convergence is uniform over the choice of starting point in any compact subset of  $\overline{\mathbbm{H}}$ .
We now use an argument of absolute continuity between the above  $\frac{3\gamma}{2}$ -quantum wedge and a singly marked quantum disk  $\mathcal{D}$  with unit area and unit boundary length.
Let us choose a parametrization  $(\mathbbm{H},h^{\mathcal{D}},\infty)$  of  $\mathcal{D}$  so that the marked point is at  $\infty$  and the  $\nu_{h}$ -lengths of  $(-\infty,0]$  and  $[0,\infty)$  are each equal to  $1/2$ .
Using the definitions of the quantum wedge and the quantum disk from [DMS21, Sections 4.2 and 4.5], it is easily verified that the law of the restriction of  $h^{\mathcal{D}}$  to any fixed ball  $B=\mathbbm{H}\cap B(0,R)$  centered at 0 with  $R<C$  say, is absolutely continuous with respect to the law of the field  $h^{\mathcal{W}}_{C}$  (here it is important that we are considering the fields away from the marked points, since they have different logarithmic singularities at their respective marked points).
Note, however, that the reverse absolute continuity statement is not true since, e.g.,  $\mu_{h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}}(B)$  can be greater than 1.
Let  $\eta^{\mathcal{D}}$  be a space-filling SLEκ loop in  $\mathbbm{D}$  based at  $\infty$ , parametrized by  $\mu_{h^{\mathcal{D}}}$ -mass.
Let  $\preceq_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}$  (resp.  $\preceq^{\mathcal{D}}$ ) be the total ordering on  $\mathbbm{Q}^{2}\cap B$  induced by  $\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}$  (resp.  $\eta^{\mathcal{D}}$ ).
By Proposition A.10, we know that  $\preceq_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}\rightarrow\preceq^{\mathcal{D}}$  in the total variation sense as  $C\rightarrow\infty$ .
Note that  $\preceq_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}$  determines each segment of  $\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}$  which is contained in  $B$  viewed modulo time parameterization, as well as the order in which  $\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}}$  traces these segments; a similar statement holds for  $\eta^{\mathcal{D}}$ .
Let  $\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\mathcal{W},\varepsilon}$  be the  $\sigma$ -algebra generated by the space-filling SLE cells  $\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$  for  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{N}$  which intersect  $B$ . Note that  $\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\mathcal{W},\varepsilon}\subset\sigma(h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}},\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}})$ .
We now combine the total variation convergence in the preceding paragraph with the absolute continuity in the paragraph before that, each applied with  $B$  replaced by a slightly larger ball  $B^{\prime}\supset B$  (which contains all of the cells which intersect  $B$  with probability tending to 1 as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ ).
We infer that there is an event  $E_{C}^{\varepsilon}$  such that  $\mathbbm{P}[E_{C}^{\varepsilon}]\rightarrow 1$  as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  and then  $C\rightarrow\infty$ , such that the following is true.
For any  $p\in(0,1)$ , there exists  $q=q(p)\in(0,1)$  such that if  $F\in\mathcal{F}_{C}^{\mathcal{W},\varepsilon}$  has probability at most  $q$  and  $\widetilde{F}$  denotes the corresponding event defined with  $(h^{\mathcal{D}},\eta^{\mathcal{D}})$  in place of  $(h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}},\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}})$ , then  $\mathbbm{P}[\widetilde{F}\cap E_{C}^{\varepsilon}]\leq p$ .
Liouville Brownian motion started from  $z\in\mathbbm{H}$  leaves the upper half plane almost surely in finite time and its law depends continuously on its starting point.
From this, we infer that for any fixed compact set  $K\subset\overline{\mathbbm{H}}$  we can choose the ball  $B$  to be sufficiently large so that the infimum over all  $z\in K$  of the probability that Liouville Brownian motion w.r.t.  $h^{\mathcal{D}}$  started from  $z$  hits  $\partial\mathbbm{H}$  before leaving  $\overline{B}$  is as close to 1 as we like.
Due to this fact and the preceding paragraph, we see that the analog of Theorem 1.2 for  $(h_{C}^{\mathcal{W}},\eta_{C}^{\mathcal{W}})$  discussed above implies the corresponding analog of Theorem 1.2 for  $(h^{\mathcal{D}},\eta^{\mathcal{D}})$ .
We now change coordinates back to  $\mathbbm{D}$ . By a slight abuse of notation we do not change our notation for fields / curves, so that now  $h^{\mathcal{D}}$  is a field on  $\mathbbm{D}$  and  $\eta^{\mathcal{D}}:[0,1]\rightarrow\overline{\mathbbm{D}}$ . From the preceding paragraph and the invariance of LBM under LQG coordinate change [Ber15, Theorem 1.4], we infer that the statement of Theorem 1.4 holds (at least in the case  $\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}$ ) but with the SLE/LQG embedding  $x\mapsto\eta^{\mathcal{D}}(x)$  instead of the Tutte embedding. As we recalled in (1.5), the Tutte embedding  $\psi_{\varepsilon}$  of the mated-CRT map associated with  $(h^{\mathcal{D}},\eta^{\mathcal{D}})$  satisfies
$\max_{x\in\mathcal{VG}^{\varepsilon}}|\psi_{\varepsilon}(x)-\eta^{\mathcal{D}}(x)|\to 0$
in distribution; see (3.3) in Section 3.4 of [GMS21]. We thus obtain Theorem 1.4.
We now discuss the thin case where  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$ . The idea is to apply a similar argument except we restrict ourselves to a given bead of  $\mathcal{W}$ . One issue with this is that it is not obvious how to describe the law of the bead containing a given point  $z$ . However, since we assume the statement of Theorem 1.2 (which holds uniformly over an arbitrary compact set  $K$  of the wedge embedded into  $\mathbbm{H}$ ), the idea is to consider the first time that some bead of  $\mathcal{W}$  has area greater than one, say. We then have a quenched invariance principle uniformly over points of the intersection of  $K$  with this bead, and by choosing  $K$  sufficiently large, we can ensure that with probability as close to one as desired, this intersection contains some given arbitrary compact set of the bead.
Moreover, since the beads of  $\mathcal{W}$  have a Poissonian structure, the first bead with area greater than one has a law which is mutually absolutely continuous w.r.t. the law of a doubly marked quantum disk conditioned to have area at least one away from their respective marked points [DMS21, Section 4.4] (for  $\gamma=\sqrt{8/3}$ , the beads are exactly quantum disks but for other values of  $\gamma$  they have different log singularities at the marked points).
The proof in the case when  $\gamma\in(\sqrt{2},2)$  then follows from the same local absolute continuity argument as in the case when  $\gamma\leq\sqrt{2}$ , except that we use this single bead instead of the whole of  $\mathcal{W}$ .
Appendix A Appendix
In this appendix we prove some basic facts about the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure.
The proofs of these facts are standard and do not use any of the other results described in the paper, so are collected here to avoid distracting from the main argument.
A.1 Basic estimates for the LQG area measure
Let  $\gamma\in(0,2)$  and let  $h$  be the circle average embedding of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone, as in Definition 2.2.
In this subsection we record some basic estimates for the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure  $\mu_{h}$  associated with  $h$ .
Lemma A.1 (LQG mass of Euclidean balls).
Fix a small parameter  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ .
With polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}/2+\zeta}\leq\mu_{h}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in B_{1-\delta}.$
(A.1)
Proof.
Let  $h^{0}$  be a whole-plane GFF with the additive constant chosen so that  $h^{0}_{1}(0)=0$ . It is shown in various places in the literature, e.g., [DG18, Lemma 3.8], that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ , one has
$\delta^{(2+\gamma)^{2}/2+\zeta}\leq\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in\mathbbm{D}.$
(A.2)
Now let  $\widetilde{h}:=h^{0}-\gamma\log|\cdot|$ .
Then  $\widetilde{h}|_{\mathbbm{D}}\overset{d}{=}h|_{\mathbbm{D}}$ . Hence it suffices to prove that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ , the bound (A.2) holds with  $\widetilde{h}$  in place of  $h$ .
The lower bound for  $\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{\delta}(z))$  in (A.2) with  $\widetilde{h}$  in place of  $h$  is immediate from (A.2) since  $(\widetilde{h}-h^{0})|_{\mathbbm{D}}$  is a non-negative function.
So, we only need to prove the upper bound.
We do this using (A.2) and a union bound over exponential scales. The argument is entirely standard but we give the details for the sake of completeness.
For  $k\in\mathbbm{N}_{0}$ , let
$\widetilde{h}_{k}:=\widetilde{h}(e^{-k}\cdot)-\widetilde{h}_{e^{-k}}(0)\quad\text{and}\quad A_{k}:=B_{e^{-k}}(0)\setminus B_{e^{-k-1}}(0).$
(A.3)
By the scale invariance of the law of  $h^{0}$  modulo additive constant,  $\widetilde{h}_{k}\overset{d}{=}\widetilde{h}$ .
The restriction of  $\widetilde{h}-h^{0}=-\gamma\log|\cdot|$  to the annulus  $A_{0}$  is bounded above by a finite  $\gamma$ -dependent constant.
We can therefore apply (A.2) with  $e^{k}\delta$  in place of  $\delta$ , followed by a union bound over all  $k\in[0,(1-\zeta)\log\delta^{-1}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$ , to get that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\mu_{\widetilde{h}_{k}}(B_{e^{k}\delta}(z))\leq(e^{k}\delta)^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in A_{0},\quad\forall k\in[0,(1-\zeta)\log\delta^{-1}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}.$
(A.4)
By the coordinate change formula for the LQG area measure [DS11, Proposition 2.1] and the definition of  $\widetilde{h}_{k}$ , a.s.
$\mu_{\widetilde{h}}(B_{\delta}(z))=e^{\gamma\widetilde{h}_{e^{-k}}(0)}e^{-\gamma Qk}\mu_{\widetilde{h}_{k}}(B_{e^{k}\delta}(e^{k}z))=e^{\gamma h^{0}_{e^{-k}}(0)}e^{-\gamma(Q-\gamma)k}\mu_{\widetilde{h}_{k}}(B_{e^{k}\delta}(e^{k}z)),\quad\forall\delta>0,\quad\forall k\in\mathbbm{N}.$
Therefore, (A.4) (note that  $z\in A_{k}$  if and only if  $e^{k}z\in A_{0}$ ) implies that
$\mu_{\widetilde{h}}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq e^{\gamma h^{0}_{e^{-k}}(0)+[(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta-\gamma(Q-\gamma)]k}\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta},\quad\forall z\in A_{k},\quad\forall k\in[0,(1-\zeta)\log\delta^{-1}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}.$
(A.5)
Since  $\gamma\in(0,2)$  we have  $(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\gamma(Q-\gamma)=\gamma(2-\gamma)<0$ , so the exponential term in (A.5) is at most  $e^{\gamma h^{0}_{e^{-k}}(0)}$  for a small enough choice of  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ .
Furthermore, since  $t\mapsto h^{0}_{e^{-t}}(0)$  is a standard linear Brownian motion it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$
that for any fixed  $\zeta>0$ ,  $h^{0}_{e^{-k}}(0)\leq(\zeta/\gamma)\log\delta^{-1}$  for each  $k\in[0,(1-\zeta)\log\delta^{-1}]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$ .
From this and (A.5), we get that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ ,
$\mu_{\widetilde{h}}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-2\zeta},\quad\forall z\in\mathbbm{D}\setminus B_{\delta^{1-\zeta}}(0).$
(A.6)
It is easily seen from a scaling argument that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ , one has  $\mu_{h}(B_{\delta^{1-\zeta}}(0))\leq\delta^{(1-\zeta)\gamma(Q-\gamma)-\zeta}$ , which is smaller than  $\delta^{(2-\gamma)^{2}/2-\zeta}$  for a small enough choice of  $\zeta\in(0,1)$ .
By combining this with (A.6), we get the upper bound in (A.2) with  $\widetilde{h}$  in place of  $h^{0}$  and with  $2\zeta$  in place of  $\zeta$ .
This is sufficient since  $\zeta\in(0,1)$  is arbitrary.
∎
Lemma A.2.
Fix  $c\in(0,1)$ .
For each  $\zeta>0$ , it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$  that
$\sup_{z\in B_{1-\delta}}\sup_{w\in B_{\delta}(z)}\frac{\mu_{h}(B_{\delta}(z))}{\mu_{h}(B_{c\delta}(w))}\leq\delta^{-\gamma^{2}/2-\zeta}.$
(A.7)
See also [BGRV16, Theorem A.1] for a related (and in some ways more precise) statement.
Proof of Lemma A.2.
We first prove the lemma with  $h$  replaced by a whole-plane GFF  $h^{0}$  with the additive constant chosen so that  $h^{0}_{1}(0)=0$  and with  $B_{1-\delta}$  replaced by  $\mathbbm{D}$ .
For each  $w\in\mathbbm{D}$ , the random variable  $\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{c}(w))$  has negative moments of all orders which are bounded above by constants which depend on  $c$ , but not on  $w$  [RV14a, Theorem 2.12]. A union bound therefore shows that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\inf_{z\in\mathbbm{D}}\mu_{h}(B_{c}(w))\leq\delta^{\zeta/2}}}\right]=O_{\delta}(\delta^{p}),\quad\forall p>0.$
(A.8)
Since  $\mu_{h^{0}}(\mathbbm{D})$  has positive moments up to order  $4/\gamma^{2}$  [RV14a, Theorem 2.11],
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mu_{h^{0}}(\mathbbm{D})>\delta^{-\gamma^{2}/2-\zeta/2}}}\right]\leq\delta^{2+2\zeta/\gamma^{2}+o_{\delta}(1)}.$
(A.9)
Therefore,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sup_{w\in\mathbbm{D}}\frac{\mu_{h^{0}}(\mathbbm{D})}{\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{c}(w))}>\delta^{-\gamma^{2}/2-\zeta}}}\right]\leq\delta^{2+2\zeta/\gamma^{2}+o_{\delta}(1)}.$
(A.10)
Due to the translation and scale invariance of the law of  $h^{0}$ , modulo additive constant, the law of  $\sup_{w\in B_{\delta}(z)}\frac{\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{\delta}(z))}{\mu_{h^{0}}(B_{c\delta}(w))}$  does not depend on  $z$  or  $\delta$ . We may therefore apply (A.10) and take a union bound over  $O_{\delta}(\delta^{-2})$  points in  $\mathbbm{D}$  to obtain that with polynomially high probability as  $\delta\rightarrow 0$ , the bound (A.7) with  $h^{0}$  in place of  $h$  and  $\mathbbm{D}$  in place of  $B_{1-\delta}$ .
The lemma statement statement for  $h$  follows from the preceding estimate for  $h^{0}$  via a multiscale argument as in the proof of Lemma A.1.
∎
Lemma A.3.
Fix  $\rho\in(0,1)$ .
There are constants  $c_{0},c_{1}>0$  depending only on  $\rho$  and  $\gamma$  such that for each  $A>1$ , it holds with probability at least  $1-c_{0}e^{-c_{1}A}$  that
$\sup_{z\in S}\int_{S}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)\,d\mu_{h}(w)\leq A\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mu_{h}(S)+e^{-c_{1}A}}}\right),\quad\text{$\forall$ Borel sets $S\subset B_{\rho}$}.$
(A.11)
Proof.
For a Borel set  $S\subset B_{\rho}$ ,
$\int_{S}\log\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\frac{1}{|z-w|}}}\right)\,d\mu_{h}(w)\leq\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}k\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{e^{-k+1}}(z)\setminus B_{e^{-k}}(z)}}\right)\cap S}}\right).$
(A.12)
By Lemma A.1 and a union bound over dyadic values of the radius  $\delta$ , we can find constants  $c_{0},c_{1}>0$  depending only on  $\rho$  and  $\gamma$  such that with probability at least  $1-c_{0}e^{-c_{1}A}$ ,
$\sup_{z\in B_{\rho}}\mu_{h}(B_{\delta}(z))\leq\delta^{c_{1}},\quad\forall\delta\in(0,e^{-A}].$
(A.13)
If (A.13) holds, then simultaneously for each  $S\subset B_{\rho}$  and each  $z\in S$ , the right side of (A.12) is bounded above by a constant (depending only on  $\rho,\gamma$ ) times
$A\mu_{h}(S)+\sum_{k=\lfloor A\rfloor}^{\infty}ke^{-c_{1}k}\preceq A\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\mu_{h}(S)+e^{-c_{1}A}}}\right),$
(A.14)
where here the implicit constant in  $\preceq$  depends only on  $\rho,\gamma$ .
Plugging this into (A.12) gives (A.11).
∎
A.2 Comparing sums over cells to integrals against LQG measure
Assume that we are in the setting of Section 2.3, so that  $h$  is the circle average embedding of a  $\gamma$ -quantum cone,  $\eta$  is a space-filling SLE ${}_{16/\gamma^{2}}$  sampled independently from  $h$  and then parametrized by  $\mu_{h}$ -mass,  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  is the associated  $\varepsilon$ -mated CRT map, and  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}:=\eta([x-\varepsilon,x])$ .
We also recall the constant  $\rho\in(0,1)$ .
In this subsection we will give a quantitative version of the intuitively obvious statement that the counting measure on cells of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  approximates the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure when  $\varepsilon$  is small.
Lemma A.4.
There exists  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0$  and  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the following is true. Let  $D\subset B_{\rho}$  be a Borel set and let  $f:B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)\rightarrow[0,\infty)$  be a non-negative function which is  $\varepsilon^{-\beta}$ -Lipschitz continuous and satisfies  $\|f\|_{\infty}\leq\varepsilon^{-\beta}$ .
For  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$ , let  $w_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  be an arbitrary point of  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\cap\overline{D}$  (e.g., we could take  $w_{x}^{\varepsilon}=\eta(x)$  or take  $w_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  to be the point where  $f$  attains its maximum or minimum value on  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$ ).
If we let  $\mu_{h}$  be the  $\gamma$ -LQG area measure induced by  $h$ , then
$\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{D}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)-\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}\leq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}$
(A.15)
simultaneously for every choice of  $D$  and  $f$  as above.
Proof.
Fix  $q\in\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(0,\tfrac{2}{(2+\gamma)^{2}}}}\right)$  chosen in a manner depending only on  $\gamma$  and let  $\beta\in(0,q/2)$ .
By Lemma 2.4, it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\operatorname{diam}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}}\right)\leq\varepsilon^{q},\quad\forall x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(B_{\rho}).$
(A.16)
By a standard tail estimate for the  $\gamma$ -LQG measure (e.g., [GHS19a, Lemma A.3] together with the Chebyshev inequality), it holds with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$  that
$\mu_{h}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(B_{\rho+\varepsilon^{q}}}}\right)\leq\varepsilon^{-q/2}.$
(A.17)
Henceforth assume that (A.16) and (A.17) hold.
Let  $\beta\in(0,q/2)$ . We will show that (A.15) holds simultaneously for any choice of  $D$  and  $f$  as in the lemma statement.
Since  $f$  is  $\varepsilon^{-\beta}$ -Lipschitz continuous and  $\mu_{h}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon$  for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ , the bound (A.16) implies that for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$ ,
$\displaystyle f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})=\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\,d\mu_{h}(z)$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-\beta}\operatorname{diam}(H_{x}^{\varepsilon})$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{q-\beta}\quad\text{by~\eqref{eqn-cell-sum-diam}}.$
(A.18)
Similarly, we also have
$f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\geq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)-\varepsilon^{q-\beta}.$
(A.19)
By (A.16), for each  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  we have  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}\subset B_{\varepsilon^{q}}(D)$  and the intersection of any two of these cells has zero  $\mu_{h}$ -mass.
We can therefore sum (A.18) over all  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  to get
$\displaystyle\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}f(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{q}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{q-\beta}\#\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$
$\displaystyle\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{q}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-1+q/2-\beta},$
(A.20)
where in the last line we used (A.17) and the fact that each cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  is contained in  $B_{\rho}$  and has  $\mu_{h}$ -mass  $\varepsilon$ .
This gives the upper bound in (A.15) with  $\alpha=\min\{q,q/2-\beta\}$ .
Since  $D$  is contained in the union of the cells  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$ , we can similarly obtain the lower bound in (A.20) by summing (A.19) of all  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$ .
∎
We will also need a variant of Lemma A.4 where we weight each cell by its degree, whose proof is somewhat more involved.
The extra factor of 6 in this case comes from the fact that  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  is a planar triangulation, so it has average degree 6 (see e.g. e.g. [AHNR16] where the same factor 6 occurs for similar reasons).
Lemma A.5.
There exists  $\alpha=\alpha(\gamma)>0$  and  $\beta=\beta(\gamma)>0$  such that with polynomially high probability as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , the following is true.
Let  $D\subset B_{\rho}$ ,  $f:B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)\rightarrow\mathbbm{R}$ , and  $w_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for  $x\in\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)$  be as in Lemma A.4.
Then
$6\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{D\setminus B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(\partial D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)-\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha}\leq\sum_{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}(D)}f^{\varepsilon}(w_{x}^{\varepsilon})\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\leq 6\varepsilon^{-1}\int_{B_{\varepsilon^{\alpha}}(D)}f(z)\,d\mu_{h}(z)+\varepsilon^{-1+\alpha},$
(A.21)
simultaneously for every choice of  $D$  and  $f$  as above.
We note that Lemma A.5 implies the following corollary.
Corollary A.6.
For  $\varepsilon>0$ , let  $\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}$  be the measure whose restriction to each cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  for  $x\in\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  is equal to  $\operatorname{deg}^{\varepsilon}(x)\mu_{h}|_{H_{x}^{\varepsilon}}$ .
Then as  $\varepsilon\rightarrow 0$ , we have  $\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}\rightarrow 6\mu_{h}$  in probability w.r.t. the vague topology.
Proof.
It is immediate from Lemma A.5 that  $\mu_{h}^{\varepsilon}|_{B_{\rho}}\rightarrow 6\mu_{h}|_{B_{\rho}}$  weakly.
The corollary follows from this and the scale invariance property of the  $\gamma$ -quantum cone (Lemma 2.3).
∎
The idea of the proof of Lemma A.5 is as follows.
Recall that a triangulation with boundary is a planar map  $\mathcal{T}$  whose faces all have three edges, except for one special face called the external face.
The perimeter  $\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T})$  is the degree of the external face.
Due to the Euler characteristic formula, if  $\mathcal{T}$  is a triangulation with boundary whose perimeter is much smaller than its total number of vertices  $\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})$ , then  $\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})$  is close to  $3\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})$  (Lemma A.7), which implies that the sum of the degrees of the vertices of  $\mathcal{T}$  is close to  $6\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})$ .
Now assume for simplicity that  $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$  is an integer.
We consider for each  $y\in\varepsilon^{1/2}\mathbbm{Z}$  the subgraph  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon}$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  induced by the set of vertices  $x\in(y-\varepsilon^{1/2},y]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$ . Equivalently, this is the subgraph of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  induces by the vertices of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  whose corresponding cells are contained in the cell  $H_{y}^{\varepsilon^{1/2}}$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon^{1/2}}$ ).
Then  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon}$  is a triangulation with boundary, having  $\varepsilon^{-1/2}$  vertices in total (not just on its boundary).
Furthermore, a basic Brownian motion estimates shows that the perimeter of  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon}$  is extremely unlikely to be much larger than  $\varepsilon^{-1/4}$  (Lemma A.8).
Consequently, the sum of the degrees of the vetices of  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon}$  is typically of order  $6\varepsilon^{-1/2}$ .
Combining this with Lemma A.4, applied with  $\varepsilon^{1/2}$  in place of  $\varepsilon$ , then leads to Lemma A.5.
Lemma A.7.
Let  $\mathcal{T}$  be a triangulation with boundary, so that the degree of each face of  $\mathcal{T}$  except for the external face is equal to 3.
Let  $\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T})$  be the degree of the external face.
Then
$\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=3\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})+3-\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}).$
(A.22)
Proof.
Let  $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})$  be the set of faces of  $\mathcal{T}$ , including the external face.
By the Euler characteristic formula,
$\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})+\#\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})-2.$
(A.23)
Each edge of  $\mathcal{T}$  either lies on the boundary of exactly two faces in  $\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})$  or lies on the boundary of a single face but has multiplicity 2 there.
Therefore,
$\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{f\in\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})}\operatorname{deg}(f)=\frac{3}{2}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(\#\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})-1}}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}).$
(A.24)
Re-arranging (A.24) shows that
$\#\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{T})=\frac{2}{3}\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})+1-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}).$
(A.25)
Plugging this into (A.23) gives
$\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})=\#\mathcal{V}(\mathcal{T})+\frac{2}{3}\#\mathcal{E}(\mathcal{T})+1-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{Perim}(\mathcal{T}),$
(A.26)
which gives (A.22) upon re-arranging.
∎
We now define the triangulations with boundary to which we will apply Lemma A.7.
For  $\varepsilon>0$ ,  $n\in\mathbbm{N}$ , and  $y\in n\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ , we let  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$  be the subgraph of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  induced by  $(y-n\varepsilon,y]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$ .
Then  $x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$  if and only if the cell  $H_{x}^{\varepsilon}$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  is contained in the cell  $H_{y}^{n\varepsilon}$  of  $\mathcal{G}^{n\varepsilon}$ .
We also define
$\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}:=\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}:\text{$x\sim x^{\prime}$ in $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$ for some $x^{\prime}\notin\mathcal{V}\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$}}}\right\}.$
(A.27)
Then  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$  is a planar triangulation with boundary.
Lemma A.8.
There are universal constants  $c_{1},c_{2}>0$  such that the following is true.
Let  $\varepsilon>0$ , let  $n\in\mathbbm{N}$ , and define  $\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$  for  $y\in n\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$  as in (A.27).
Then
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\#\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}>m}}\right]\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}},\quad\forall m\in\mathbbm{N}.$
(A.28)
We will prove Lemma A.8 using the Brownian motion representation of the mated-CRT map.
For this purpose we need the following lemma.
Lemma A.9.
Let  $\mathcal{B}$  be a standard linear Brownian motion.
For  $n\in\mathbbm{N}$ , let  $\mathcal{K}_{n}$  be the number of intervals  $[k-1,k]$  for  $k\in[1,n]_{\mathbbm{Z}}$  which contain a running minimum of  $\mathcal{B}$  (relative to time 0).
Then for  $m\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\mathcal{K}_{n}>m}}\right]\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}}$
(A.29)
for constants  $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ .
Proof.
Let  $\tau_{0}=0$  and inductively let  $\tau_{m}$  for  $m\in\mathbbm{N}$  be the first time after  $\tau_{m-1}+1$  at which  $\mathcal{B}$  attains a running minimum.
We observe that
$\mathcal{K}_{n}\leq 2\max\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{m\in\mathbbm{N}:\tau_{m}<n}}\right\}.$
(A.30)
By the strong Markov property, the increments  $\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1}$  are i.i.d.
By a standard Brownian motion estimate,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{m}-\tau_{m-1}>t}}\right]\asymp t^{-1/2},\quad\forall t>1.$
(A.31)
Therefore, for  $m,n\in\mathbbm{N}$ ,
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\tau_{m}<n}}\right]\leq\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\sup_{j\in[1,m]_{\mathbbm{Z}}}(\tau_{j}-\tau_{j-1})<n}}\right]\leq\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left(1-c_{0}n^{-1/2}}}\right)^{m}\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}},$
(A.32)
for universal constants  $c_{0},c_{1},c_{2}$ . Combining this with (A.30) gives (A.29) (with  $c_{2}/2$  in place of  $c_{2}$ ).
∎
Proof of Lemma A.8.
Recall the Brownian motion  $(L,R)$  used to define  $\mathcal{G}^{\varepsilon}$  in (1.2).
From (1.2), we get that  $\partial\mathcal{T}_{y}^{n,\varepsilon}$  is the same as the set of  $x\in(y-n\varepsilon,y]\cap(\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z})$  such that either
$\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}=\inf_{t\in[y-n\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}\quad\text{or}\quad\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,x]}L_{t}=\inf_{t\in[x-\varepsilon,y]}L_{t}$
(A.33)
or the same is true with  $R$  in place of  $L$ .
By Brownian scaling and the translation invariance of the law of  $(L,R)$ , it suffices to prove (A.28) in the case when  $\varepsilon=1$  and  $y=n\varepsilon$ .
By (A.33) and the symmetry of the law of  $(L,R)$  under reversing time and/or swapping  $L$  and  $R$ , it suffices to prove that
$\mathbbm{P}\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left[\#\mathopen{}\mathclose{{\left\{x\in[1,n]_{\mathbbm{Z}}:\inf_{t\in[x-1,x]}L_{t}=\inf_{t\in[0,x]}L_{t}}}\right\}>m}}\right]\leq c_{1}e^{-c_{2}m/n^{1/2}}$
(A.34)
for universal constants  $c_{1},c_{2}>0$ . This is precisely the content of Lemma A.9.
∎
Proof of Lemma A.5.
Step 1: regularity event.
Let  $n_{\varepsilon}:=\lfloor\varepsilon^{-1/2}\rfloor$ , so that  $n_{\varepsilon}\in\mathbbm{N}$  and  $n_{\varepsilon}\varepsilon\approx\varepsilon^{1/2}$ .
For  $y\in n_{\varepsilon}\varepsilon\mathbbm{Z}$ , we define the triangulation with boundary  $\mathcal{T}_{y}^{\varepsilon}:=\mathcal{T}^{n_{\varepsilon},\varepsilon}$  as in the discussion above Lemma A.8.
